Could Tupac verdict inspire new efforts to find killer of his rival the Notorious B. I. G.?

BBC News Tue, 01 Sep 2026 19:25:20 GMT

The conviction of Duane "Keffe D" Davis in Las Vegas has brought an end to one of the world's most famous unsolved murder cases.

He was found guilty of the murder of rapper Tupac Shakur, who died when the black BMW he was travelling in was sprayed with bullets in a drive-by shooting in 1996.

"This is huge. It was a tough case. It's a cold case," former prosecutor Neama Rahmani told the BBC. "We're talking about the greatest rapper of all time, an icon, and not a single arrest or prosecution for 30 years."

The conviction gives closure to Shakur's family, and has prompted questions from observers as to what it could mean for an almost identical case - the unsolved murder of Notorious B. I. G. or Biggie Smalls, also known by his legal name of Christopher Wallace.

Wallace, a New Yorker, was once one of Shakur's friends, but the two became rivals and embodied the East Coast-West Coast feud that dominated 1990s hip-hop. Wallace was killed in Los Angeles a few months after Shakur and in similar circumstances - a drive-by shooting. No one has ever been charged.

"Tupac's murder and Biggie's murder are two of the great cultural touchstones of our lives," said Justin Tinsley, a journalist for ESPN's Andscape and the author of "It Was All a Dream: Biggie and the World That Made Him."

"Those two men, they were so unique, talented, and impactful, separately," Tinsley told the BBC. "But it's impossible to tell each of their stories without telling the other's."

"When you talk about these cases, they're always going to be connected because there are so many mutual figures involved with them, and ancillary figures," he said.

Theorists have long believed the two murders were linked. Wallace's name came up during Duane Davis' trial. He and Davis were at the same party the night Wallace was killed, and police interviewed Davis about it.

The investigator who conducted that interview even testified at the Tupac murder trial.

The breakthrough in finally solving the Shakur case largely came down to one thing: Davis' own words.

Through documentaries with the media, his own memoir, podcasts and even a secret police interview, he acknowledged his role in Shakur's death.

Davis said he tossed a firearm in the backseat and his nephew, Orlando Anderson, used the gun to fatally shoot Shakur as they pulled up alongside his vehicle in Las Vegas on 7 September, 1996.

Anderson was shot dead in 1998, having denied killing Shakur.

During the trial, there were no eye-witnesses to place Davis as being in the car, no murder weapon presented, no video or photo evidence. His defence team went as far as to argue there wasn't even proof that he was in Las Vegas that night.

Rahmani said it was a difficult case to prosecute. He noted the rumours and speculation surrounding Davis were nothing new and had been around for decades - but the decision to charge him and go to trial was an "uphill climb" - a gutsy move - for prosecutors.

"Look, when you're a prosecutor, you're expected to win every time. They made a difficult decision to charge a case that a lot of people thought might be a loser," he explained. "And they got justice, where other people didn't even bother trying."

Davis' attorney Michael Sanft asked the jury to consider "what facts do you have?" He urged the panel, before they decided their guilty verdict, to discredit his client as a liar who told tales to sell books and make money.

"There's no proof," he argued to the jury.

The moment the guilty verdict was read in court, there was an outpouring of emotion among Shakur's family. Some cried and wiped tears with tissues. Others hugged and held hands. A family member embraced one of the prosecutors in the case.

At a press conference on Tuesday, Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson thanked the judge, prosecutors and Shakur's family members, who he said were very relieved and "finally have justice."

"Their loved one was murdered," he said. "They waited 30 years for a trial. It's very understandable that they were relieved."

Trial lawyer attorney Shaun Kent said the case really evolved with each interview and moment that Davis decided to talk about the case.

"There are no other witnesses, besides him," Kent told the BBC before the trial, noting that the "strongest witness against him, is him".

Rahmani believed Davis likely would have never faced charges if he had stayed silent.

"He really couldn't stop himself," Rahmani added. "Even when he was arrested and in custody, he was giving interviews."

Much of the Shakur trial forced the jury to place themselves back in the 1990s, at a time of intense gang violence that had infiltrated roots into hip-hop music and rivalries between East-Coast and West-Coast rappers.

It was a time of deep-rooted mistrust in policing and a street code that forbade reporting to authorities.

Even Shakur, after being hit multiple times in the drive-by shooting that would later kill him, refused to talk to authorities. "We'll take care of it," he said in an ambulance as an officer tried to question him.

The silence was echoed months later in the shooting death of Biggie Smalls.

Biggie, one of the biggest East Coast rappers, was leaving an after-party in Los Angeles for the Soul Train Music Awards, when a black Chevrolet pulled up to his vehicle at a red light and opened fire on 9 March, 1997. It was almost exactly six months after the shooting that killed Shakur, one of the biggest West Coast rappers.

Both were Grammy-nominated artists at the top of their genre, making millions and receiving constant radio play. Their fued spilled over into their lyrics, and also led to threats and physical violence.

Violence erupted on the streets of Los Angeles following both shootings, as street gangs sought to hold one another accountable for the rappers' deaths.

For years, neither murder led to arrests or convictions, just rumours and conspiracies.

"People will search for closure in any way they can get it," Tinsley said. "People are trying to make sense of it for 30 years."

Like Shakur's death, countless theories and names have surrounded the death of Biggie in Los Angeles, but the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) have not made any arrests.

"It's really a stain on the LAPD. The fact that this could happen and not a single arrest was made and no one was prosecuted," Rahmani said, noting Biggie's killing happened on a public street in the middle of the second most populous US city.

"Prosecutors don't like to lose," Rahmani explained. "But, maybe this [Tupac's conviction] will embolden folks in Los Angeles to maybe take another look at it, a cold case that's coming up on 30 years."

Asked about the cases and whether the Tupac murder conviction could revive Biggie's death, the LAPD told the BBC that it was aware of the conviction and the investigation into Biggie's case remained active.

"The murder of Christopher Wallace remains an open, unsolved case within LAPD's Robbery-Homicide Division," Lt Elpidio Orozco said, urging anyone with any tips to call authorities.

Though Wallace's case has gone cold, the public's interest has not.

"They've been gone longer than they've been alive," Tinsley said, "But the enduring mythology around these guys and their deaths will always be a topic of conversation."

Kayla Epstein contributed to this report.

Five takeaways from Burnham's Commons debut as PM

BBC News Tue, 01 Sep 2026 18:17:41 GMT

Andy Burnham has taken questions from MPs in the House of Commons for the first time since taking over as prime minister.

The statement on his future plans for power comes six weeks after he took over from Sir Keir Starmer in July, just before Parliament's summer recess.

Here are the main points from what he said.

Burnham told MPs his time as mayor of Greater Manchester had given him a "clear theory of growth" that further devolution of power away from Westminster would help boost the UK's economic prospects.

But he said he wanted to avoid a "two-tier England" - where areas that have already been given greater powers pull away from those that have not.

He announced that work was under way with Cornwall council and its six MPs on a devolution deal, "with or without" an elected mayor, to help the rural economy.

Burnham's move to grant the county greater powers, without requiring it to team up with councils in neighbouring areas, could open the door to more devolution for other single counties.

Burnham also said he would meet leaders in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to explore more local powers there.

The statement was the first chance for Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch to grill Burnham on defence spending following headlines on the issue over the summer.

Chancellor John Healey was appointed by Burnham after quitting as defence secretary under Sir Keir Starmer, calling for the UK to spend 3% of gross domestic product (GDP) on defence by 2030.

However, since entering the Treasury, Healey is yet to attach a date to this spending target, and has faced pressure to do so in recent days.

Healey has said a target date for increasing spending to 3% of GDP will be set out at the next government spending review, expected in spring next year.

But in a potential signal of his intentions in this area, Burham said the arguments Healey had made about defence spending in his former role were a key reason why he had put him in charge of the Treasury.

Burnham confirmed he would attend the COP31 climate summit in November, as he vowed to "meet the climate challenge".

The annual UN climate change conference will take place in Antalya, Turkey, allowing Burnham to come face to face with many world leaders and senior officials.

While Sir Keir attended COP summits when he was prime minister, Rishi Sunak was criticised in 2022 for not going because he had "other pressing domestic commitments".

Burnham's pledge to attend the summit comes as he faces a looming decision about whether to allow drilling to start in the Rosebank oilfield and Jackdaw gasfield, in the North Sea, which have been in legal limbo for a year.

Labour's 2024 election manifesto promised to "finally bring the feudal leasehold system to an end", after campaigners said it was unfair that flat owners had little control over spiralling property costs.

A draft Leasehold and Commonhold Reform Bill published by Starmer's government earlier this year included plans to cap ground rent at £250, ban the sale of new leasehold flats and give homeowners greater control over how their buildings are managed.

Under the bill, leasehold would be banned "except in limited cases", and developers would no longer be allowed to sell new flats as leasehold.

That bill is yet to be introduced to Parliament, but Burnham confirmed he intended to "bring forward" a Commonhold and Leasehold Bill during the current session of Parliament, which began in May and would normally last around a year.

Burnham kicked off his Commons statement by paying tribute to his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, who had announced he was resigning as MP for Holborn and St Pancras just hours earlier.

Sir Keir had given the UK "a lifetime of service", Burnham said, including delivering the Hillsborough Law which demands more accountability from public officials during official inquiries, as well as work to achieve peace in Ukraine.

He also praised Sir Keir for leading Labour to one of its "best victories" in the 2024 election.

He said Sir Keir had "created a platform to change this country for the better" which the new government would "use well".

Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP

BBC News Tue, 01 Sep 2026 17:04:29 GMT

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has announced he is to stand down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.

The move will trigger a by-election in the London seat of Holborn and St Pancras, long a Labour stronghold, which he has represented since 2015.

Sir Keir, who left Downing Street in July, had previously said he would stay on as an MP until the next UK general election, which is not due until 2029.

But in a surprise statement hours before his successor Andy Burnham made his debut in the House of Commons, he said he was resigning to work on issues such as international affairs and violence against women and girls.

Paying tribute to his predecessor, Burnham highlighted Sir Keir's work with Ukraine and the Hillsborough Law drawn up under his government to improve the accountability of public officials, which is going through Parliament.

"He has given this country a lifetime of public service, particularly for those fighting for justice," he added.

"His leadership took our party from one of its worst defeats to its best victories and created a platform to change this country for the better. We will use it well, and we wish his family the very best for the future."

Announcing his resignation, Sir Keir told the Camden New Journal it had been a "huge honour and privilege" to represent the London constituency for 11 years, ending weeks of speculation about whether he would remain an MP.

He added he was ready to "pass the baton to a successor", telling the newspaper it was the "right time" for him to leave Parliament.

He said: "I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.

"I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, to work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely.

"It's work I started before I became an MP and it's work I'm keen to continue after I'm an MP. So international affairs on the one hand, and continuing my work on violence against women and girls on the other."

Sir Keir became prime minister after winning a landslide majority at the 2024 election, but quit No 10 after pressure from Labour MPs to stand aside.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch wished Sir Keir the best for the future adding: "I can understand why he would not want to spend time with the Labour MPs who treated him so badly after he won them their seats."

Tory Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake accused Sir Keir of making "another U-turn having pledged to stay on", prompting a "costly by-election for taxpayers".

A date will not be set for the by-election until Sir Keir formally resigns his Commons seat.

This will only be confirmed once the government has given him a crown appointment, the mechanism that disqualifies him from being an MP.

Labour expects to select a candidate for the by-election by 9 September, according to the party's website.

Holborn and St Pancras has long been a Labour stronghold, with Sir Keir securing a more than 11,000-vote majority at the last general election in 2024.

Labour's main challenger in the seat is likely to be the Greens, who came second by vote totals at this year's local elections in wards that make up the constituency - with 29.8% of the vote to Labour's 39.5%.

Reform UK came a distant third by these vote totals, and the Greens' share was higher if they are given the votes in two wards where they stood aside.

Candidates for the by-election will not be confirmed until a later stage, but the Greens hinted that leader Zack Polanski was considering a run at the seat.

A spokesperson for the party said Polanksi, currently a member of the London Assembly, had "always made it clear he would like to be a London MP".

While it is unclear exactly what type of international affairs role Sir Keir may take up, global issues and diplomacy dominated his time as PM.

In his departure interview in July, Sir Keir was asked if he had another big political or international job in him, to which he replied: "I don't know is the honest answer to that."

By standing down so soon after quitting as PM, Sir Keir has departed from recent precedent for those in Downing Street before him.

Rishi Sunak is still the Tory MP for Richmond and Northallerton two years after leaving No 10, and his precedessor Liz Truss stayed on as a backbencher until she lost her seat to Labour at the 2024 election.

Theresa May stayed on as MP for five years after leaving Downing Street.

However, both Boris Johnson and David Cameron quit the Commons shortly afterwards.

UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget

BBC News Tue, 01 Sep 2026 16:36:42 GMT

Long-term government borrowing costs have risen to a 28-year high, putting further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ahead of his first Budget next month.

The yield on a 30-year gilt — a loan to the British government — rose to 5.89% on Tuesday, the highest since 1998.

Borrowing costs in the US, Japan and Europe have hit similar highs in recent days, reflecting investors' concerns about inflation, state borrowing levels and spending levels by large tech companies on AI.

Burnham told the House of Commons his government's "bedrock", as it seeks to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, will be "fiscal responsibility".

All of those factors will make the Budget process trickier for Burnham, who on Tuesday addressed MPs for the first time as prime minister, and his Chancellor John Healey.

Burnham told the House of Commons the economy and the cost of living were "the biggest issues facing the country".

Higher borrowing costs will reduce the amount of headroom the government has against its self-imposed fiscal rules, limiting the amount Healey can spend on consumer-friendly measures to ease the cost of living.

Despite the squeezed public finances, Burnham said said he would bring about "more substantial change" to ease living costs.

"Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Burnham of "living in the past".

"His diagnosis is completely wrong," she told the House of Commons. "His theory of growth is completely wrong. He thinks that if Government spends more money, we will all get richer.

"That is not how this works."

The chancellor has previously said he will stick to a set of fiscal rules imposed by his predecessor Rachel Reeves that restrict borrowing. These rules are designed to help markets have clarity about the path of borrowing.

The more that is forecast to be spent on interest payments, the more likely that there will be a squeeze on spending or some form of tax rise to meet these rules.

On top of that, higher government rates can feed through to higher business and household borrowing costs, and so weigh on the economy.

Burnham was already facing a tough balancing act with taxing and spending, due to pressures on defence and the cost of living.

As well as the rise to 30-year gilt yields, the yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt rose to 5.22% on Tuesday. This is its highest rate since June 2008, at the height of the global financial crisis.

Gilt yields move counter to the value of the bonds, meaning their prices fall when yields rise.

Around the world there are warning lights flashing from the markets for government debt.

Global markets reacted in particular after suggestions in the US that its central bank could raise rates. Japan is also facing pressure to raise rates.

The Chancellor is in the USA attending a meeting of global finance ministers and central bankers. He told the G20 that the UK had the fastest growth in the G7 in 2026 so far, that productivity was improving and that the UK was cutting its borrowing at the fastest rate of the major economies.

US borrowing costs hit a fresh high on Tuesday as renewed strikes in the Middle East pushed up oil prices and heightened concerns over inflation.

Karen Ward, JP Morgan's chief market strategist for Europe, said governments around the world want to increase spending and are turning to borrowing to fund it.

And she told the BBC's World at One they are increasingly having to compete with major technology companies raising money to invest in the AI revolution, pushing up the amount of interest being charged.

"Markets are getting a lot more choice about who they are going to lend to and at what interest rates," she added.

Burnham has rolled out a series of interventions to support consumers and businesses since entering Downing Street, and is expected to prioritise further measures to ease the cost of living in the Budget on 28 October.

Ward urged Burnham and Healey to set out how they will fund any fresh spending on defence and the cost of living, and how those lending the government money will be paid back.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at investment company XTB, told the BBC News Channel: "Of course, this is red lights flashing."

"We are used to pockets of volatility, it has been volatile few months," she says.

But record levels of government debt and a record tax take mean "these are not comfortable times for the new government and the new chancellor," she says.

Every time bond yields rise, the UK has to pay more on the debt interest, she says.

Pistol in a lake gives hope for French cold case

BBC News Tue, 01 Sep 2026 16:33:29 GMT

Police investigating the unsolved murder of a British family in France 14 years ago have an unexpected new clue with the discovery of a Luger pistol in the waters of a nearby lake.

One of the few certainties in the killings of Saad al-Hilli with his wife and mother-in-law – as well as a passing cyclist – is that they were shot through the head with a Luger model P06, a type used by the Swiss army until around 1960.

Now France's cold case unit has confirmed the discovery of a Luger in Lake Annecy, in the Alps, not far from the scene of the murders in September 2012.

According to Marianne magazine, which broke the story, it was British tourists on 20 August who found the weapon lying in two metres of water.

At first they thought it was a water pistol, but realised their mistake when they felt its weight.

The discovery was made near the very camping site – Le Solitaire du Lac – where the al-Hillis were staying in their caravan, Marianne reported.

Forensic experts are now examining the weapon, which has been badly damaged by its time under water, to see if it is indeed a P06 model.

It is estimated that around 60,000 Luger P06s were manufactured. But the number of Luger pistols in general that were made is more like three million.

Exhaustive investigations in France and the UK have left police no closer to understanding who carried out the al-Hilli murders and why. Over the years a series of leads have been pursued then dropped.

A British national of Iraqi birth, Saad al-Hilli was holidaying with his family in the picturesque countryside of Lake Annecy in eastern France.

On the afternoon of 5 September, his body with those of his wife and mother-in-law were found in their car, its motor still running, on a forest road near the village of Chevaline. A passing cyclist had – like the other victims – been shot through the head.

Poignantly, the two al-Hilli daughters, aged four and seven, survived. The older girl had been hit on the head with a pistol butt and was badly hurt. The younger, lying in the car under her mother's skirts, was not discovered till forensic experts began examining the scene many hours later.

It was fragments from the pistol butt which enabled police to identify it as a Luger P06. The model is regarded more as a collector's item than a working weapon, which made the theory of a professional hit against the family seem less likely.

Lake Annecy is only 50km from Switzerland, where the Luger P06 will have been familiar to older people from their military service. French police said many examples of the gun have been kept by families on either side of the border.

Among the theories that have been entertained are that the murders were linked to a family row over money; that they were the work of a motiveless crank; and that the main target was the cyclist.

Police were also briefly intrigued by the fact that al-Hilli's wife's first husband – an American – died of a heart attack just hours before the killings in France.

River water smashed into tunnel and chased me for 20 minutes, Nepal worker tells BBC

BBC News Tue, 01 Sep 2026 16:11:18 GMT

Nepalese hydropower workers have told the BBC about the catastrophic moment water from the Trishuli River crashed into their tunnel as the region was inundated by deadly flash floods last week.

It started with a sudden, strong gust of air, says Pemba Dundu Tamang, whose team of about 30 was constructing the tunnel's concrete lining.

The blast of wind sent plywood flying through the air and dislodged heavy machinery. Just outside, houses had already been swept away.

"I ran towards the tunnel entrance," he said. "The water was chasing behind me and I was running ahead of it."

Tamang lost several family members who were at home at the time. Nepal's death toll has exceeded 1,000 after last week's devastating floods, and officials say about 4,000 are missing.

A number of the missing - potentially in the hundreds - are labourers like Tamang, working in a vast network of tunnels at hydropower sites along the river. Engineers have been pumping air into these tunnels as part of a huge rescue operation.

"We are focused on search-and-rescue efforts at the tunnels, our work is continuing," Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP news agency.

"Our soldiers are also deployed to collect bodies and prevent the spread of disease."

The army said 119 people had been rescued on Tuesday.

Tamang says he ran for about 20 minutes to flee the violent deluge, which followed him uphill.

"I was almost unconscious with shock. I could not think clearly."

His colleague, Itha Ghale, says the powerful gust of air almost blew them away as they sprinted.

Over 99% of the electricity generated in Nepal comes from hydropower, and Tamang and Ghale had been working at a major production site helping to build the Upper Trishuli 3B Hydropower Project.

The plant, which was due to open next year, was designed to re-use water from a hydroelectric plant further upstream to generate additional electricity for Nepal's national grid.

There were several different teams operating there - and Tamang says the one operating the large tunnel-lining machine was the last to come out.

But soon afterwards came a crushing realisation.

"I could see where my house should have been. There was nothing left. That was when I realised everything was gone."

Six of Tamang's relatives - his mother, elder brother and sister-in-law and three of their children - are gone, he said. They were at home on the riverside when the floods hit.

Only his wife, son and one nephew survived.

"I feel life is meaningless now. Surviving feels miserable. I do not know where to eat or where to go," Tamang says.

"The dead are at peace. It is those of us who survived who suffer."

Ghale, who lost eight members of his family, says he does not know why he survived. "Perhaps it was not my fate to die."

The eight family members include his mother and eldest daughter. His three sons and wife survived.

Tamang dreads what the future may bring, especially if these hydropower projects are shut down. "If things continue like this, we will go hungry. Sometimes I feel it would have been better not to survive."

Tamang ultimately managed to take refuge with a few others in the village of Shanti Bazar for two days until the army came to rescue them.

He estimates about 50 to 60 workers were able to escape the tunnel alongside him.

He says more people could have been saved if proper resources had been in place.

This is echoed by a new report which says there was evidence of growing instability around the glacier in the days before the disaster - and that better early warning systems could have saved lives.

Satellite images suggest the glacier surface was moving faster, meltwater was turning brown and a crack was developing in the surrounding rock, according to experts from the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance, the Stimson Centre and China's Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment.

These are all possible signs the mountainside was becoming unstable.

The avalanche itself moved too fast for conventional warnings to help those closest to it, the scientists say.

But further downstream, where the flood took 10 minutes or more to arrive, they say a comprehensive warning system could potentially have saved a significant number of lives.

Right now, however, specialists from China, India and Nepal are continuing to use excavators and heavy machinery to blast through debris from the hydropower projects to try to reach workers still trapped at several hydropower sites.

"There are probably still some survivors inside. I would be happy if they were rescued quickly," Tamang says.

"I know many people who are still trapped there."

Additional reporting by Justin Rowlatt, climate editor

Sexual assaults happening almost every day in Ceuta, prosecutors say

BBC News Tue, 01 Sep 2026 15:33:14 GMT

Spanish prosecutors say 23 sexual assaults, including nine against children, have been recorded in Ceuta since the mass influx of migrants into the Spanish exclave at the end of July.

That number meant there was almost one case every day, Ceuta's chief prosecutor Silvia Rojas said.

She told El País newspaper migrant girls were "particularly vulnerable because of their irregular status in the territory".

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July and although most have returned, as many as 5,000 remain - leading to unrest in the autonomous city in North Africa and a crisis for Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Between 1,400 and 1,600 of the estimated 5,000 migrants still in Ceuta are children, according to Rojas.

Among the suspected attackers are four Moroccans, three Spaniards and a Belgian, Efe news agency reports.

There have been scenes of violence in recent days as tensions flare up between migrants and local residents.

Sánchez called the second meeting of his national security council in a week on Tuesday to tackle the issue.

Rojas said the influx had led to an exponential increase in sexual assault, and many victims did not file a report, either out of fear of because of their "current situation in Ceuta".

The Spanish Society of Epidemiology said the border crisis had highlighted the difficulty in detecting and tackling violence against migrant women and girls.

One 24-year-old woman from Morocco told the BBC she had "put her life in danger" by travelling to Ceuta, and described being sexually assaulted while sleeping among a group of men and women. "I was shocked… If I had known this, I wouldn't have come."

Emergency doctor Susana Ascaso said last month her department at Ceuta University Hospital had treated several sexual assault victims, including one who was just 10 years old.

Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said a multi-million euro aid package had been approved by the cabinet that would help provide essential services and cover care for unaccompanied children.

The territory's conservative mayor, Juan Jesús Vivas, has called on Spaniards to take part in demonstrations across mainland Spain in support of Ceuta on Wednesday, which coincides with the city's annual holiday.

The Spanish government is facing bitter criticism from its opponents for its handling of the crisis. The hard-right Vox party said Sánchez had not "lost control of Ceuta - he has handed it over".

Arantxa Campos, president of the Ceuta Employers' Confederation, told the BBC: "We can't do anything unless these people leave.

"We don't have a plan from the government. We don't have anything. We don't even know when they're going to finish screening everyone."

The prime minister said on Monday that King Felipe VI would visit Ceuta "as soon as conditions allow", seen as an attempt to assert Spanish authority over the exclave.

Morocco has a long-standing claim over Ceuta and its fellow autonomous city of Melilla. The last time a Spanish head of state visited the territories in 2007, Rabat pulled its ambassador from Madrid, and another royal visit may cause further diplomatic tensions.

In an interview with Spanish radio channel Cadena Ser, Sánchez made a point of saying the king had not visited Ceuta for 20 years - even though Felipe has only been on the throne for 12 years and it was Juan Carlos who visited in 2007.

He also asserted he was the only prime minister to have made an official visit to Ceuta while in office, having travelled there on 31 July as the crisis took hold.

Some Spanish commentators noted that his remarks appeared to criticise the king, whom he then met later in the day.

Unlike his political opponents, Sánchez has been careful to avoid blaming Morocco for stoking the surge of migrants. He said on Monday that no intelligence reports pointed to "any involvement in one way or another" from the Moroccan authorities.

Instead he focused on disinformation on social media "associated with both Russia and Israel and an international far-right movement that always uses migration, not only to attack Spain but also Europe".

He told Cadena Ser it did not mean "it must come from a state actor" and appeared to indicate the crisis had been stoked after the influx. Government spokeswoman Elma Saiz later confirmed his allegation, saying there was evidence that "various digital forums amplified what happened with the intention of fracturing and polarising Europe".

Russia and Israel have both denied any involvement. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar accused the Spanish prime minister of "a blatant lie" and Russia's foreign ministry spokeswoman demanded proof to support Sánchez's allegations.

A large number of social media posts appeared in August portraying the border fence between Morocco and Ceuta as safe and easy, even though at least 100 people died while trying to swim around the border fence, according to figures from the mayor.

Spanish fact-checking website Maldita said before 30 July, when the influx began, messages circulated on Moroccan social media encouraging people to attempt the crossing, after a June ruling by Spain's Supreme Court.

The opposition People's Party (PP) has criticised Sánchez for "exonerating" Morocco and pointing the finger in other directions. Borja Sémper, a spokesperson for the party, said tens of thousands of people could not have moved towards the Ceuta border without Morocco's knowledge.

Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.

Why did Modi urge Putin to end Ukraine war - and will he listen?

BBC News Tue, 01 Sep 2026 11:55:51 GMT

Russian President Vladimir Putin has been urged by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a close ally, to end Moscow's war against Ukraine.

"Every day spent in war pushes humanity back, and every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm," Modi said on Monday.

Modi, whose country's economy depends heavily on discounted oil from Moscow, has made several similar pleas to Putin since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

BBC correspondents in Delhi and Moscow look at what lies behind Modi's renewed appeal for peace, and Putin's response.

Modi's comments on ending the war in Ukraine are not surprising and don't suggest any tactical change in India's foreign policy.

In fact, speaking on the sidelines of a regional summit in 2022 - less than a year into the conflict - Modi told Putin publicly that "now is not the time for war".

But it would be an oversimplification to suggest that Modi's current or past statements on the war can be seen as a rebuff to Putin or Russia's strategy.

Western countries have pushed Modi hard to take a clear stand on the war - but Delhi has largely stayed neutral, urging dialogue to end the war instead.

The stand hasn't made many Western capitals happy but they have continued to court Modi and India - it's just too big and too fast-growing an economy to be ignored.

In this context, Modi's current statement cannot be seen as an attempt to please a third country.

If anything, it is very much in line with India's policy of strategic autonomy. Which then begs the question: why would Modi say something on the war so publicly?

The answer lies in the long-standing Russia-India ties - the two countries have generally found a way to work together, even when they see geopolitics through different lenses.

Moscow has continued to be one of India's strongest allies despite Delhi forging closer relationships with Europe and the US in the past three decades.

Delhi is one of the founding members of the Brics grouping of nations along with Russia and China, and it is also a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation with the two countries.

But at the same time, Delhi is also a member of the Quad group with Australia, Japan and the US - Moscow has not been happy about this association.

Still, Moscow and Delhi tend to work through these differences. Moreover, Russia still supplies around 40% of India's defence imports and it has also been a steady supplier of Delhi's energy needs.

So, Modi's latest statement is not expected to cause any rift in Moscow-Delhi relations and analysts say it's unlikely that it would have come as a surprise to Putin or his diplomats.

As for the West and Modi's critics in India, they will feel that the prime minister should have been even more direct in his criticism of the war.

This isn't the first time a foreign leader has publicly urged Putin to end the war in Ukraine.

Just five weeks ago the President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev suggested Putin freeze the conflict and return to the negotiating table.

He didn't. And he hasn't.

There's no sign of these public calls for peace changing Putin's calculations.

To Modi's call for a cessation of hostilities, the Kremlin leader replied:

"Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path."

Polite, but vague. And non-committal.

After all, a path can be short. But it can also be long. Very long.

And "moving forward" at what pace?

And, crucially, on which path?

All the evidence suggests that Russia's leadership remains convinced it is on a path to military victory in Ukraine. To frame that in terms of peace, "moving forward" to peace on Russia's terms dictated by military success.

Therefore, for now, the fighting goes on.

Despite the fact that, after more than four-and-a-half years of war and huge military losses, the Kremlin has yet to secure victory.

And despite Ukraine's success in bringing the war back home to Russians: for example, through long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries that have sparked fuel shortages and petrol queues across the country.

In recent days Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine.

"After [Russia] intensified its strikes on Ukraine's military-industrial facilities and critical infrastructure," wrote the Kommersant newspaper this morning, "the Russian side is convinced that in the military confrontation time is working against Kyiv."

While Putin believes that, he'll be reluctant to pause his so-called "special military operation".

'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban

BBC News Tue, 01 Sep 2026 05:00:34 GMT

The elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind.

"It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan.

The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins.

"But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags.

Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran.

They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world.

Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021.

Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt.

The expulsions show no sign of stopping.

The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR.

"In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan.

"We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border.

It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go.

Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all.

"I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry.

"We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says.

"But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police."

Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan.

The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law".

Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden.

The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants".

In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025.

The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel".

The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified".

But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in".

Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children.

Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university?

Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried."

Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified.

"I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house.

"We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside."

He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work.

"I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country.

Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights.

Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN.

But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000.

At the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face.

"There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan."

In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide.

The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition.

"No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive.

But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support".

Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve.

The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule.

But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states.

As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?"

He answers his own question: "Nothing."

We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense.

All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.

Are you made of real-world quarks or virtual-world qubits?

New Scientist September 01, 2026

The following is an extract from our Lost in Space-Time newsletter. Each month, we dive into fascinating ideas from around the universe. You can sign up for Lost in Space-Time here.

You can blame my youngest child for the existential crisis that I’m about to drag you into. When he gazed up with his innocent wide eyes to ask, “Mum, do you think we could be living inside a computer game?”, little did I know that my search for an answer would require a three-year journey of discovery! Could this all in fact be a computer simulation of a virtual reality so perfect that it appears to be real in every sense?

Day one of my quest started with an epic internal battle between the part of me that wears my Astronomer Royal for Scotland hat, and the other part of me who is still a toddler.

Advertisement

Astronomer Royal: “If a scientific question cannot be directly tested, it is, by definition, worthless. Move on.”

Inner toddler: “Why? How? What? Who? Are you real? Am I real? What is real?”

It took a week before I settled on a position. The ability to simulate reality hinges on the question of whether everything in our universe is mathematical – maths is the only language that computers speak – and the Astronomer Royal could certainly interrogate that.

Let’s start by celebrating the particle physicists who revolutionised our understanding of the building blocks of reality with their “shut up and calculate” prescription for quantum mechanics, (an approach that handily evades all the problematic philosophical questions that arise when you zoom into the quantum realm). In the 1970s, they gave birth to a single algebraic equation, the so-called standard model, that predicts the number of subatomic particles, their properties and how they interact with each other. Using this mathematical model, they predicted what should be observed when two protons smash into each other at close to the speed of light and break apart to reveal their innards. To carry out this challenging particle-smashing experiment, they built CERN, a 27-kilometre ring of superconducting magnets buried 100 metres under the France-Switzerland border. The perfect accuracy of the theorists’ predictions compared with the precision of CERN’s experimental measurements is breathtaking. The resulting discovery of the long-searched-for Higgs boson affirms our hypothesis that the universe is very mathematical.

Why banishing irrational numbers could trigger a revolution in quantum theory

But then the astronomers came along, throwing several spanners in the works. For example, particles called neutrinos change their personality – switching from one so-called flavour to another – in the eight and a half minutes it takes them to travel from the sun’s core to our detectors. This is an impossible feat according to the standard model. And, as a scientist who has made her name using giant telescopes to map invisible dark matter and dark energy across the cosmos, I find it deeply disappointing that the standard model also has nothing to say about these mysterious dark entities.

And what about gravity? Albert Einstein’s theory of general relativity concludes that our experience of gravity arises from the way clumps of matter warp the entirety of space and time, an exceptionally well-tested theory that appears to be true whenever astronomers look out into the universe. But how can this mass-bending-space-time version of gravity work when we zoom into the quantum world? Here, particles can essentially be anywhere and everywhere all at once, until the moment we observe them. Our “shut up and calculate” prescription for quantum physics doesn’t have an answer for that. If the universe is wholly mathematical, it’s clear that we have yet to uncover the full story.

That shouldn’t prevent us from looking to the future though. If you are willing to assume that a mathematical theory of everything is just around the corner, with advanced quantum computing available to run the calculations, what are the chances that our observable universe, and everything in it, is a digital by-product of such a simulation? In 2016, tech billionaire Elon Musk answered that question by blithely stating “there is a one-in-billions chance that this is base reality”: a one-in-billions chance that you are living in the real world that will, at some point in the future, develop the technology and scientific know-how to simulate perfect virtual worlds. The argument goes that, once simulators develop this skill, they won’t create just one virtual world, but billions of realisations played like computer games, over and over again throughout cosmic space-time. The total number of virtual humans would then dramatically outnumber the real-world humans in the “base reality”, creating the tiniest probability that you are one of the few that physically exist.

If our universe is truly mathematical, then it is possible that the quarks and all the subatomic particles we believe we are made from are in fact qubits, quantum bits of data that are currently encoding your reality within a futuristic quantum computing data centre. Let me reassure you, however, that contrary to the opinion of the world’s richest man, the probability of this is vanishingly low. Looking carefully at the practicalities of simulating a perfect virtual world, you’ll find that any futuristic software engineer would require an incredible amount of energy to succeed. Step aside Darth Vader, with your puny planet-killing Death Star! Meet my Galaxy Annihilator, which will harness the energy of the entire Galactic Empire to simulate our virtual universe: highly, highly implausible.

Does gravity create reality? A shocking path to a theory of everything

Does this mean that I can now confidently answer my son that we cannot be living inside a computer simulation, because creating our world would require far too much energy? Unfortunately, no. Take a moment to assess your experience of reality at this precise moment. Can you see the four walls of your room? Perhaps a cat is purring on your lap? Your experience, right here, right now, knows nothing of the goings-on in the far reaches of the universe, let alone what is happening in, say, Buckingham Palace. If you are living in a virtual reality, it does not need to be a perfect replica of everything that we can see when we look out into the cosmos, nor a complete simulation of all the 8 billion individuals who inhabit planet Earth. What if an energy-intensive, full-quarks-and-all simulation exists, but it features only you? AI is already sufficiently advanced to create realistic faces, places and conversations to paint in for everyone and everything around you. Could you be the centrepiece of a scientific experiment run by, say, a futuristic neuroscientist interested in studying your consciousness? It’s not impossible, but again it’s unlikely, as scientists are fairly efficient when conducting their experiments: the total number of simulations like this would be small.

On the off chance that your computational overlord has sent you this article to spark your curiosity, however, you might like to give them a little wave. But do not despair. The techno-philosopher David Chalmers has said that a virtual reality where you feel free will, love and laughter is as genuine a reality as any real world, and I agree with him. At the end of the day, it doesn’t really matter whether we are real, so long as we feel real.

Catherine Heymans is Scotland’s Astronomer Royal, and professor of observational cosmology at the University of Edinburgh, UK. Read about her three-year-long journey to find an answer for her son in her new book How to Design a Universe: The science of real and virtual worlds, published in September 2026 by Bloomsbury.

How Ukraine created world-leading prostheses amid the chaos of war

New Scientist September 01, 2026

In the early 1980s, military forces from the Soviet Union went to war in Afghanistan in an effort to prop up a failing Marxist regime. At the time, Ukraine was part of the union, and many of its people were conscripted. Plenty of soldiers ended up losing legs in the fighting – and back then, their options weren’t good.

Shockingly, the Soviet authorities’ response was to offer them a medical version of a skateboard to get around. “That was your only option,” says Antonina Kumka, a former adviser to Ukraine’s government. “They were just rolling on wooden boards with wheels around the cities.”

Fast-forward to today, and Ukrainians have again been thrust into a war they didn’t choose. This time, the conditions of modern warfare mean that unprecedented numbers of people are losing limbs, presenting the country with a huge challenge. The response, however, has been very different. Kumka, who is a co-founder of Protez Hub, an initiative to improve the lot of Ukrainians with amputations, has been stepping up her work. And her organisation is just one part of a sprawling network of clinics, start-ups and research labs that has sprung up to help the injured.

Advertisement

The AI expert who says artificial general intelligence is nonsense

Thankfully, no skateboards are involved. But questions abound. Does Ukraine really have what it needs to help the legions of injured people – many of whom will need prostheses for decades to come? Is this newly created industry always acting in the best interests of those it assists? And it is worth asking what the rest of the world can learn from Ukraine’s booming prosthetics industry.

Unsurprisingly, statistics on the number of Ukrainian amputations are murky. Figures of up to 100,000 are often mentioned in news reports, apparently based on government estimates. But Ukraine has an interest in exaggerating this number to bolster international empathy and support. Kumka, who can access official statistics as part of her work, tells New Scientist the real number is around 24,100, counting from the beginning of 2021 to the end of 2025. (Neither the Ukrainian Ministry of Health nor the Ministry of Social Policy responded to requests to confirm this number.)

However, even that lower estimate represents a tragic loss for a whole generation of Ukrainians. For context, 12,000 UK service members lost limbs in the six years of the second world war, while around 1705 US service members had limbs amputated as a result of injuries sustained during 16 years of fighting in Iraq and Afghanistan. For Ukraine, which had one of the lowest incomes of any European country even before Russia’s invasion, the necessary medical response is an enormous challenge.

The nature of the war today means that not only are amputations more common – on both sides – but they also tend to be particularly difficult cases. The front lines are shrouded in a wide no-man’s-land, known locally as the Kill Zone, in which drones dominate and no vehicle can move without attracting deadly attention. Anyone from Ukraine injured in this zone faces a difficult extraction that is only partially being addressed with ground drones at the moment.

Yakov Gradinar works at Protez Foundation (which translates as Prosthetics Foundation), a non-profit clinic in Ukraine that supplies and fits prostheses (and which isn’t connected to Protez Hub). He says one person recently came in having been stuck on the front line wearing a tourniquet for 60 days. These devices stem blood loss in the short term, but create complications in the long term. They were simply never designed to be used for such lengthy periods. “Tourniquets are saving lives, but losing limbs,” says Gradinar. He estimates that as many as 95 per cent of these patients would be dead without the life-saving devices, but that they also lead to amputations much higher up the limb because the flesh below them rots once it is deprived of blood flow.

One of the reasons the prosthetics industry in Ukraine now extends far beyond Gradinar’s organisation comes down to money. Before Russia’s invasion in 2014, Ukraine had only a small number of prosthetics workshops dealing with cases from car accidents and medical amputations. The government would pay almost $700 per limb, which the individual could use as they saw fit. Since then, Kumka has been a leading figure in campaigning for greater investment and better legislation. Now, the Ukrainian government will pay $100,000 to soldiers for each lost limb, allowing them to go to any of the country’s increasingly numerous private clinics, or even abroad, and choose a limb that suits their needs. When limbs wear out after two to five years, they can receive the payment again. (It is a similar situation for civilians who lose a limb, albeit with less money available.) Over the coming years, this will cost the government “billions and billions and billions of dollars”, says Kumka.

This investment has catalysed the development of new clinics, labs and more. Former doctor Dima Gazda launched a company called Esper six years ago – before the full-scale invasion – to develop sensor technology that could be licensed to other companies for use with prostheses. But when the war ratcheted up, Gazda wondered whether this technology could be adapted so the company could create its own prosthesis for wounded soldiers. “The Ukrainian prosthetics market is definitely shaped by war. We as a company, also, we are shaped by war,” he says.

Could a new approach to AI finally deliver artificial general intelligence?

Since then, Esper has developed an advanced robotic prosthetic hand that has six motors controlled by sensors, allowing the wearer to move the hand faster or slower as needed. It is more dextrous and capable than most prosthetic hands. Around 60 per cent of its nearly 250 components are made in Ukraine. The Esper Hand is waterproof, can carry loads of up to 35 kilograms and is highly modular, so breakages can be easily repaired without having to ship it to a service centre. It is also 10 per cent lighter than a human hand – although Gazda says everyone who holds it thinks it is heavy, largely because they have never held a human hand in the same way.

Esper now employs 65 staff, and although its head office is in New York, most of them work in Ukraine. More than 600 soldiers have been fitted with at least one Esper Hand, and more than 50 of those are back on the front line. According to Gadza, one soldier called Volodymr, who lost both arms in a drone attack, has now been fitted with a pair of Esper Hands. He subsequently qualified on an elite sniper course, which he put down to the hands no longer having a pulse running through them, allowing him to be unnaturally still and precise. He also started to paint, and has held his first exhibition.

Another example of Ukraine’s burgeoning prosthetics industry is Gradinar’s Protez Foundation. Amputations higher up a limb generally lead to a harder rehab, and any prostheses with a knee, which are more difficult to learn to use, are more complex to build and fit, and therefore more expensive. We have long known that higher amputations also result in greater energy use when walking. Not only is Ukraine seeing huge demand for prosthetics care, but it is also seeing the most challenging cases imaginable.

Gradinar says that many new clinics take only the easier cases, but he prides himself on never saying no. He has fitted devices from Icelandic company Össur, which uses resin and glass fibre to mould a socket that fits the user closely, on shorter amputations than the company had ever previously seen done – pushing the boundaries of what was believed to be possible.

Other Ukrainian companies are emerging all the time. Kyiv-based Allbionics makes an electronic hand with 3D-printed construction, backed up by aluminium where needed, which runs for two days on a single charge. A smartphone app helps users learn to operate the device and track usage stats. Syla makes a prosthetic knee that uses AI to help the wearer control it intuitively and lets them walk at up to 10 kilometres an hour, with a battery life of 24 hours. There are also treatment clinics, such as Superhumans Center, which has three sites across Ukraine and more than 600 staff.

However, it isn’t a uniformly positive picture. Kumka says some prosthetics clinics are spending a great deal on marketing and PR, and are prioritising their bottom line and patient numbers over quality of care. “Prosthetics and amputations in general are very lucrative for charities right now, I’ll be honest,” she says. Patients face multiple pitfalls, she reckons, including clinics that fraudulently fit cheaper devices while claiming the cost of more expensive ones, or charities that seek foreign aid but also apply for government reimbursement for treatment. Gradinar concedes there are problems in places. “It’s corruption, but it’s survival mode,” he says. “It’s getting, each day, better and better.”

The economics of medical devices in wartime can also be jarring. For instance, many prostheses currently fitted in Ukraine come from German company Ottobock. But it also openly sells to Russia. The company told New Scientist that Russia represented 8.8 per cent of its global revenue in the first half of 2025, up from 5 per cent in 2023. A report from a US analytics firm puts the figure at closer to 35 per cent, and says that despite claiming to sell only to civilians, Ottobock’s devices have been seen in footage of Russian soldiers. Ottobock refuted that figure and told New Scientist it doesn’t work directly with the Russian military, but cannot rule out that its devices may end up on its front lines.

On top of that, there’s a more direct worry: that the swift innovation going on in Ukraine may result in Ukrainians being fitted with untested devices in a manner that would be considered unethical in peacetime. “There are so many different companies going into Ukraine with their less-than-perfect solutions and trying to use Ukrainians as [experimental] material,” says Kumka. “They would never pass ethical board regulations [in other countries], and they would never be approved, but in Ukraine, they can do that because nobody stops them. They’re using it as a testing ground.”

Subscriber-only newsletter

Finally, despite the number of start-ups and new clinics working on advanced devices, many prosthetics experts believe there remains a critical shortage: medical expertise. On average, someone with an amputation requires nine medical visits in the first year alone, whether that be fittings, physiotherapy appointments or psychological support. And even when the prosthesis is in place, that isn’t the end. Amputation surgery causes a great deal of swelling, so the person being treated often finds that their first prosthesis quickly becomes ill-fitting as the limb heals and reduces in size. Given all of this, prosthetics engineer Alex Dickinson at the University of Southampton, UK, says the biggest problem in Ukraine isn’t necessarily to do with the prosthetics hardware. “It’s the [lack of] trained clinicians,” he says.

In the medium term, there will be further changes, as muscles that once had a strenuous job find themselves doing much less, or even nothing at all, and atrophy, while others get stronger. So, someone may have three prosthetic limbs in their first year.

Then, in the longer term, prostheses simply wear out. Once an individual has adapted, this can happen every two to five years, meaning they may get through a dozen or more in their lifetime. “It’s a really good sign [when a prosthetic] leg falls apart, because it shows the person’s working really hard on it. It actually got them back to really good physical activity,” says Dickinson. “So, it’s lifetime care that these people need.”

Ukraine has already shown itself capable of building a drone industry from scratch, reducing its reliance on politically problematic supply chains, then becoming a global expert and exporting its knowledge and products around Europe and the US. It is possible the same could happen with prostheses – the fact that Esper now has a head office in the US may be a sign of that.

You can now buy a humanoid robot housekeeper for less than the price of a second-hand car. But before splashing out, there’s something you need to know

Still, it is fair to say that helping people with amputations adapt to their new lived reality goes far beyond fitting a prosthesis or even providing ongoing mental health support. Take the fact that cities in Ukraine aren’t exactly known for their ease of access for people with disabilities. On a recent reporting trip to Kyiv, I was struck by the city’s beauty, but surprised by how car-centric and hostile to pedestrians parts of it were.

Many of those who have lost limbs are young men with long lives ahead of them, which perhaps explains why there is now plenty of talk about addressing this problem. The military veteran and double amputee Oleksandr Budko has a YouTube show in which he takes Ukrainian celebrities to different cities to test them for accessibility. In one episode, he and television presenter Masha Efrosynina roll through Lviv in wheelchairs, growing increasingly frustrated by the cobbled streets and their inability to get up the steps into cafes.

Making old cities accessible is vital in every country, but for Ukraine, the need is being thrust into the mainstream by a young generation of recently injured people. As the country rebuilds in the coming years, it will need to ensure that it is done with accessibility first and foremost in mind – and Budko has found that city governments contact him after his shows air for advice. All this will take time, no doubt, but we have already come a long way from those medical skateboards.

The first signs of dark matter particles may finally have been spotted

New Scientist September 01, 2026

Researchers may have spotted the first signs of a dark matter particle. If the result is confirmed, it could be one of the most monumental discoveries in the history of physics.

Dark matter makes up about 85 per cent of the universe, but for decades physicists have been unable to determine what it itself is made of. Hypotheses have ranged from different sorts of particles and forces to strangely behaving gravity and everything in between – but the leading idea has always been that of the weakly interacting massive particle, or WIMP. As we have built more and more powerful detectors to search for WIMPs, though, their failure to show up has led many to doubt their existence and move on to more exotic ideas.

That doubt may soon come to an end. A new analysis of data from the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment in South Dakota has revealed a single particle that may be the first WIMP ever detected. “This result is certainly an exciting one, because it provides some potential positive hint for what dark matter could be, not just what dark matter could not be,” says JiJi Fan at Brown University in Rhode Island, who wasn’t part of the analysis.

Advertisement

LZ looks for dark matter using a 7-tonne tank of liquid xenon, surrounded by several layers of shielding and buried more than a kilometre down to keep out other types of particles. When an outside particle hits a xenon atom, it creates a tiny burst of light that is measured by sensitive detectors surrounding the tank. Researchers can then use that light to reconstruct the path of the incoming particle and the energy level of the interaction.

In the search for WIMPs, we generally look for events with energies below about 30 kiloelectronvolts (keV), says LZ spokesperson Richard Gaitskell, also at Brown University. That assumes the simplest sort of interaction, in which the WIMP is essentially bouncing off an individual nucleon in the xenon nucleus. Having not found any hints of WIMPs in that energy range, the LZ team decided to reanalyse the first 220 days of data from the detector, searching for events with higher energies.

That is where they found their dark matter particle candidate, at about 248 keV. “You must never make an assumption that nature is going to do something the easy way,” says Gaitskell. “Nobody can accuse our universe of making the simplest and most natural-seeming choices.”

Strange gamma-ray signal could be most direct evidence of dark matter yet

Such a high-energy event can’t have come from the most simple type of interaction between a WIMP and a nucleon – instead, it must have happened through a more complicated coupling between the WIMP and the entire xenon nucleus. If that is the case, the WIMP must have a mass more than 200 times the mass of a proton.

“It’s not just that they’re seeing something, but that there’s a hint at what the underlying mechanism might be,” says Wick Haxton at the University of California, Berkeley, who wasn’t involved in the analysis. “If this all stands up, our learning curve is going to be pretty steep from now on.”

Actually detecting a dark matter particle could reveal some of the universe’s most closely held secrets, including information about the early universe that is otherwise nearly impossible to determine, and drastically shake up our standard model of particle physics. But as Haxton says, this detection is not yet certain.

In particle physics, the statistical threshold for a finding to go from an intriguing hint to a solid discovery is a number called 5 sigma, which means there is about a 1-in-3.5 million chance that a signal like this would show up as a fluke rather than a true sign of dark matter. Right now, this detection from LZ sits at 2.6 sigma, which means that there is about a 1-in-200 chance it could appear as a fluke.

Subscriber-only newsletter

That might still seem fairly secure, but in the search for dark matter it is far from enough. “In science we sit down and we do so many damned experiments, I’m afraid you come across a 1-in-100 event fairly often,” says Gaitskell.

“Before one can declare victory, you need a few more data points, but now they have something to aim for, they know where to look,” says Haxton. The good news is that this analysis only covered about one-third of the data that LZ has already taken, and other dark matter detectors around the world have their own data, as well. A few more events in the same energy range could bump the discovery of WIMPs up to 5 sigma – and change our understanding of physics and the universe forever.

The UK just had its hottest summer ever

New Scientist September 01, 2026

The UK’s dry, hot and sunny summer has provisionally entered the record books as the hottest season for the country since records began in 1884.

The average temperature for the months of June, July and August was 16.5°C (61.7°F), the national weather service, the Met Office, said on 1 September, blowing through the previous summer record of 16.1°C (61°F) set just last year.

“The conditions we’ve seen this summer have broken UK climate records once again,” said Amy Doherty at the Met Office in a statement.

Advertisement

Britain’s only desalination plant remains idle during drought

Summer in the UK began with the second warmest June on record, followed by the second-warmest July. But the heat remained almost constant throughout the three-month period, with 38°C (100.4°F) recorded for the first time in June in Norfolk, and 38.1°C (100.6°F) recorded at Kew Gardens in London on 13 August.

Much of England is now in the grip of a severe drought after rainfall vanished from many parts of the country during July. The hot, dry conditions have damaged crops, strained healthcare systems and triggered severe wildfires.

Fossil fuel emissions fuelled the high temperatures, with climate change making a summer like 2026 around 130 times more likely to occur, the Met Office said.

Free newsletter

“In a climate unaffected by human emissions of greenhouse gases, a summer like this would be exceptionally unlikely, i. e. 1 in over 1,000 years,” Mark McCarthy at the Met Office said in a statement. “In our current climate, which is changing because of the effect of burning of fossil fuels, we should now expect this to be roughly a 1 in 9 year event.”

The top five warmest summers for the UK have all occurred since 2003. This trend will only intensify in the future as rising global temperatures cause summers in the UK to be increasingly hot and dry. Under 4°C of warming, the summer just gone would be considered cool or below average for the UK, the Met Office said.

In response to the announcement, Ruth Fuller at the World Wildlife Fund said in a statement: “These stark figures prove what we have been experiencing first hand, we are getting hotter and hotter. And the climate will continue to heat up until we cut our emissions to net zero.”
