Mountain warming means there will be more disasters like the Nepal flood

New Scientist September 01, 2026

The terrible disaster in Nepal isn’t a one-off event, but a harbinger of things to come. There will be more catastrophes of this kind as mountainous regions around the world continue to warm fast, researchers warn.

“In coming years, we can expect more of these events happening,” says Gunjan Silwal at Newcastle University in the UK. “Maybe this is just a trailer.”

How our bodies adapt to extreme temperatures – until it gets too hot

Initial analyses suggested the cause of the flash flood in Tibet and Nepal on 26 August was the collapse of a glacier. Better satellite images now show that an entire slope collapsed, with huge amounts of rock below and around the glacier also falling.

Advertisement

“It’s not just a glacier detachment; it’s like a large landslide with a glacier on top of it,” says Bethan Davies, also at Newcastle University.

The rock and ice plummeted into the valley below, leading to a catastrophic wave of water and debris that swept down the river. It is still not entirely clear where such a huge volume of flood water came from, says Daniel Shugar at the University of Calgary in Canada. But it appears the falling rock and ice landed on other ice left by retreating glaciers.

“So the ice in the valley bottom, as well as the ice on the glacier, is probably a lot of the water that we’re seeing in those videos,” says Shugar.

Researchers are now discussing to what extent global heating contributed to this disaster in informal online forums. Davies, who has been studying glaciers in the area with Silwal and others, thinks climate change could have played a substantial part. “We do know the area is warming very rapidly,” she says. “Pictures from the 1970s show a much more substantial glacier.”

Free newsletter

That glacier would have helped support the rock slope down which it was flowing, so its thinning and retreat may have destabilised the slope to the extent it gave way. “The term we use is debuttressing,” says Davies.

Another factor could be the degrading of permafrost. Ice in cracks helps hold rocky slopes together, and helps glaciers stick to the surfaces they flow over. “The permafrost acts like a glue that holds everything together,” Davies says.

The glacier involved in this disaster is just one of many retreating glaciers in the region. What’s more, the rate of retreat is increasing – it was 1.5 times higher from 2000 to 2023 than from 1964 to 2000.

The large glaciers on valley floors are relatively stable because of their size, but the smaller ones that flow down steep slopes and feed the valley glaciers are more vulnerable. In many cases, their lower parts are vanishing, disconnecting them from the valley glaciers. “We’re seeing this really significant fragmentation, and that’s leaving lots of glaciers perched high up in the same way as this one that collapsed was,” says Davies.

The fundamental problem is that the region is warming fast, at around 0.3°C per decade compared with a global average of under 0.1°C per decade, says Silwal. The same is happening in other mountainous regions around the world, a phenomenon called elevation-dependent warming.

The devastating wildfires in Europe demand urgent measures to make landscapes more resilient, but without action to reduce use of fossil fuels, the danger is only going to increase

There are three reasons for this, says Mike Byrne at the University of St Andrews in the UK. Firstly, land areas in general warm faster than the seas.

The second reason is the loss of snow and ice cover. High-elevation areas are usually covered in snow, even in the tropics, which reflects the most sunlight. When warming melts snow, the darker surfaces absorb most of the sunlight, leading to yet more warming. “It’s a positive feedback loop,” says Silwal.

The third reason is more complex. As atmospheric carbon dioxide levels increase, more longwave radiation – heat – is being bounced back to Earth’s surface instead of escaping to space. Hot regions that are already radiating lots of heat have to warm only a little before the extra heat they radiate balances out the extra heat coming back down. This Planck feedback, as it is known, is why Earth would stop warming if CO2 levels stopped rising.

But cold regions aren’t close to radiating enough heat to balance out the extra heat arriving, so they warm more. “Elevated regions, because they’re colder, somewhat counterintuitively warm up more rapidly,” says Byrne.

The bottom line is that mountainous regions will keep warming fast for the foreseeable future, leading to many more disasters. “We will continue to see bigger and more events in mountain ranges around the world,” says Shugar. “Will they be bigger than this one? I don’t know.”

So what can be done to prevent them? “Stopping emitting carbon dioxide would be the single most effective measure that we can deploy,” says Davies.

Referring to the flood in Tibet and Nepal, Davies says, “If this is something that’s been caused by warming, then this is something that we did, and therefore I wouldn’t call it a natural disaster.”

Climate scientists constantly warn us about the need to prepare for extreme weather, but people rarely pay attention when the heat fades. That needs to change

In the absence of stopping CO2 emissions, an effective early warning system is needed so people can move to higher ground in time.

That is going to be expensive, and the high-income countries that are mostly responsible for climate change should pay, says Davies. “Nepal has contributed very little to the climate crisis, yet is suffering a lot of consequences.”

We tend to think of climate change as gradual, says Byrne, but events like the disaster in Nepal and Tibet and the recent wildfires in Europe show that very dramatic events can be triggered by gradual change. “It’s been a very sobering summer in the context of climate change,” he says.

The best new science-fiction books of September 2026

New Scientist September 01, 2026

If there was a paucity of new science fiction in August, then September more than makes up for it, with everything from a long-awaited piece of speculative fiction from China Miéville to a short story collection paying tribute to the genius of Ursula K. Le Guin, with contributions from names including Ann Leckie and Kelly Link. Then there’s a new near-future novel from Station Eleven author Emily St John Mandel, a fresh sci-fi series from the bestselling Brandon Sanderson (and co-author Janci Patterson) and a strange but intriguing tale from one of my favourite writers, Naomi Alderman.

This is something I absolutely cannot wait to read: a collection of 15 new short stories, inspired by the work of the one and only Ursula K. Le Guin and intended to honour her amazing legacy. The names contributing are super impressive, including Karen Joy Fowler and Charlie Jane Anders: what a treat.

China Miéville is one of our great contemporary writers, master of the weird and author of masterpieces including The City and the City and Embassytown (my personal favourite). New book The Rouse comes in two whopping volumes, and its publisher promises it is a “decade- and continent-spanning epic of grief, global tumult, and grim conspiracy”. I can’t tell you for sure that it’s science fiction, as I’ve yet to tackle the two doorstopper tomes I’ve been sent, but I can predict it will definitely be weird, and speculative. Michael Moorcock, no less, calls it “completely without parallel”. Exciting times.

Advertisement

Free newsletter

In my younger days, I was an avid reader of Garth Nix’s young adult Old Kingdom series, so I’m interested to see what this excellent author’s first venture into sci-fi will be like. It’s a military space opera, set in a universe where interstellar war rages between Earth and Mars – and where for over two centuries, humans have travelled into space on huge sentient mountain ranges known as Massifs. Then the crew of the ship Sassafras starts asking questions about why the Massifs carry humans to the stars – and talking to the powerful avatars piloting the ships.

This is the first in the new Skyward Legacy series from the mighty Sanderson, co-written with Janci Patterson. It’s a complicated set-up: humans have warred against alien oppressors for decades. Now they’re free, and Arturo Mendez, leader of Skyward Flight, is sent on a mission to make contact with a settlement of humans isolated during the long war. But Blightfall, the planet he’s sent to, is more dangerous than he’d anticipated.

I am such a Naomi Alderman fan. We read her previous novel, The Future, with the New Scientist Book Club, and I loved it. This latest sounds much stranger and more speculative, but I’m here for anything from this author (her recent non-fiction book, Don’t Burn Anyone at the Stake Today, is also a big recommendation from me). Anyway: the plot here is that the novelist Naomi Alderman, grieving the loss of her mother, sets up a wildlife camera in her parents’ garden, and takes the first photo of a new animal, the “mimmoth”. These creatures spread across the world, harmless apparently, but strangely intelligent – what will their eventual impact be?

Emily St John Mandel, author of Station Eleven, is very good at thoughtful, near-future tales, and here comes another. Set in 2031, this is a world where America is in the middle of a civil war – but where something even stranger might be going on. Ari, newly out of prison, goes to a party in Los Angeles, where she meets someone who looks exactly like her friend, but isn’t… Living in Paris a long time later, Ari is haunted by what happened at the party, and by what might lie beyond the boundaries of her world. I’ve started this one, and it’s living up to its promise so far.

This collection of short stories from the award-winning speculative author moves between science fiction and fantasy – from techno-witches battling a world ruled by machines, to a consciousness on a starship watching the cosmos die and be reborn.

This new Doctor Who novel sees the Fugitive Doctor and Martha investigating a strange object in the British Museum. Apparently a medieval toy, it refuses to stay in one place, time or identity.

This novel by the heavyweight literary author Hernan Diaz, winner of the Pulitzer Prize, takes place centuries in the future, following the adventures of a pincher, someone who steals electricity from the grid and sells it on the black market. This pincher, an orphan, goes on to discover an experiment that, if she can power it, could “change the fabric of reality itself”.

Laurel is a biologist turned dishwasher at an Antarctic research station. She doesn’t tell anyone in her new life about the tragedy which made her leave her old one – but she becomes convinced that the mysterious Arc that appears across the ice could lead her to a new world where she could turn back the clock. I’m halfway through this one and am loving the biology and the Antarctic side of it. Can’t wait to see how the physics holds up.

This sci-fi thriller is set in a world where the poor die young, and the rich live forever. Assassin Azure is usually hired to kill the richest of people – but then he’s given a job to protect one of them. The publisher promises that this fuses “the dystopian morality of cyberpunk with the explosive action of anime”, which sounds pretty cool.

Abby, suffering the burden of being in her 30s without having achieved any of her dreams, decides she has a new purpose: becoming the first person on Mars. Luckily for her, a Danish entrepreneur is planning a one-way mission.

Jiang, who also has a story in the Ursula K. Le Guin anthology out this month, sets this piece of “science-fantasy” in a world where the royal advisors are plotting to overthrow emperor Yun. Yun’s sister Xilian escapes to the drowning continent of Opera, a place filled with strange tech and dreams of immortality.

It’s 2026, and time travel is a luxury commodity. So, Rachel, who killed Oliver in a car crash in 1997 when she was 18, goes back to save him – only for the future to change in bad ways that may have something to do with Oliver, with whom she’s now fallen in love…

Taj is a scrapper, living in a junkyard and keeping his family alive with the scrap he finds there. His one salvation? A “construct”, or robot, that he built himself, and which he hopes will win big in the construct fighting circuits.

How our bodies adapt to extreme temperatures – until it gets too hot

New Scientist August 31, 2026

During recent video calls with my UK colleagues, I have noticed a common theme. Their cheeks are pink, damp hairs stick to their brows and they sigh a lot. The unprecedentedly hot summer in Europe is taking its toll. “How do you cope, living in Australia?” they ask glumly.

Earlier this summer, the temperature in the UK reached 38°C (100.4°F), breaking the record for June and many people’s spirits. But that doesn’t sound too bad when you have grown up in Australia, where it usually gets into the 40s in summer. I remember times when it has surpassed 45°C (113°F) in Sydney. I don’t love these scorching days, but they don’t bother me too much, despite working from home in a small un-air-conditioned room.

This has sparked several conversations about why the heat affects us differently. I have British and German ancestry, so I don’t have any kind of genetic advantage for tolerating Australia’s heat. One possibility is that my repeated early-life exposure to heat has somehow primed my body to cope better with it. But it turns out that my UK colleagues are just as equipped as me for adapting to heat on a physiological level, and that the advantages of growing up in Australia are merely psychological and behavioural. There are also techniques we can all use to help our bodies adapt to the rising global temperatures (spoiler alert: you may want to switch off your air con).

Advertisement

Alzheimer’s, stroke, depression: The preventative power of sauna

Our bodies function optimally with a core temperature of around 36.5° to 37.5°C (97.7° to 99.5°F), and our organs start to shut down at anything above 40°C (104°F). As a result, we have evolved ways to constantly monitor the temperature of the outside environment and our insides, and cool ourselves down when needed.

We sense external heat via thermoreceptors in our skin, which communicate with the brain. “Thermoreceptors are the body’s first responders, detecting and relaying to the brain what is happening at the body’s surface,” says neuroengineer Clarissa Whitmire at the University of Queensland in Australia. If the brain considers the heat to be a threat to the body’s core temperature, it produces a conscious feeling of being uncomfortably hot and bothered, so that we peel off a layer of clothing, rest in the shade or engage in other cooling behaviours.

The brain also activates unconscious cooling mechanisms in response to heat. For example, it tells the heart to beat harder and faster to move blood from the body’s core to the skin. “We’re basically trying to bring warm blood from the central circulation to the periphery, where, if air temperature is lower than skin temperature, we can lose heat via convection,” says Julien Périard, an environmental physiologist at the University of Canberra in Australia. This explains why my veins bulge out so much on hot summer days that I look like an anatomical drawing of the circulatory system.

We can’t lose heat via simple convection if the outside temperature is the same or hotter than us, like when it recently reached 38°C in the UK, so we have also evolved the ability to sweat. As sweat beads evaporate off our skin into the air, they draw heat away.

So far so simple, but things get interesting when you compare people who live in different climates.

In hot climates, people become gradually better at self-cooling over the course of summer because their bodies undergo what is known as “seasonal acclimatisation”. Studies show that, at the end of summer, people who are asked to exercise in a hot room redirect blood to their surface faster, start sweating sooner and produce more sweat overall compared with when they were tested before the season. They also have a greater volume of plasma – the liquid portion of blood – to supply more water for sweat. These changes allow them to maintain a lower core temperature, skin temperature and heart rate while in a hot environment. Because of this seasonal acclimatisation, heatwaves tend to result in fewer deaths when they occur at the end of summer compared with the beginning.

We must adapt to climate change while also tackling the root cause

Another response to regular heat exposure is the expression of heat shock proteins. Our bodies produce these when we get hot to repair and refold other types of proteins in cells that might be damaged by the increased temperature. Their upregulation then helps to protect cells from thermal stress during subsequent heat exposures.

The good news is that anyone can undergo this kind of heat acclimatisation, regardless of their genetics or their level of heat exposure growing up, if they spend enough time in a hot climate, says Périard. “We evolved as tropical animals, so we have the systems in place for dealing with heat,” he says. “Everybody can adapt, and the adaptations develop quite quickly.”

For example, Périard and his colleagues conducted an experiment in which they brought nine Danish cyclists to Qatar. In Denmark, it had been below 10°C (50°F) for months, but in Qatar, it was in the high 30s. “Their initial performance on an outdoor time trial was atrocious, but after training outside every day for two weeks, their performance got much better,” says Périard. “So even people from Denmark, who are not used to really hot summers, can adapt in a short time.”

When I relay this information to my UK colleagues, however, they are unconvinced. They swear that even after enduring months of baking weather, they still don’t feel like they are getting used to it. But this could just be a trick of the mind.

According to Carolyn Broderick, who is a sports medicine physician at the University of Sydney, if people in the UK were to do an exercise test in a hot room right now, they probably would show signs of being more physiologically heat-adapted than before the hot summer – for example, they would likely produce a greater volume of sweat to more efficiently cool themselves down. However, they might not consciously feel any better because there is a difference between physiological adaptation and thermal perception. Research shows that even when people become physiologically acclimatised to heat during summer, they often don’t report feeling any more comfortable when placed in a hot room than they did before summer, for reasons that are unclear.

There is also an expectation effect, says Broderick: “If you grow up in a hot climate, you see it as normal.” In Australia, everyone knows that summer is going to be blisteringly hot, so they are psychologically prepared. From a young age, you also learn ways to cool yourself down, like running under a sprinkler or sleeping under a towel soaked in cold water. Conversely, when I spent a year in Montreal in my early twenties, the sub-zero winter came as a shock because I had never known anything like it. It took time for me to work out that it was unwise to go out in ballet flats and that late-night poutines were vital for warming my insides and laying down insulative fat tissue.

In these psychological and behavioural senses, therefore, early-life exposure to hot or cold may be important for coping with it later on, says Broderick. Children growing up now in the UK and other traditionally cool countries will probably become better at dealing with the heat than their parents because they will have greater exposure, she says.

The urgency of the climate crisis could also be affecting our psychological responses to peaks in temperature. Notably, one of the previous hottest years in the UK’s history – 1976 – is often remembered as its happiest ever, despite the temperature reaching 35.9°C (96.6°F) and surpassing 32°C (90°F) for 15 consecutive days (although it was less humid than this summer’s heatwave). “There was that long, hot summer… Everyone in the country was happier and more relaxed,” recalled writer Will Self when describing 1976 to the Guardian newspaper. Photos of the time show children gleefully splashing in paddling pools and shirtless adults sunning themselves in parks. But now that climate change is front of mind, our perception of heatwaves has changed, and we tend to find them worrying and ominous rather than enjoyable.

Since summers are only going to get hotter, I ask Périard and Broderick how we can improve our heat resilience. They both say that the most helpful thing we can do is regular exercise. This is because physical activity raises our internal heat, which naturally stimulates heat acclimatisation.

Exercising outdoors on hot days is even better because the external heat boosts the acclimatisation effect, says Broderick, who is chief medical officer of Tennis Australia and the Australian Open, as well as the medical director of the Australian Olympic team. “You should go out into the heat – start with small doses of low-intensity activity and build up a bit more each day,” she says. People over the age of 65 need to be careful because they are at risk of developing heat stroke if they do strenuous exercise in the hot sun, but walking in shaded areas is usually safe. A recent study found that during pregnancy, brisk walking or moderate-intensity jogging or cycling is also safe when the outside temperature is 32°C or lower.

For people who can’t exercise easily, there is also growing evidence that regular sauna bathing builds up similar physiological mechanisms for coping with heat, like expanding plasma volume to support more sweating.

While exercising in the heat, it is important to stay hydrated to replace fluids lost through sweating and to quickly implement cooling measures if you feel like you are overheating, says Broderick. “For example, you can put a cold towel around your neck where the large blood vessels are or use a misting fan.”

Air conditioning is also useful for cooling down, but Périard cautions against spending too much time in artificially cooled environments, since we need heat exposure to promote acclimatisation. This makes me think of some British friends who have lived in Australia for over 10 years but still suffer badly in summer. They cope by blasting their home air con, but perversely, this may be one reason why they have never properly acclimatised to the outdoor climate. “Air con is good at night because we want to be able to sleep, but in the day, it might be better to set it at 24°C [75°F] rather than 18°C [64°F],” says Périard. Personally, I have air conditioning in my bedroom for occasional nighttime use, but not in the rest of the house.

Tellingly, even though climate change is making the planet hotter, people in the US are actually experiencing cooler temperatures on average nowadays because of the widespread adoption of air conditioning in homes and workplaces. Modelling shows that the average temperature experienced by Americans is 1.4°C cooler than in 1960. “It’s kind of alarming because we’re spending more time inside in air conditioning and exercising less, so it’s not the ideal scenario for helping us adapt to climate change,” says Périard.

Unfortunately, heat acclimatisation is also temporary, so you have to build it up again each summer. Research shows that it gradually decays over a period of around six weeks once heat exposure ceases, like when winter sets in. This suggests that if I was to travel to the UK right now, having come from winter in Australia, I would perform worse in a heat stress test than locals, who have undergone seasonal acclimatisation over summer.

What’s more, there is a limit to how much heat the human body can acclimatise to and survive. If a person’s core temperature exceeds 43°C (109°F), death is almost certain. Core temperature starts to rise to this fatal level if the air temperature is very high, because the skin can’t lose heat via convection. High humidity makes things worse because the moist air hinders the evaporation of sweat.

According to modelling led by Jennifer Vanos, an environmental health researcher at Arizona State University, a young healthy adult could survive for a maximum of 6 hours in the shade if the relative humidity was 25 per cent and the air temperature was 50°C (122°F). If the relative humidity increased to 50 per cent, they could only withstand 43°C for 6 hours. “Our survivability model identifies conditions beyond which even the fittest young adults, at best, will perish over 3 or 6 hours without access to cooling resources,” Vanos and her colleagues write.

Older people are more vulnerable to heat because, as we age, our hearts become less efficient at pumping blood to our skin and we sweat less. Vanos and her team estimate that regardless of humidity, a person over the age of 65 couldn’t withstand anything above 46°C (115°F) for more than 5 hours. Older people can also succumb to temperatures in the 30s if they are repeated over many days, because of the prolonged pressure on their hearts, which is why thousands are estimated to have died in the European heatwave in June.

A new measure of health is revolutionising how we think about ageing

If current rates of global warming continue, some places on Earth will go above the survivable limits of heat and humidity modelled by Vanos and her colleagues, says David Romps, who studies the climate at the University of California, Berkeley. “Homo sapiens has been around for 300,000 years and over that time, the Earth has been 100 per cent habitable, meaning I could put you anywhere on the planet, in any one of those 300,000 years, at any time of day, and you would be fine with the heat, humidity or cold, so long as I gave you adequate shade, water or clothing. You wouldn’t necessarily be happy, but you would survive,” he says. But if things continue as they are, he says, “parts of the Earth will become uninhabitable for the first time in human history”.

These no-go regions could include parts of India, China, Australia, Africa, South America, the Middle East and the US Midwest, says Romps. In these places, people might be able to live inside artificially cooled buildings, but going outside for extended periods would be fatal.

On our current climate change trajectory, the first place on Earth to become unsurvivable will likely be the Persian Gulf, says Romps. Modelling has found that Kuwait City could experience temperatures above 60°C (140°F) by around 2070. The outlook for Australia is also alarming, with some studies forecasting that Sydney and Melbourne will experience 50°C days by 2060 if there is 2°C of global warming above pre-industrial levels. With 2.5°C of warming, even the UK could experience 45°C days by 2056.

I might be able to bear 40°C days, but 50°C or 60°C sounds unimaginable. We all have the ability to adapt to a bit more heat than we are used to now, but ultimately there is a limit to what we can stand. As Romps says, “the human body has adapted to deal with the worst conditions the planet has historically doled out to us, but we’re not that far away from conditions in which the human body runs out of tricks.” At that point, no amount of exercise or sauna bathing will be able to prepare us.

Should we all be taking low doses of lithium to prevent Alzheimer’s?

New Scientist August 31, 2026

In the 1880s, a newly dug well in Texas became known as the “Crazy Well” after a woman who drank from it daily allegedly overcame dementia. Her legendary recovery has since been suggested to be due to the naturally occurring lithium in the area’s groundwater. This lithium-containing “Crazy Water” is still available to buy in the local town of Mineral Wells.

Strange as it may seem, the idea that lithium, a simple metal, might have a role in treating and/or preventing dementia is starting to gain traction. Starting next month, lithium orotate, a type of lithium salt, will be tested for the first time in people with early Alzheimer’s disease in a clinical trial at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland. This comes on the back of research published last year by Bruce Yankner at Harvard University and his colleagues showing that lithium orotate reversed memory loss in mouse models of Alzheimer’s disease, the most common cause of dementia.

Game that reduces dementia risk may clear amyloid from men’s brains

Yankner’s team also found that the brains of people who died of Alzheimer’s disease had lower levels of lithium than those who didn’t have any cognitive impairment when they died. And earlier this year, a study of more than 2000 US counties led by Hyeong-Moo Shin at Baylor University in Texas revealed that counties with low levels of naturally occurring lithium in their public water supplies had higher rates of dementia than those with high lithium levels in the water.

Advertisement

These findings don’t prove a causal link between lithium deficiency and dementia; however, they are certainly intriguing, and they have inspired many people to rush out and buy lithium supplements. Is it too early to jump on this bandwagon? And are there any risks of boosting your lithium levels with supplements?

Lithium is the lightest metal element on Earth and is named after the Greek word lithos for “stone” because it naturally occurs in rocks. It is best known for its use in rechargeable batteries, but also has a long history of use in psychiatry, particularly in the treatment of bipolar disorder. Interestingly, the soft drink 7UP started out in the 1920s as a lithium-containing lemon-lime-flavoured beverage marketed for curing hangovers and boosting energy. No one knows why “7” was included in the name, but one theory is that it referred to the approximate atomic mass of lithium.

Since lithium is highly reactive, it is usually paired with other substances like orotate or carbonate to form lithium salts. Lithium carbonate is the type typically prescribed for bipolar disorder. However, Yankner’s team found that lithium orotate was far better for treating Alzheimer’s-like disease in mice. This was thought to be because lithium orotate is less likely to be taken up by amyloid plaques – the abnormal clumps of protein in Alzheimer’s-affected brains – leaving more lithium available in the healthy parts of the brain.

We still don’t know exactly how lithium protects against neurodegeneration, but one mechanism seems to involve the fact that it inhibits an enzyme called glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK-3 beta). Animal studies have found that blocking this enzyme reduces the build-up of amyloid plaques and helps to regulate inflammation.

So far, only lithium carbonate has been investigated for slowing cognitive decline in humans. The latest trial, conducted by researchers at the University of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, disappointingly found no benefit of taking a daily lithium carbonate pill for two years in adults aged 60 and over with early signs of memory loss. I hope, and I’m sure many others do too, that the upcoming trial of lithium orotate will be more successful, but we won’t know the results for years because the trial is scheduled to run until 2029.

In the meantime, lithium orotate supplements are already available to buy, leading some people to try to get ahead of the curve and start taking them now just in case they are eventually proven to work.

Caution is warranted, however, because taking too much lithium can cause side effects like tremors, thirst, nausea and headache, as well as thyroid and kidney toxicity. In Yankner’s study, the dose of lithium that was given to mice was much lower than the lithium dose typically prescribed in bipolar treatment, so it is hoped that similar “microdoses” might ward off neurodegeneration in people too. However, no studies have examined the long-term safety of lithium orotate supplementation, even in low doses. There is also no agreed definition of lithium deficiency or standard test for it, so there is no way to know if your levels are too low.

Beyond its potential role in preserving cognition, lithium may also reduce the risk of suicide and committing crimes. A Lithuanian study found that municipalities with high levels of lithium in their drinking water had lower suicide rates than those with low lithium levels, after adjusting for socioeconomic factors. Another study found that people who died of suicide had lower levels of lithium in their bodies than those who died of other causes. In Japan, meanwhile, municipalities with high levels of lithium in the water have been found to have lower crime rates after adjusting for employment rates and age. More research is required, though, to confirm a causal link.

Personally, I think I’ll wait for the results of the clinical trial of lithium orotate to come out before I consider taking supplements. But if I ever find myself in Texas, I will definitely stop in at Mineral Wells for a big glass of Crazy Water.

Need a listening ear? UK Samaritans: 116123; US 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: 988; hotlines in other countries.

Healed fang wound found on 520-million-year-old apex predator

New Scientist August 28, 2026

Even top predators weren’t safe in Cambrian seas around 520 million years ago. An extraordinary fossil shows a healed wound where one predator took a bite out of the side of another.

“I would never have expected to see something like this preserved in the fossil record,” says Stephen Pates at University College London.

The predator with a bite taken out of it is called Amplectobelua symbrachiata, which belonged to a long-extinct group of strange arthropods known as the radiodonts that looked a bit like a cross between squid and lobsters. They had two vicious, grasping appendages on their heads for catching prey, and a line of swimming flaps protruding from their sides that decreased in size towards their rear.

Advertisement

Extraordinary ichthyosaur fossil shows its last meal was a pterosaur

They grew to nearly a metre long, which might be tiny compared with modern marine predators, but back in the Cambrian Period, it made them one of the biggest predators around.

The swimming flaps of radiodonts were softer than their grasping appendages, resulting in very few fossils of them. But a team recently found a single flap at a site in China called the Yu’anshan Formation, where soft tissues are exceptionally preserved.

It is recognisable as a radiodont flap because of a characteristic pattern of lines on its surface. If it was the largest swimming flap, the animal would have been at least 23 centimetres long. If it was one of the smaller flaps, it could have been much larger.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The researchers noticed an odd W-shaped feature on the edge of the flap – the kind of shape typically left when two fangs tear through flesh.

But is it really a bite wound? The researchers in China got in touch with Pates because he has studied similar injuries in trilobites. “You want to rule out that it’s been broken during the fossilisation process,” says Pates.

X-ray fluorescence mapping shows that the chemical composition of the W-shaped part is consistent with the rest of the fossil, which means it’s not an artefact caused by flaking. “This is telling us that this is likely a flap that was preserved like this, rather than altered later,” says Pates.

What’s more, there is a black band visible around the edges of the W-shape that appears to be a sign of healing. “In modern arthropods, you see this melanisation, this darkening around areas where they’re regrowing,” he says. “I think we can be fairly confident this happened while the animal was alive.”

It is an extraordinary find because only around 10 isolated radiodont flaps like this have ever been found, says Pates. “With more complete specimens, even if these wounds were there, you wouldn’t necessarily be able to see them.”

So, what took a chunk out of this ancient predator? The team can’t be sure, but it could have been another species of radiodont, or even a member of the same species, says Pates.

Palaeontologists have found new evidence that the early ancestors of amphibians, reptiles and mammals did not have a larval stage with external gills like modern frogs or salamanders

Hundreds of likely predation wounds have been found on trilobites, but their fossils are much more common because of their hard exoskeletons and because they survived until 250 million years ago, whereas radiodonts were all extinct by around 480 million years ago. Trilobites were also much smaller and nearer the bottom of the food chain.

“There have been other reports of healed injuries in Cambrian animals, though never in a radiodont,” says Joe Moysiuk at the Manitoba Museum in Canada. “With only one specimen, I don’t think we can rule out other potential causes.”

For instance, it’s not unusual for arthropods to suffer injuries while shedding an exoskeleton, and so this flap might have been damaged during moulting, says Moysiuk.

“You can’t rule it out, but it’s [a] balance of probabilities,” says Pates. For instance, a moulting wound is most likely to be a singular tear, whereas the W-shape points more towards a bite mark, he says. The location on the flap is also what would be expected if the radiodont was fleeing an attacker, whereas a moulting wound could occur anywhere on the animal’s body.

“For us, the best interpretation for this injury is a predation injury,” says Pates.

bioRxiv DOI: 10.64898/2026.08.01.742255

NASA’s huge Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is about to launch

New Scientist August 28, 2026

NASA’s next flagship space telescope is getting ready to launch. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which will probe some of the cosmos’ most vexing mysteries, is set to take off from Cape Canaveral in Florida on 30 August.

This new observatory gets its name from NASA’s first chief of astronomy, who helped plan the Hubble Space Telescope and built the agency’s space astronomy programme. It and the previous major telescope to be launched, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), are designed to work together to investigate the universe in infrared-light wavelengths.

But while JWST was intended to probe deep into distant space with a relatively small field of view, Roman will take a broader, shallower view, capturing an area of the sky equivalent to the full moon in each observation.

Advertisement

Planned satellite launches could ruin Hubble Space Telescope images

Using its Wide Field Instrument, Roman will take images with the same resolution as the Hubble Space Telescope, but over an area of sky 100 times larger, making it 1000 times faster at gathering data than Hubble. This broad view is intended to allow Roman to map the distribution of dark matter across the universe and measure the effects of dark energy.

“The goal is not necessarily for Roman to take a picture of dark matter or dark energy, but to measure their effects with far greater precision,” said Kristen McQuinn at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Maryland, one of the science leads for the mission, in a statement. “That could help us understand what the universe is made of, how it developed and what may happen to it in the distant future.”

Subscriber-only newsletter

These broad surveys will also enable it to spot a huge variety of cosmic objects. JWST can then follow up on the most interesting of them to get deeper, more detailed data, or Hubble can observe them in a wider variety of wavelengths of light.

Over the course of its five-year primary mission, Roman is expected to observe about 12 per cent of the sky, unveiling the universe going back to just 2 billion years after the big bang. Space telescopes tend to have their missions extended – Hubble, for example, was only expected to last about 15 years and has now been operating for more than 36 years. This means Roman may well end up observing a much wider swathe of sky.

The observatory’s other scientific instrument is its coronagraph, designed to directly image planets orbiting other stars. By blocking the light from the stars themselves, it will allow the reflections of that light off any planets to shine through.

This will enable it to see planets that are 100 million times fainter than stars, far more than any existing space-based coronagraph can accomplish. Spotting all those planets will set the stage for NASA’s next proposed flagship space telescope, the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

If the launch goes smoothly, Roman should reach its final position at L2 – a gravitationally stable point about 1.5 million kilometres further from the sun than Earth – in about a month. It will then undergo another three months or so of instrument testing and calibration before beginning its science phase, so the first scientific observations are expected to begin around the start of 2027.

One job ad, 1000 applicants: How do you stand out in a world of AI job hunters?

New Zealand Herald September 01, 2026

Applicants need to ensure their own voice is still in the job application. Photo / 123rf

By Susan Edmunds of RNZ

Job hunters using AI to help with their applications are flooding listings, leaving some recruiters sifting through thousands of potential hires for each position advertised.

Squirrel chief executive David Cunningham said he had noticed a “tsunami” of job applications in response to advertised positions, most clearly generated using AI.

“We’ve had numerous roles where we have received hundreds of applications, and in one case, over 1000. AI is good at ‘match my current CV to this job, update accordingly, and write a cover letter’.”

He said Squirrel had to use an AI tool to filter them and look for people who were a fit.

“We tend to look more at their work experience, the cover letters are a waste of time now really, because you can write a cover letter to make it sound like you’re a perfect fit for any job.

“We tend to use AI tools to analyse the job versus the work experience.”

He said Squirrel would also usually give preference to people who were based in New Zealand, and run screening interviews to come up with a shortlist.

University of Otago associate professor and human resources expert Paula O’Kane said she had had a similar experience reviewing applications. “This is the problem, how do you actually get through all of those cover letters that are written relatively similarly and what can you do to stand out from the crowd from a candidate’s point of view … I really think that’s what candidates have to think about.”

She said people should try to keep their cover letters “short and sweet”.

“So what are the really key things that are important to the job, how do you bring your skills, your attributes and your personality into your cover letter?

“That’s the thing that’s going to make you stand out. For candidates there’s still a role to use AI in that initial thinking about it and thinking how they write but they need to bring it back to themselves in the final iteration of their cover letter. I think that’s what employers are going to look at more and more … bring your own voice into it and think about who you are and how you want to come across.”

She said employers would be most worried about false negatives – people not making it through the screening process who would have been a good fit.

“Whereas when you have false positives you will probably catch them later. Yes, they’re a waste of your time but you’re going to move on to the next level of selection tools, which are probably going to be more face-to-face and personal. So it’s the people who miss that are the biggest risk rather than the people you put through that you shouldn’t have put through.”

Hayley Pickard, managing director of recruiter Fortitude Group, said she saw the problem particularly when advertising for technical and engineering positions.

“AI has made it incredibly easy for someone to produce a polished CV and cover letter and apply for a large number of vacancies very quickly. The problem is that it hasn’t necessarily improved the relevance or quality of those applications. It has simply removed much of the effort that previously went into submitting one,” she said.

“I regularly receive applications that use the exact terminology from the job advertisement but provide no real evidence behind it. Skills and responsibilities mentioned in the advert suddenly appear in the application, but the person provides no specific examples of when, where or how they gained that experience.

“When I ask the applicant for further details, it can become clear that the polished wording has overstated their actual level of experience – or, at the very least, made it extremely difficult to distinguish what the candidate genuinely knows from what AI has added.

“I don’t think the answer is for applicants to avoid AI completely. It can be very useful for improving spelling, structure and presentation, particularly for people who don’t naturally find writing easy or whose first language isn’t English. However, it should be used as an editing tool, not as a substitute for the applicant’s own experience, judgment or voice.”

She said high application volumes created screening fatigue for recruiters. “When an employer is working through dozens or hundreds of similar-looking applications, they are not necessarily looking for the most beautifully written one. They are trying to quickly establish: Can this person do the job? Are they genuinely interested? Can I trust what they have told me?

“Ironically, a straightforward, specific and recognisably human application can now stand out more than an extremely polished one. Applicants shouldn’t try to compete with AI-generated applications by producing even more generic AI content. They should compete through relevance, evidence and authenticity.”

She said employers also had to be careful not to confuse polished writing with a strong application. “A capable person may not have the strongest writing skills, while someone with little relevant experience can now produce an impressive-looking application in seconds. Screening therefore needs to focus increasingly on verifiable examples and well-targeted follow-up questions.”

The Green Party is refusing to apologise after one of its MPs made a false claim about a National MP in the House, with a clip of the comment racking up more than one million views.

National’s Northland MP Grant McCallum is requesting an apology from Green MP Tamatha Paul after she incorrectly claimed he had bought a house in Wellington to take advantage of an accommodation allowance given to MPs.

In a heated general debate speech last month, Paul took a swing at MPs who she said had bought property since the Government’s changes to property taxes this term.

The interest deductibility scheme, often described by the Opposition as “tax cuts for landlords”, was reinstated in 2024 after Labour phased it out over the previous two terms.

Property owners can claim 100% of the interest incurred on residential property mortgages as a tax expense.

In her speech, Paul said Act Party MP Parmjeet Parmar, who owns the largest number of properties of any MP this term, bought five new houses since the coalition was elected.

National MP Katie Nimon was listed as having bought three residential properties.

“Let’s talk about the National and New Zealand First MPs” Paul said. “Including Grant McCallum, who bought a house in Wellington, so they can pay themselves the accommodation allowance while taxpayers pay their mortgage off.”

Clips of the speech were posted by Paul to TikTok and Instagram, with the former version attracting more than one million views.

McCallum corrected the record in the House, denying he had purchased a property in Wellington and was paying it off with the accommodation allowance.

McCallum later took to Facebook to deny the allegations again.

“I did buy another home in Paihia. The reason is simple. It was so I had somewhere to stay when I was working in the mid and far north of my electorate. I do not rent it out,” the post said.

He said his own investment in the property saved taxpayers money because he didn’t need to stay in motels when he travelled to the Far North.

McCallum requested Paul apologise for the mistake, “preferably in Parliament”.

In a statement request, Newstalk ZB asked Paul whether she planned to apologise to McCallum.

A copy of his assets declared in pecuniary interests were included in the request, which didn’t list property in Wellington.

The statement Newstalk ZB received listed a number of donations from “the property industry” the coalition received during the 2023 election, which Paul said were “all on the public record”.

Paul also included that landlords received a “$2.9 billion tax cut” since interest deductibility was reinstated.

“National can play games through the media if they want, but the Green Party stands by calling out their record on housing and who’s actually benefiting from it,” the statement said.

It did not include any mention of McCallum or his request for an apology.

Paul declined Newstalk ZB’s requests for an interview.

Newstalk ZB followed up with Green Party co-leaders Marama Davidson and Chlöe Swarbrick.

Davidson said the record had been corrected and was happy for the issue to be left at that.

“In the heat of the moment in the chamber, things are often said off the cuff by MPs across the House,” she said.

This morning Davidson was challenged over whether the Greens believed mis- and dis-information was bad for political discourse.

“We do, and that has been corrected in the house,” she told Herald NOW’s Ryan Bridge Today.

“What about online? What about in the court of public opinion? What about the internet?” Bridge pressed.

Davidson responded that the party had “put up the correct information into the dialogue”, though she did not elaborate.

“The principle remains the same - it’s to show how disconnected privileged MPs are from the experiences of ordinary people,” she said.

“Even more so when you can buy a whole extra property and you don’t need any help to pay it off. You can just have an extra property in your back pocket, in your handbag.”

McCallum said he was disappointed the Green Party’s leadership was letting the matter go.

“I think it reflects poorly on them and their leadership.

“The people of New Zealand, they want to hold other politicians to a high standard and have them do it to themselves,” he said.

McCallum said he still believes an apology from Paul would be appropriate.

Act leader David Seymour, who appeared alongside Davidson on Ryan Bridge TODAY, said anyone who had watched the clip could judge for themselves.

“The facts don’t need to be wrong, right, because the principle is right, except the principle was based on the facts which are wrong. So if you can work that out, good luck.”

Troy Matich is a political reporter with Newstalk ZB, working from Parliament’s press gallery. She joined NZME in 2025, previously working for RNZ as a producer for Morning Report.

Central Hawke’s Bay’s Charlie Laird to fly fish at world youth championships in Slovakia

New Zealand Herald September 01, 2026

Charlie Laird is part of a New Zealand team of five to compete in the World Youth Fly Fishing Championship in Slovakia in July 2027.

Central Hawke’s Bay College student Charlie Laird has been selected to compete in the world youth fly fishing championship in Slovakia.

The 16-year-old is part of a New Zealand team of five teen anglers who will, in 2027, rotate across five venues, catching and releasing as many fish over 20cm as possible.

Laird said the anglers had about three hours to fish a 100m to 300m section of four rivers plus a lake.

He said points were given per fish and per centimetre.

Laird said he was expecting some differences compared to his usual practice spots on the Waipawa River.

This included a shift in his target species from rainbow and brown trout in New Zealand to grayling in Slovakia.

He said the grayling species was not as scared as trout.

“You can walk through the water and they will come right up to your feet.”

Laird said he had a mix of nerves and excitement for the July 2027 competition.

He said practice came in the form of getting down to the river as often as possible.

“I enjoy it, just being out there; you never know when the next fish is going to be like the biggest fish you have ever caught.”

Laird said the Waipawa River had a good number of fish to perfect his skills before his monthly squad meet-ups, with mentors to train him for the rivers in Slovakia.

He was modest in saying there was always room for improvement.

“I would like to get my skill level up for when I go.”

He said his selection came after a late entry into the Sport Fly Fishing New Zealand’s (SFFNZ) youth development plan.

He took part in workshops in Rotorua in July and August.

“I wasn’t expecting to have a spot because that development squad was going for a bit ... when I joined.”

Sport Fly Fishing angler development officer Aaron West said Laird came to his attention through the weekend camps where active younger anglers mentor keen kids to share their passion for the sport.

“Charlie stood out due to his natural ability to find and catch fish, plus his willingness to ask questions and learn.

“Since being part of the development squad, he has shown how determined and committed he is.”

West said SFFNZ would support Laird and the team through training weekends, and hoped to attract others like Laird to future events.

He said they are excited to have selected the first full New Zealand youth team for the competition.

“We have had individuals compete before, but these events are primarily a team event with five youths per team.

“To have a full team heading off next year is a big deal.”

SFFNZ is a small volunteer organisation and is unable to fully fund the team, which has a Givealittle with a $50,000 target to help cover flights, accommodation, competition fees, equipment and travel.

Michaela Gower joined Hawke’s Bay Today in 2023 and is based out of the Hastings newsroom. She covers Dannevirke and Hawke’s Bay news and loves sharing stories about farming and rural communities.

Mayor says Nepal disaster should spur planning over Milford Sound tsunami risk

New Zealand Herald September 01, 2026

Milford Sound draws a million visitors a year, Southland Mayor Rob Scott said. Photo / Supplied

By RNZ

Southland’s mayor says the tragedy in Nepal should prompt practical preparation for the threat of a tsunami at Piopiotahi/Milford Sound.

The death toll from the devastating Himalayan glacial floods has crossed the grim 1000 mark.

Nearly 4500 people are missing after the gigantic wave of freezing water, rocks and debris from a high-altitude glacial collapse roared downstream last week.

Glaciers melting or falling, climate change, large-scale erosion and the possibility of tsunamis are all factors in parts of New Zealand.

A new report from Emergency Management Southland highlights the risks of a landslide down the cliffs surrounding the water at Milford Sound and then causing a tsunami.

Large landslides had occurred in the past, and an Alpine Fault earthquake could trigger those in the future, the report said, “potentially creating tsunami that reach visitor and village areas within minutes”.

Problems identified included a very short response time and limited evacuation options.

Mayor Rob Scott told Morning Report the tragedy in Nepal was an eye-opener for people in this country and a similar event in an area like Milford Sound could become the country’s worst natural disaster.

“What attracts everybody there is the greatest risk.”

As soon as the Nepal flash floods occurred, Scott said he was among those realising how much of a wake-up call it was and it could easily be repeated here.

“It’s trying to weigh up what we can actually do ... there is a likelihood it’s going to happen and I guess we’ve got to look as a country as to what we can do to be the most prepared we can be.”

He didn’t wish to catastrophise the risk, however, Milford Sound attracted a million visitors a year so at any given point in a day there could be 3500 people visiting.

One possibility would be limiting the number of visitors to reduce the scale of any possible disaster.

There wouldn’t be much warning and even if an earthquake provided some clues it would still leave people with only two or three minutes to get to higher ground, Scott said.

“I think Usain Bolt would probably even struggle to get to higher ground in that short timeframe so the risk is real and I think we need to look at what practical things we can do to mitigate it.”

While practical advice could be given to residents, it was much harder trying to prepare visitors for such an emergency, Scott said.

Milford Sound is part of the Department of Conservation’s estate.

However, emergency management falls to councils to fund, but Milford Sound was a nationally significant attraction, he said.

“This becomes a national responsibility rather than a local one to fund.”

He said someone at a high level needed to take ownership and responsibility for the risks.

“This whole ‘it’s not my responsibility, not my job’ kind of thing isn’t going to land here after the event.”

Scott said some of the funding could come from the International Visitor Levy and paying for some escape routes might need to be one priority.

“We need to look at whatever measures we can to minimise the harm from something that’s just happened in Nepal.”

- RNZ

Associate Justice Minister Nicole McKee is rejecting suggestions her firearms law reforms were an attempt to move New Zealand towards a United States-style “right to bear arms”.

The second amendment of the US constitution protects this right, permitting anyone who legally owns a firearm to carry it in their home for self-defence purposes.

Last month McKee, Act deputy leader and former Council of Licensed Firearms Owners spokeswoman, progressed the Arms Bill into law to replace the 43-year-old Arms Act, a commitment in the National-Act coalition agreement.

The original bill would have broadened a licensed holder’s right to carry firearms in a non-public area. However, this was changed at the 11th hour after McKee acknowledged concerns from NZ Police.

Cabinet had agreed to carry over the relevant clause in the old law: section 45, requiring a “lawful, proper and sufficient purpose” for carrying or possessing “any firearm, airgun, pistol, prohibited magazine, restricted weapon, or explosive”.

The original bill copied this clause but only applied it to explosives. Other clauses applied to firearms and firearms parts but only in a public place.

“This creates gaps in the law, for example there is no offence if a licence holder carries or possess a firearm in a private place,” police said in McKee’s Cabinet paper about the issue.

This could potentially lead to thousands of fewer charges per year.

“Between April 2019 and May 2026 there were over 12,500 prosecutions for this offence. The impact of not carrying over the entire section cannot easily be determined but will decriminalise some behaviour.”

It’s unclear how many of those charges were for ”carrying" offences, which weren’t covered unless for explosives, and how many were for “possessing” offences, which were.

McKee acknowledged a possible gap, and when the bill passed into law, all the section 45 provisions were retained, including the onus of proof of a “lawful, sufficient and proper” purpose falling on the person with the firearm.

She described in her Cabinet paper the characteristics of a scenario that wouldn’t be covered if the bill was unchanged, where a person:

It is this kind of scenario that prompted Labour’s police spokeswoman Ginny Andersen to raise questions about whether the original bill was an attempt to move New Zealand towards the US-style “right to bear arms”.

Andersen said McKee appeared to be trying to give licensed firearms holders greater freedoms on their own properties while weakening the reach of police in those homes or vehicles.

“This is what New Zealand gets when a [former] firearms lobbyist is the minister in charge of firearms policy.”

Without the “intervention” from police, Andersen said there would have been scenarios compromising public safety that the law wouldn’t have covered.

“She only changed it when forced to at the 11th hour.”

McKee said Andersen’s comments did not align with her actions.

“Ginny Andersen claims to be concerned about this issue, but when I put forward changes to fix it, she voted against them,” she said.

“That tells you everything you need to know. She is an opportunistic merchant of misinformation, desperate for any crumb of attention she can get.

“If Ms Andersen genuinely wanted to scrutinise firearms policy, she has every opportunity to question me in Parliament. Remarkably, she has not asked me a single oral question on firearms in almost two years.”

In her Cabinet paper, McKee said the bill had originally been worded so there wouldn’t be multiple provisions “potentially applying to the same conduct”.

“Officials therefore did not carry section 45 over in full, on the basis that the conduct it addressed would be adequately covered by other offences in the bill.”

Police had not raised any concerns until after the bill had been introduced, she said in her paper.

She told the Herald it was “difficult to identify a situation in which conduct that put public safety at risk could not have been prosecuted under the bill, even without this amendment”.

“However, [the change] now provides additional clarity and preserves a distinct offence, with an updated penalty, for carrying or possessing a firearm or other specified item without a lawful, proper, and sufficient purpose.

“This is an area that would benefit from further analysis, and I intend to have it reviewed next term.”

Through a spokeswoman, Police Minister Mark Mitchell said he endorsed police raising concerns about public safety.

“A lot of work has been done to modernise the [Arms] Act in line with the coalition agreement to improve public safety. The Police Minister has advanced safety issues as part of this process when police have indicated a possible risk to the public.”

Derek Cheng is a senior journalist who started at the Herald in 2004. He has worked several stints in the press gallery team and is a former deputy political editor.

Christchurch City Council’s attempt to create abandoned shopping trolley map fails

New Zealand Herald September 01, 2026

Christchurch councillors say shopping trolleys are being abandoned. Photo / RNZ, Louis Dunham

By Rachel Graham of RNZ

A Christchurch City Council attempt to create a map of hotspots for abandoned shopping trolleys has failed because staff could not obtain retailers’ information about where the trolleys were dumped.

In May last year, councillors asked staff to examine ways to address the issue of abandoned trolleys, after a report showed that 6313 trolleys had been abandoned between October 2024 and October 2025.

RNZ was told trolleys cost an average of $300 but could cost up to $700 each, with Woolworths spending more than $1.5 million per year on abandoned trolleys nationwide.

One of the suggestions was to create a heat map for locations where shopping trolleys were frequently abandoned and compare them with bus routes.

The report, which would go to the full council on Wednesday, said staff could not produce the requested heat map because information gathered by Send Snap Solve, an app that logged maintenance problems such as dumped rubbish, graffiti and abandoned trolleys, belonged to the retailer and could not be shared with the council.

The report said Retail NZ members generally felt they already had sufficient systems to manage trolley retrieval and were not keen to develop a memorandum of understanding with the council on best-practice trolley recovery.

Retail NZ also said retailers objected to the term “abandoned trolleys” because trolleys were stolen, rather than left behind.

The report recommended that council staff liaise with Retail NZ to consider a public awareness campaign to encourage people to report abandoned trolleys.

It also recommended including trolleys in an upcoming council campaign about illegal dumping.

Retail NZ advocacy manager Denise Garland said stolen shopping trolleys were a serious and expensive issue for retailers around the country.

She said most retailers collected dumped trolleys within 24 to 48 hours of being notified that a trolley had been found.

“What we feel it comes down to is the reporting of stolen shopping trolleys. Retailers don’t know where their shopping trolleys have gone unless it is reported,” she said.

Retailers primarily relied on members of the public reporting stolen trolleys, which was where the system was failing, Garland said.

She said Retail NZ would support a public campaign, with the council, encouraging people to report stolen trolleys.

Auckland’s Pet Refuge is at capacity after 17 dogs were brought in during unprecedented demand over the second half of August.

The charity said all available spaces at its Auckland shelter and across its network of external boarding providers are now full, with at least six dogs waiting for a safe place.

Founder Dame Julie Chapman said the sudden influx showed how quickly demand could change the charity’s capacity when many needed care at once.

“Seventeen dogs in two weeks is an extraordinary number for our team to accommodate.”

The charity provides temporary shelter, veterinary care and support for pets while their owners escape family violence, before reuniting them when their families find somewhere safe to live.

Chapman said finding a suitable placement is not simply a matter of finding an empty bed.

“Dogs that come to us are often highly traumatised and we need to consider their size, temperament, health and individual needs, to ensure we’re placing them where they can be safely and appropriately cared for by our team.”

Chapman said pets were often used as a tool of coercion and control, and it was a frightening option for women to leave them behind.

“Research from Women’s Refuge found 53% of women delayed leaving violence out of fear for their pets, and 23% have had a pet killed as part of family violence. Our job at Pet Refuge is to give people certainty that their pet will be safe and cared for while they are in refuge or emergency housing.”

A family violence survivor who depended on the pet refuge to escape her circumstances said the only thing stopping her from leaving was her dog.

“I wasn’t willing to give my dog up. Being asked to choose between a home for my kids and keeping our dog, it didn’t feel like a real choice. I felt stuck,” she said.

Another said leaving an abusive home meant leaving behind her dog she described as part of her family.

“Knowing [that my dog] was finally safe meant I could focus properly on getting myself and my children secure without constantly worrying about him,” she said.

Alongside its Auckland shelter, Pet Refuge worked with boarding partners across the country to provide additional safe spaces when its own facility was full.

With the skyrocketing demand, Chapman was calling on pet lovers to help get dogs on their waitlist to safety by giving to the Safe Bed for Pets programme charity through regular monthly donations.

Since opening in 2021, Pet Refuge has provided more than 80,000 nights of safety to 979 pets from 561 families.

West Ham fight off Wolves as Divine Mukasa double eases pressure on Nuno

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 21:01:15 GMT

It was a match between two disjointed sides, two teams trying to carve out new identities following the drop into the Championship. In the end West Ham won thanks to a bit of luck, a degree of resolve and, crucially, a sharpness in front of goal that took them away from Wolves and reduced the pressure on Nuno Espírito Santo, for a few days at least.

First half goals from Divine Mukasa and Jarrod Bowen from the penalty spot were complimented by two more in the second, as Mukasa secured his brace alongside a goal for Konstantinos Mavropanos. The defender doubled up himself too, albeit by scoring in his own end, as Wolves tried to claw their way back into contention. The visitors could also claim a decent goal from midfielder Marshall Munetsi to their tally. For all their obvious technical ability, however, Cesar Peixoto’s side lacked the hosts’ sang froid at the crucial moments and that proved the decisive factor.

Nuno’s mantra after the match was “I think we can do better”, but he was clearly grateful for the win. “We all know that it was much needed”, he said. “Looking back even on today, we have mistakes again but we’ve been much more effective in our attacking actions.”

With West Ham’s uncertainty extending beyond the field of play, there was much interest taken from the appearance of Amanda Staveley in the stands here. The former Newcastle shareholder remains in the running to acquire a stake at West Ham and could be seen punching the air at Mukasa’s first-half banger. The City loanee was not the only new recruit to impress, with Arne Engels impressive alongside him in midfield.

What gave off the vibes of being an uninspiring opening half ended up being blessed by three goals. West Ham were on the back foot for much of the opening half hour but established a two-goal lead by the 40th minute after a short spell of improved play. The opening goal was a memorable one, hit by Mukasa from 25 yards and cannoning into the net off the underside of the bar. It was a memorable way for the teenager, signed on loan Manchester City, to open his account, and it came after a piece of smart attacking play that got Kyle Walker-Peters behind Wolves’ defensive line. Seven minutes later, Bowen converted a penalty after swift feet from Joel Piroe confused André into an untimely tackle.

Before Nuno could get his troops into the dressing room and preach the importance of a clean sheet, Wolves hit back. With West Ham’s defense pushing up, a fortunate deflection off the previously-bewildered Andre opened up the opportunity for Marshall Munetsi to run into space, check inside Mavropanos and finishing coolly inside Mads Hermansen’s left hand post.

With nascent enthusiasm tempered by the late concession, the atmosphere among the home support quietened as the second half began, perhaps in anticipation of further trials for West Ham. Instead they extended their lead in short order and it was Mukasa who struck again. This was a lovely move, starting with a cute through ball from Bowen that Pablo dummied to take four Wolves players out of the equation. Receiving on the edge of the box, Mukasa stood up Toti Gomes, shifted to his left and hit a shot that deflected off the Wolves skipper and beyond the despairing José Sá.

“I’m delighted by the way he played,” Nuno said of Mukasa. “All the young lads, not just those who joined this summer, have brought us energy and talent. There’s a lot of things to improve but I’m delighted to have him.”

Wolves responded to the third goal by grabbing hold of possession once more, but the sprightly Fer López spurned two chances. Up the other end, however, and an Engels’ corner was deep and dangerous and after Mavropanos saw a towering header crash off the bar, the Greek defender smashed the rebound home on the volley. Six minutes after celebrating, Mavropanos got the final touch to a cross from Jackson Tchatchoua to turn it into his own net.

Yiannopoulos on Tuesday appeared on Piers Morgan Uncensored, a YouTube show presented by Piers Morgan, the British broadcaster and media personality. Yiannopoulos, 41, described the experience in the US as “humiliating and disorientating”, “physically degrading” and “frightening”.

He also said that he was “ashamed” of his previous support for Donald Trump, who has pursued an agenda of mass deportation throughout his second presidency.

“I didn’t really understand the physical reality of how institutionalized the brutality is in America” he said, adding: “It’s like everybody that’s arrested is an MS-13 gang member, and it hurts a lot more than it looks like on television.”

His remarks came just days after he was deported from the US, after being arrested on Thursday by ICE officers at New Orleans airport.

In a statement last week, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the parent agency of ICE, said Yiannopoulos had “legally entered the country” in May 2019, but “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.

The homeland security department said Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”.

In the Piers Morgan interview, Yiannopoulos disputed the government’s account and denied previously overstaying a visa. He said he is married to an American, and claimed he held a green card that he was “renewing on a two-year basis”.

The Guardian has contacted homeland security and the White House for comment on Yiannopoulos’s remarks.

Yiannopoulos also said that while he was detained, “no one would tell me anything” – a common complaint from people held in ICE custody.

“I don’t think I’ve ever been frightened like that before” he told Morgan. “I think maybe in the past I’ve been a little bit blasé when people talked about their trauma, a little bit cavalier when people talked about stuff kind of lingering with them, but I get it now … I wouldn’t wish it on anyone.”

Last year, in posts on social media, Yiannopoulos had been supportive of Trump’s crackdown on immigration.

In one post, he wrote: “There is one concrete thing we must insist on this administration delivering. It matters a lot more than debts measured in imaginary money. We have got to deport millions and millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters.”

In another post, Yiannopoulos had said that California “needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally”.

During Tuesday’s interview, Yiannopoulos said of his past support for Trump: “If I had any clue that anything remotely like this was even possible, I would never have gotten involved in supporting Trump in the first place and I’m very ashamed that I did.”

Peekaboo island: the floating forest confounding nature watchers in western Canada

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 20:06:49 GMT

A 150-metre-long island appeared from nowhere on Williston Lake, British Columbia; vanished, then reappeared 20 miles away

A thickly forested island appeared mysteriously on a western Canadian lake. Nearly 150 metres (500 feet) long and 75 metres (250 feet) wide, the land mass took local people and experts by surprise. It wasn’t on any maps or navigation charts.

One boater approached and took a video of the island, capturing nearly 100 trees undulating in the chop of the lake.

And then, within days, it disappeared.

On Monday, the island made its second appearance – nearly 20 miles from its location earlier in August – in stunning aquatic displacement that has left residents wondering how an entire island can seem to simply vanish.

The mystery has unfolded in the middle of Williston Lake, a long and narrow reservoir created after the W. A. C Bennett dam flooded the region in the early 1970s. At nearly 1,700 sq km (650 sqmiles) it is the largest body of freshwater in the westernmost province.

Bob Gammer, a spokesperson for BC Hydro, the government-owned utility that operates the reservoir and dam, said the island was “quite something and rather unbelievable” when he first saw the images.

“In the days of AI, you really needed another form of verification or evidence like a corroborating eyewitness account,” he said. “And soon, we got that.”

Satellite imagery confirmed the island was in fact real, and floating in the main body of the reservoir, roughly 60 miles west of the dam.

BC Hydro believes the island is the result of years of trees and plants growing largely undisturbed on the woody debris along sheltered sections of the reservoir’s shoreline.

Similar islands have shown up across the globe, including Wisconsin’s famed Forty Acre Bog. The giant, floating island on Lake Chippewa is knitted together by peat, mud, roots and trees.

Measuring roughly 12,000 sq metres (14,000 sq yards) in size, the British Columbia island is also bursting with life: birds and small animals are living among the mix of coniferous and broadleaf trees. Observers suspect the root system in the water hides some of the lake’s best fish.

Gammer likened the growing conditions to hydroponics and said: “Well-fed trees growing on a decaying food source with lots of water … they could grow pretty quick.”

The reservoir, he added, is higher than it has been in 14 years, as a result of high winter snowpacks and consistent summer rains that have raised water levels in the Peace River and the lake.

“Suddenly, there are all of the right conditions to potentially lift this kind of little island from where it was, and bring it out into open water,” he said.

Between sightings, the island may have drifted to shore. Its seeming disappearance “doesn’t mean it’s gone to the bottom of the reservoir”, Gammer previously told CBC. “It may have returned to a more sheltered area along the shoreline.”

BC Hydro doesn’t know how old the trees on the island are, but with the right conditions the forest could “just stay there for years” and grow. Local people speculated the trees could be decades old.

“It’s not like they’re just a bunch of little shrubs. This is an island with larger trees and it’s something you really have to wrap your mind around,” said Grammar. “It’s not an everyday thing. This is really really unusual.”

Rocky Avery, a friend of the boater and a longtime resident of the area who first posted the clip to social media to warn others about a possible hazard, said he would “totally jump on that island if I could”.

“It’s probably a bit shaky on the outer sections, but with those huge trees in the centre, I imagine someone could walk on it,” he said.

Gammer cautioned boaters from attempting to become the first to set foot on it, warning that video shows trees moving back and forth on a “delicate, thin layer of logs”, adding it is “very unsafe” and “very unstable”.

Avery’s social media posts about the island prompted a flurry of excitement and a seemingly inescapable nod to the current political situation in Canada. Recently, the US president, Donald Trump, chose to rename Lake Ontario after trade talks collapsed between the two countries. The announcement has prompted anger, frustration and mockery from the Canadian public.

“I’m surprised Trump hasn’t named [the island] and claimed it,” commented one user on Avery’s post.
