A federal judge on Tuesday dismissed the remaining claims in a well-publicized lawsuit against Lizzo’s production company, declaring that the case brought by her former wardrobe stylist could not proceed.

The ruling by US district judge Fernando L Aenlle-Rocha comes nearly two years after he dismissed Lizzo as an individual defendant from the case brought by Asha Daniels against the About Damn Time singer and her production company, Big Grrrl Big Touring, Inc Daniels first filed her lawsuit in September 2023, alleging that she was subject to bullying as well as sexual and racial harassment in an “unsafe, sexually charged workplace culture”.

Lizzo denied all allegations and called the lawsuit, as well as a separate suit filed by three backup dancers in August 2023, “false” and “outrageous”. At the time of filing, her lawyers characterized Daniels as a “disgruntled” employee with “meritless and salacious” accusations.

In his ruling, Aenlle-Rocha said Daniels failed to identify conduct by company employees that would constitute “general hostility” toward women or disparate treatment between men and women at the workplace. “This alleged conduct and these alleged incidents, while inappropriate and unprofessional, fall within the scope of what the Supreme Court has held to be outside the protection of Title VII as part of the ‘ordinary tribulations of the workplace,’” he wrote.

Daniels also claimed disability discrimination, citing an injury from a wardrobe manager who allegedly rolled a heavy clothing rack over her foot and pushed her. But while “the court does not seek to minimize or disregard the pain plaintiff felt from these injuries,” the judge decided that said injuries did not meet the requirements set forth by the American Disabilities Act (ADA).

In a statement, Daniels’ lawyer Ron Zambrano expressed disappointment with the ruling. “While we respect the court and the judicial process, we believe the decision improperly weighed evidence that should have been evaluated by a jury,” he said. “We disagree that an employee twisting her ankle and limping while trying to work does not meet the legal standard of a disability under the ADA. These are important issues because these claims often depend on how a jury evaluates the full workplace environment, the surrounding context, and disputed facts. We respectfully disagree with the Court’s approach and are considering appropriate next steps.”

Daniels’ lawsuit followed on the heels of a separate suit by three former backup dancers who accused the Grammy winner of creating a hostile work environment through sexual, racial and religious harassment. The lawsuit further claimed that the singer, an outspoken advocate for body positivity and self-love, berated a dancer for gaining weight, pressured another dancer to touch a nude performer at a club in Amsterdam and subjected several dancers to an “excruciating” 12-hour audition after making false accusations that they drank while working.

The fat-shaming claim was dismissed by a judge in December 2025. In a social media post celebrating that dismissal, Lizzo said she is “not settling” and will fight “every single claim until the truth comes out”. The case remains ongoing.

“I could have settled, but I’m a woman who is not afraid of the truth coming out, so I’m continuing to fight,” she told the Today show in June. “I’m really excited for all of the claims to be dropped and for us to just move forward.”

Nigel Farage is facing questions about why he claimed his finances were the subject of a second standards investigation, as he was sworn in again as Clacton’s MP.

The Reform UK leader said when he resigned in July that the standards system had become a “political tool” because “yet another standards investigation is under way” into his finances.

He argued he wanted the people of Clacton to be the judge of his actions, rather than “the establishment”, after revelations in the Sunday Times that his friend and convicted fraudster George Cottrell had paid for social media work, accommodation and security before the 2024 election.

However, it is understood the parliamentary standards commissioner had not launched another investigation or widened the scope of the existing one at that point.

The commissioner is believed still not to have decided whether to widen the inquiry as recently as two weeks ago, when it was reopened as Farage was returned as MP for Clacton with an increased majority.

The commissioner launched his first investigation in May into Farage’s £5m gift from the Thailand-based donor Christopher Harborne before the 2024 election, which was not declared on the MPs’ register of interests and was first revealed by the Guardian. Initially Farage said the money was given to pay for his security, then he described it as a reward for campaigning for Brexit.

At least two complaints were then submitted in July about Farage’s funding by Cottrell. Farage called a byelection on 7 July and the initial investigation was paused.

However, Westminster sources said the standards commissioner was assessing information. There is no official confirmation that he has widened his inquiry to include the Cottrell donations, and the commissioner’s list of investigations currently only includes the one launched in May.

The sources said the commissioner wanted to see further evidence that Farage had broken the rules in relation to donations from Cottrell in the year before the 2024 election, including his payments for social media work.

Farage has maintained the videos were personal and likened his public role before that election to the work of an influencer. However, a number of the videos were political in nature, campaigning on immigration issues.

Critics say these should be declared under rules that say donations related to politics must be registered in the 12 months before an MP is elected.

The standards commissioner declined to comment on the status of the investigation into Farage and whether any decision had been made on widening the inquiry.

If there is no second investigation nor a widened scope, it is possible the first investigation into Farage could conclude sooner than expected. The Times reported in July that the Reform leader would be interviewed within weeks but the byelection paused the process.

In relation to the investigation, Alex Burghart, the shadow chancellor of the duchy of Lancaster, said: “The questions surrounding Nigel Farage’s £5m gift from Christopher Harborne and the donations from George Cottrell simply aren’t going away.

“Farage has already tried to run away with his farcical byelection in Clacton, but he can no longer hide from these questions. He needs to come clean … The public deserves answers and Farage can’t keep hiding.”

If the standards commissioner finds a breach of the rules, and the separate standards committee of MPs recommends a sanction of more than 10 days of suspension from parliament, Farage could end up facing a second byelection.

As he was sworn in again on Tuesday, Farage told GB News that he planned to spend less time in parliament and would be leaving more Westminster work to [the Reform deputy leader] “Richard Tice and the gang” while he goes on a tour of the country.

Farage will set his priorities for the year ahead when he gives his speech at the Reform party conference at the end of this week, where he is expected to attempt to draw a line under the focus on his finances.

Burnham blames Brexit and Thatcher for ‘wrong turns’ in first Commons speech as PM

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 18:52:32 GMT

The prime minister said Britain needed to be brutally honest about the mistakes of the last 40 years of UK politics

Andy Burnham has blamed Brexit and Margaret Thatcher for a decade of low growth in the UK, arguing that Britain needs to be brutally honest about having taken “a series of wrong turns” in the last 40 years.

In his first Commons appearance since he took over as prime minister about six weeks ago, Burnham told MPs he wanted to build a new sense of optimism so “we can make this next decade better than the last”.

The British people wanted “much more substantial change” on the big issues facing the country, he said. “That is what I will bring. Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be. Things are not working as they should.”

The UK economy has taken a 6% hit from the effects of Brexit, according to economists’ analysis of internal Bank of England data on thousands of British companies since the referendum a decade ago.

Shortly before Burnham’s Commons address, Keir Starmer, his predecessor, announced he would stand down as an MP, saying he wanted to focus on international affairs, triggering a tricky first byelection test for Burnham in a seat where the Greens fancy their chances.

The cabinet was told on Tuesday that the government will have three key priorities: cutting costs of essentials like childcare and mortgages; the regeneration of communities; and greater public control of water, housing and energy.

Burnham’s deputy, Louise Haigh, will lead task forces on each of those issues, the Guardian understands. He told his ministers they must be “relentless” in fulfilling his priorities.

His plans are set against a tough economic backdrop. The chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s fiscal rules could be halved at his first budget if the current global bond sell-off persists, and economists warn mortgage rates could go up this autumn.

In his Commons statement, the prime minister also:

Hinted that he would commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, saying he had appointed John Healey as his chancellor “precisely because” of his position on military spending.

Signalled he is open to renationalising the water industry – saying he is looking at “all possible solutions”, as the sector is a “leaking monument” to the failures of privatisation.

Opened the door to looking again at electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto. “I do believe there needs to be a mandate to make that change. There are different views in this house, but I believe we will need to get a consensus at the next election. And if there is that consensus, then a change can be made in the next parliament.”

Announced he would attend the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey and continue pursuing green energy – but that he would be “pragmatic” on supply, amid expectations he will approve the Jackdaw gasfield. “The mistake is saying it’s got to be one or the other for political purposes. The truth is, it’s going to have to be both.”

Flanked by Healey and Haigh, Burnham suggested to MPs the Brexit vote had been a response to “a series of wrong turns” made by Britain in the 1980s onwards, that were then compounded by leaving the EU.

The prime minister, whose Makerfield constituency voted for Brexit, has previously argued it would be a mistake to rerun the referendum – but has said that he wants the UK to rejoin in his lifetime. He suggested the next UK-EU reset summit could take place in November.

“Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country de-industrialised. Austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this,” he said during a three-hour stint in the Commons.

“And then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration. Change begins with honesty … Unless we are blunt about what went wrong, we won’t turn things around.

“Far from taking back control, the combination of these policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain for 40 years. Too many places have been drifting.”

He added: “The government I lead will be relentless in giving people and places what they were promised 10 years ago: ownership and control, and from that control over their destiny comes change and growth.”

The Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, accused the prime minister of “living in the past” over his attacks on Thatcher – who was in power from 1979 to 1990 – and four decades of neoliberalism.

“The year is 2026 but the prime minister said everything has gone wrong since the 1980s, still complaining about Margaret Thatcher. He is talking about a woman who became prime minister before I was born. He is living in the past and he wants to take us back to the 1970s.”

In the statement, Burnham paid tribute to Starmer, saying he had created a platform for Britain to be fixed, “and we will use it well”. Just hours earlier, his predecessor announced he would be standing down as MP for Holborn and St Pancras, despite saying in July he planned to stay on until the next election.

“It has been a huge honour and privilege to represent the best constituency in the country,” he said. “I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs, including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.”

Starmer’s seat, long seen as a safe Labour hold, is likely to be targeted by the Greens, potentially for party leader Zack Polanski, who is a London Assembly member. “Zack has always made it clear he would like to be a London MP. London has been his home for over 20 years,” a Green spokesperson said.

Just as the Makerfield byelection was seen as a proof of concept for whether Burnham could beat Reform, so the north London seat will test his progressive credentials. Labour will choose its candidate to replace Starmer next Wednesday under an accelerated selection timetable.

Burnham’s first taskforce will be charged with finding bold solutions to tackling “everyday rip-offs”. The cost of living taskforce will look at parking charges, subscription traps and cowboy builders, as well as long-term fixed pressures like mortgages, food costs and childcare.

The second will assess the affordability and practicalities of the state taking over failing essential services. Burnham believes that greater state control of essential services is the surest way to economic growth, avoiding the potential for ineffective profiteering by privatised services.

Government sources said that Haigh, the first secretary of state, wanted to look beyond sectors such as transport and explore serious opportunities for greater state control in areas like energy and housing – if it would bring down ordinary people’s costs.

The third taskforce will explore more radical ideas to revive crumbling high streets and impoverished districts, such as potential legislative options on houses in multiple occupation, as well as devolving powers to mayors and councils to help them regenerate local high streets.

A century from Maia Bouchier led England to a record women’s one‑day international run chase against Ireland at Grace Road on Tuesday, as they passed their target of 282 with six wickets and 71 balls to spare.

Bouchier missed out on selection for the T20 World Cup in June, but she remains a key part of England’s ODI plans as they try to build a new team following the retirements of Heather Knight and Tammy Beaumont.

Bouchier initially played second fiddle to Sophia Dunkley, who smashed 73 from 61 balls. But when Dunkley drove a return catch to the leg-spinner Cara Murray, it was left to Bouchier to bring up the three-figure score which was there for the taking against a helpless-looking Irish attack.

“Obviously gutting that I missed out on the World Cup,” Bouchier said. “But it was a really good way to play some more cricket [for Hampshire] and take the positives instead of the negatives. There’s a lot of opportunity next year which is really exciting. If I can just put my name out there and score those big runs, I hope that will take care of itself.”

England are contesting the three ODIs against Ireland without several key players – the regular captain Nat Sciver‑Brunt remains injured, while Lauren Bell, Danni Wyatt-Hodge, Sophie Ecclestone, Amy Jones and Linsey Smith are being rested. The series therefore provides an intriguing glimpse into the future, with the 21‑year‑old Jodi Grewcock batting at No 3 and the off‑spinning all‑rounder Mady Villiers making a white‑ball return after two years in the wilderness.

Grewcock failed to shine, bowled through the gate by the wily Murray for nine, while Bouchier holed out to long-on for 104. But Alice Capsey and Freya Kemp continued the momentum with a flurry of boundaries, ensuring England romped home.

The Ireland captain, Gaby Lewis, said: “It’s very disappointing. You’re battling against world-class players who really took on the powerplay, and they put our bowlers off their lines and built that pressure for our bowlers and we struggled with our execution.”

Earlier there were half-centuries for three Ireland players – Amy Hunter, Lewis and Rebecca Stokell – although Stokell’s original celebrations proved premature when the umpires ruled that a boundary over fine leg had come off her helmet and counted as leg-byes. She was then given out lbw to England’s stand‑in captain, Charlie Dean, but had the decision overturned on review, allowing her to reach the milestone for real with 10 balls left of the innings.

There remain concerns about England’s lack of bowling depth. Without Bell and Ecclestone, England’s attack – spearheaded by Issy Wong and Lauren Filer – lacked penetration, allowing Lewis and Hunter to stroll to a 136-run partnership for the second wicket.

The Guardian view on the global bond shock: Andy Burnham should take note

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 18:15:24 GMT

Japan’s collision with Donald Trump reveals the dilemma facing Britain: economic independence is becoming more necessary – and more tricky to achieve

“In the midst of every crisis lies great opportunity” is an aphorism attributed to Albert Einstein. It seems to be taken to heart by this White House. A global bond sell-off sparked by an inflationary shock emanating from the Gulf sees Donald Trump seeking to restrict plans by Japan – a longtime ally – to reduce dependence on an international system America dominates.

Japan, a successful exporter, has long done things its own way. For years Tokyo saw off the bond vigilantes despite running enormous deficits and a huge national debt. It demonstrated how a central bank could fund public spending and keep interest rates low if it wanted to. This economic model was refined by Shinzo Abe, Japan’s longest-serving prime minister. However, this week the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, called time on Abenomics as his price for US help in stabilising Japan’s currency. Japan’s Sanae Takaichi, he indicated, should shrink her $2tn spending plans and raise rates. Abenomics did not suddenly become financially impossible. It became inconvenient to the issuer of the world’s reserve currency.

Kevin Warsh, Mr Trump’s handpicked chair of the US Federal Reserve, has made it clear that he will raise interest rates in response to inflationary pressures. Others will be expected to follow. In Japan’s case, Washington fears that a yen crisis could become a bond crisis. A disorderly rout could force Japan into ever larger currency interventions – and repeated appeals to Washington to help defend the yen. If such aid proved inadequate, Tokyo could end up defending its currency by dumping US treasury bonds – of which it has more than a trillion dollars worth – and put upward pressure on the very yields Mr Bessent is trying to contain. His demand that Tokyo raise rates and cut spending is not just about Japanese inflation. It is about trying to prevent Tokyo’s adjustment to the Iran shock being exported on to America’s balance sheet.

Mr Burnham’s first Commons speech as prime minister suggests an expansive programme to raise living standards and get growth through regional reindustrialisation. This, he says, rests on the “bedrock” of fiscal responsibility. Mr Burnham promises an activist state to deal with four decades of underinvestment and privatisation. But retaining Rachel Reeves’s fiscal framework leaves his investment plans hostage to interest rates, debt costs and feverish “headroom” speculation. Turmoil in global bond markets could derail his industrial strategy before it gets going.

Japan’s big bazooka spending programme was meant to do what Mr Burnham now says Britain must do on a smaller scale: use the state to rebuild productive capacity, reduce strategic dependence and build its export competitiveness. Tokyo has the fiscal firepower, a central bank able to dominate the sovereign bond market and trillions invested overseas. The UK government could mimic that and change its fiscal rules, its relationship to the Bank of England and the way investment is accounted for.

But Japan is Mr Burnham’s problem writ large. The war in Iran made it urgent to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. But the conflict’s inflationary shock makes that objective harder – though not impossible – to pursue. Mr Trump’s team is using its leverage over the yen to restrain Tokyo’s plan to make Japan resilient to external price spikes. Mr Burnham has been forewarned: the Gulf inflation shock wave bolsters the argument for economic independence while making the means of achieving it more difficult.

The Guardian view on loneliness: the decline in friendship leaves gen Z exposed

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 18:14:13 GMT

Problems with housing, jobs and technology have dented young people’s confidence in the future and each other

Hope, Raye told a crowd at Reading festival on Saturday, was the theme of a set inspired by her second album. Having established through a show of hands that most of the audience had just done their GCSEs, and after recounting her own rocky road to stardom, the 28-year-old singer led a series of upbeat chants of “it’s gonna be all right”.

For anyone who thinks adolescence ought to be a time of optimism, it was a charming spectacle. But a new report from the Institute for Public Policy Research thinktank paints a much gloomier picture. Building on existing evidence of declining wellbeing, such as Alan Milburn’s report on young people who are not in education or work, the IPPR’s researchers found that 11- to 24-year-olds in England (gen Z and older members of gen Alpha) are increasingly lonely. They have fewer friends than young people in the past and are less contented with those they do have. One in 20 say that they have no friends at all. A series of interviews produced worrying evidence of their lack of confidence about the future.

They also spoke about problems with concentration that they associated with social media. When asked what they do in their spare time, the most common answer was “doomscrolling”. But while the authors point to “deference to unaccountable tech oligarchs” as one way in which politicians have let younger generations down, their analysis goes wider. It includes housing costs, a shortage of entry-level jobs, student debt, austerity and the Covid-19 pandemic. They conclude that the social contract with youth is broken and needs fixing.

This is a deliberately broad-brush study that focuses on what the 10 million 11- to 24-year-olds in England have in common. But it does not gloss over socioeconomic differences. The steepest falls in life satisfaction over the past decade have been in deprived areas; housing is a far more serious blockage on the route to independence for those without family wealth. Noting that the average deposit has risen to £78,000, the report states that “owning a home before your mid-30s has become close to an inherited trait”. With social housing all but impossible to access for most young adults, too many are either stuck with parents or in privately rented flats. Labour has already taken steps to boost the supply of new homes, but must do more to improve young people’s prospects. It is a national scandal that so many are locked out.

Adolescence is a complicated time of life, and there is an echo of Sigmund Freud’s idea of “ordinary unhappiness” in the report’s reference to the “ordinary challenges” of growing up. It is hard to leave school and parents, and decide what to do next. This is one reason why supportive peer relationships are so important, and why research on friendship is worthwhile.

But while gen Z and gen Alpha deserve attention, their problems should not be viewed in isolation. The weakening of the social fabric around them can be seen as part of a wider pattern that the IPPR rightly links to neoliberalism’s assault on collectivism. There is no single policy lever that can be pulled to mend the missing threads. But governments and councils are far from helpless. Housing, job-market reforms (including limits on AI in recruitment) and a stronger overall emphasis on generational fairness would all make the world a friendlier place for under-25s.

Germany blames Russia for drone attack at Leipzig airport

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 18:01:07 GMT

Government says ‘dangerous behaviour’ is part of effort by Moscow to cause damage with hybrid attacks

The German government has blamed Russia for the drone attack on Leipzig airport last month, calling it “dangerous behaviour” and part of a systematic and concerted effort by Moscow to “cause great damage” through a large number of hybrid attacks.

The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, and the foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, ended weeks of speculation and the government’s hesitancy to blame Russia, saying in a brisk 10-minute briefing in Berlin that all indications were the Russian state had provided the knowhow and equipment for the planned attack and “low-level agents” were recruited to carry it out.

A drone loaded with explosives was discovered at Leipzig/Halle airport on 4 August attached to the wing of a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane used to transport weapons to Ukraine. It failed to detonate but could have caused a catastrophe, authorities said.

Russia will face a package of penalty measures, Wadephul said, adding that the German government saw “a need for appropriate and necessary action in this situation”. It would respond “to this hybrid attack in Leipzig with proportionate and measured, yet equally resolute, action”, he said. “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.”

He added: “The dangerous behaviour of the Russian Federation is part of attempts at destabilisation, disinformation, threats, sabotage and aggression.” Berlin regretted the abysmal state of its relations with Moscow, he said.

The EU expressed “full solidarity” with Germany over the attack, and Nato assured Berlin that it would defend its members.

The Russian ambassador had been summoned to the foreign ministry at that very moment to be informed of the consequences, Wadephul said. The Russian consulate in Bonn will be closed later this month, and Russian House, a sprawling cultural and science institute in the centre of Berlin, which is alleged to house Russian spies and to have been the launchpad for a number of hybrid attacks carried out in Germany over the past few years, is to be turned out of its rented building.

A clampdown on Russia’s shadow fleet – illegal ships carrying Russian oil and other supplies in the Baltic and North seas – is also planned. Sweden and Finland track and disrupt the shadow fleet but Germany does not, so vessels regularly opt to sail via German waters in its foreign economic zones.

New lists of people on a blacklist would be drawn up and tighter border controls of Russians entering Germany would be carried out, Wadephul said.

Parallel to these moves, Berlin is also backing the European Commission’s 22nd package of sanctions, to cover a further 1,600 companies and organisations with a Russian connection.

Responding to ​Germany’s announcement, ‌Russia’s foreign ministry ​spokesperson, ​Maria Zakharova, said Moscow would respond to what she called Berlin’s “anti-Russian action”, according to the Interfax news agency.

The government has previously said it does not intend to directly involve Nato by invoking article 4 of the alliance. However, its Nato and European partners were informed about the investigation and agreed on the planned consequences, Wadephul confirmed.

The Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, promised “full solidarity” with Berlin.

Rutte said Berlin had put forward clear evidence of Moscow’s role in the “hybrid attack” and welcomed the measures announced in response, while von der Leyen vowed to “keep the EU united despite these escalating and serious acts”.

Tuesday’s announcement marks the first time the German government has concretely named Russia as responsible for the attack.

It marks the lowest point in decades for relations between Russia and the EU’s largest member, which had already plunged after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

This weekend will see a critical election in the eastern states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg Vorpommern, in which the war in Ukraine and relations with Russia have been a focal point.

The far-right populist Alternative für Deutschland, which is pushing a pro-Russia agenda as it seeks to win an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt, has accused the government of double standards over its treatment of Russia. Urging the government to prove Russia’s involvement in the Leipzig incident earlier this week, it said the same rigour should be applied to investigations into the attack on the Nord Stream pipeline, for which Ukraine is alleged to have been responsible.

The drone in the Leipzig incident was carrying 600g of explosives and was discovered in the security area of ​​the airport close to Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes on the night of 4-5 August. The explosive device detonator appeared to have failed. A second drone was believed to have been part of the planned attack but investigators have since thrown doubt on that theory. Traces of the military explosive hexogen were found on the edge of the airport on 14 August along with a further drone, investigators confirmed. Had the devices exploded they could have caused a catastrophe, German officials said.

The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, who last week said whoever was behind the attack “will pay”, did not attend the briefing to the press and public on Tuesday.

Konstantin von Notz, the Green party’s security policy expert and commissioner for intelligence oversight, criticised the government before the announcement for what he described as its failure to stand up to Vladimir Putin in the face of the growing hybrid threat from Russia. “The federal government must finally stop being hesitant, reticent and timid. Things must be called by their name, and decisive action must be taken,” he said in an interview with the RND network.

Even within his own Christian Democratic Union party, Merz has faced calls to be tougher towards Russia. On Tuesday, the party’s foreign policy expert, Roderich Kiesewetter, urged the chancellor to take a tougher line against Russia, accusing successive governments of exercising “extreme caution with regard to Russian state terrorism on German soil”.

Citing sources in German intelligence, Bild Zeitung said direct connections had been made by investigators between other drone and explosives finds and incidents in Germany and across Europe, including in Romania, Italy, Poland, Bulgaria and the UK. A cache of weapons discovered recently in a Berlin forest are thought to be connected to Russian activities in Romania. Investigators in various countries are believed to be working in parallel with each other.

Five people are being held on suspicion of murder after a newborn baby died from stab wounds in Sheffield on Sunday.

Police officers found the girl at a property in Holywell Heights, in the Wincobank area of Sheffield, while responding to reports concerning her safety just before 6am on Sunday. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

Seven people were arrested on suspicion of murder. Two have since been bailed. A postmortem examination found the girl had died from stab wounds, police said on Tuesday.

DCI Tom Woodward of South Yorkshire police said first responders, paramedics and detectives now leading the murder investigation had been profoundly affected by the baby’s death.

“We recognise this is deeply distressing for those who would have loved to have a chance to love this baby girl, for the emergency services who responded and for the community who will inevitably be shocked by this incident,” Woodward said. “Our commitment to this little girl is unwavering.

“We will confront every difficult and distressing challenge and pursue every line of inquiry with determination and care to secure justice for her.”

Woodward said the investigation was fast-moving and asked the community to “avoid speculating around the circumstances of this tragic incident”.

“We know the local community will hold her in their thoughts and support us as we work through this complex investigation,” he said.

Five murder suspects remain in custody after police were granted a warrant for further detention, a force spokesperson said on Tuesday. A 26-year-old and a 37-year-old have been released on bail.

Specialist search officers will remain in the Holywell Heights area as the investigation continues.

South Yorkshire police said anyone with information about the case should contact them online or call 101, quoting incident number 993 on 30 August 2026. People can also report information to the independent charity Crimestoppers.

One last Starmer U-turn and it’s over to Andy ‘less policy, more vibes’ Burnham

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 17:43:43 GMT

What former PM could resist upstaging the new one hours before his first dispatch box appearance in 16 years?

UK politics live – latest updates

No good deed goes unpunished. Or any deed for that matter. It was only a few weeks ago that Keir Starmer was insisting he would remain an MP until the next general election. So we should all probably have guessed that he would be off at the earliest opportunity. U-turns were a distinguishing feature of his two years in office.

And what former prime minister could resist upstaging the new one hours before his first appearance at the government dispatch box for 16 years? Especially when the new one had been plotting his downfall for at least a year. It’s what everyone would have wanted. Right?

Not that Starmer was framing his decision in these terms. This wasn’t a simple matter of revenge. Or a need to still feel relevant. These were the last things on his mind. Keir has only ever wanted what was best for Andy. But he now had his own life to think about. And why tell the world about it on a bank holiday weekend when nobody is paying attention to the news, when you can wait till the first day of the new parliamentary session and grab the headlines?

Keir said in his statement that he had really meant it when he said he would remain MP for Holborn and St Pancras, but it had only latterly dawned on him that this would be incompatible with his ambitions to be a player on the international stage. Please spare us from another Tony Blair. There again, Keir is unlikely to be invited on to Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. He should use that as his calling card.

In truth though, Keir had never seemed that interested in representing his constituents or serving as a backbencher. He’s not like Theresa May, who remained, sad and alone, on the backbenches for years after being removed by her fellow Tory MPs. Nor does he have the inclination to follow the example of Rishi Sunak and turn up to work every couple of months or so. Perhaps he is more in need of the money that might come from leaving the Commons. And for a prime minister, Starmer had always seemed curiously uninterested in politics. So much so that you wondered why he had ever become a politician. It probably just felt like a normal career progression.

Meanwhile, Burnham could probably live with being pushed down the news agenda for the day. He had mixed feelings about Keir’s decision. In the long run, life would probably be easier without Starmer around to cause trouble, but the downside was a potentially tricky byelection. Especially if Zack Polanski chose to stand for the Greens. And never forgetting an almost obligatory appearance from Count Binface. But this would all be for another day. Right now he had a Commons statement on the government’s direction to negotiate.

First, it was a time to be gracious. After saying he would be following his predecessors in reaffirming his commitment to Ukraine, Burnham spent the first few minutes of his speech praising Keir. He had given a lifetime of service, had created a platform for change and had made the Labour party electable again. You could almost believe he was sorry to see him go.

Then we got to the heart of the matter. Less policy, more positive vibes. Andy hadn’t come to the Commons to pick a fight with the opposition. Rather he hoped they would listen to him, realise he was right and then work with him. It was a big ask – especially with Kemi Badenoch as leader of the opposition, and so disinhibited she can pick a fight with herself – but probably worth a go. Just on the off-chance. Andy wasn’t going to give in to point scoring without at least attempting to offer a hand of friendship.

We ran through a wishlist. The climate crisis. Surely no one was going to argue with that, not after the emergency in Nepal and the hottest summer on record? You could sense Kemi longing to intervene, to say that net zero was a con. It took all her self-control not to make an idiot of herself.

Burnham began. Small boat crossings down: tick. More prison places for the right kinds of prisoner: fingers crossed. Defence: that would be sorted later, somehow. The cost of living: we need to be honest that the country has been in decline since 1980.

“I will be relentless about achieving change and growth,” he said. First he had taken Manchester, now he takes the UK. A Britain that would work for all of us. A desire to keep upbeat. The country had had enough of being told it was falling apart. Let the good times roll. Ish.

We can make the next decade better than the last, he concluded. That suddenly didn’t feel quite so comforting. I mean, the next 10 years can hardly be worse than the shitshow of the last 10 years. Can it? Can it? Please. We need some reason to get out of bed each morning.

As for Kemi, let’s also be generous. She did at least try to sound as if she had listened and would work at doing better to find common ground. Though she couldn’t do this without sounding vaguely patronising. As if Burnham was some sort of ingenu who had been parachuted into Westminster without a clue as to what he was doing, and she was the old lag who had seen it all before.

“I’ll be gentle,” she said, as if Andy was a halfwit, before going on to say that almost everything he had said was totally wrong. The decline in small boat crossings was just a coincidence. Margaret Thatcher had taken office before she had been born, so therefore anything Thatcher had done was totally irrelevant. Kemi thinks the world began with her birth and will end with her death. The narcissist’s fantasy. She promised to help when it was in the national interest, but the national interest would only be served if she was in charge.

Andy tried to let her down gently. He was here to help too. Kemi had gone to Rome and fantasised that Giorgia Meloni had told her not to do a deal with Reform. He would happily have saved her the air fare and told her the same thing. Then he took her by surprise – by pointing out she had just picked a shadow chancellor who had been the author of Liz Truss’s mini-budget. Kemi looked a little shell-shocked. She is going to have to up her game before tomorrow’s prime minister’s questions.

UK politics live – latest updates

In Keir Starmer’s north London constituency, full of pretty pubs and elegant townhouses, few tears were being shed at the news of his departure as its MP.

One man nursing a pint outside a pub in Kentish Town simply remarked “good” when informed his MP had quit. He added: “I thought he was very nice before he became prime minister; I met him a few times. But he messed the country up and screwed over pensioners.”

Annie, a 30-year-old doctor having a coffee and pastry on a bench near the tube station, said: “I think everyone here wanted him to leave. He’s had a rough time of it, sure, but we have all had enough of him.”

Dominic Ford, a 75-year-old pensioner reading a book outside the Parakeet pub, was more sympathetic. “I think he’s sensible. It would have been tough for him to sit behind the new prime minister,” he said. “He’s a very nice, honest guy, and he was very visible around here. We used to see him going to the Arsenal with his son. He was a good local MP, and very honest. I felt very sorry for him when he resigned as prime minister.”

On a quiet street among rows of pastel-coloured terrace houses is the Pineapple, Starmer’s favourite pub. It is out of the way of the high street, and the former prime minister is frequently seen there drinking a pint.

He may have become tired of his pub visits being documented in various newspapers, because when the Guardian visited and asked regulars what they thought about him stepping down, the bar staff firmly said that questions about Starmer were not allowed. Perhaps this commitment to discretion is why he has referred to the pub as his “church” and “the best pub in land”.

Starmer announced his departure as prime minister in June after several unpopular choices including making Peter Mandelson, a friend of Jeffrey Epstein, ambassador to the US. On Tuesday, Starmer told the Camden New Journal he wanted to focus on international affairs and “pass the baton to a successor”.

Starmer had previously said he would seek to serve out his term as a backbench MP, and his decision to quit will spark a byelection. The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, is understood to be considering a run for the seat.

Laura Hyland, a 67-year-old artist, said she was pleased Starmer was stepping down and that she welcomed the prospect of a byelection. “He gave very little support for Palestine, and I hope Andy Burnham will be more supportive. Arresting people for holding signs saying ‘I support Palestine Action’ was disgraceful.”

Anita, 52, was doing her shopping on the high street. She also welcomed Starmer standing down, and said: “I can’t stand him. He was completely useless and I am glad he stood down.”

Russia targets Ukraine’s rail network as war enters deadly new phase

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 17:23:15 GMT

Six employees killed on Tuesday after Moscow escalates attacks on infrastructure and Ukrainian capital

Russia has opened a deadly new phase in its war against Ukraine by deliberately targeting the country’s railway network, with six employees killed on Tuesday in the latest strikes on Kyiv.

Ukraine’s state-owned railway company, Ukrzaliznytsia, said its workers died when a ballistic missile plunged into a locomotive depot. The Russians hit other railway facilities, it added, during a massive bombardment of Kyiv and the Kyiv region. At least 12 people died, with a dozen wounded, including three children.

“An unbearably difficult night for the entire railway family. Railway staff have been working at the scene since early this morning. The attack has caused significant damage. Rescue workers are still putting out a number of fires,” said Ukrzaliznytsia’s chair, Oleksandr Pertsovsky.

The grim strike took place as Russia escalated its attacks on the Ukrainian capital. It has carried out continuous raids for six days, beginning last week, in an attempt to disrupt daily life and demoralise the city’s inhabitants. The onslaught took place hours before Ukrainian children began a new school year.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, 58 railway staff have been killed and at least 318 injured. One wounded railway employee, Volodymyr, was taken to hospital on Tuesday, with people urged to donate blood if they were B positive – his group. “Our colleagues are by his side,” Ukrzaliznytsia said, adding it would support victims’ families.

Ukraine’s railway network is Europe’s third largest, with 15,000 miles (24,000km) of track. It has been a lifeline for the country’s wartime civilians, transporting four million people and an estimated 120,000 pets. It has brought world leaders to Kyiv, including Joe Biden and Andy Burnham, who arrived last week on an overnight service from Poland.

Serhih Leshchenko, a member of Ukrzaliznytsia’s supervisory board, described the railway as the “backbone of Ukraine’s economy”. It was the main logistical supplier for the country’s army and industry, and every week transported 600,000 people, he told the Guardian. With 170,000 workers, it was also Ukraine’s biggest company.

For these reasons Russia was trying to destroy railways, he added. In the first year of the war it attacked bridges, which could be easily replaced. Next, it targeted rails and electricity substations. Ukraine then switched to using diesel engines. This year, Russia started “direct attacks on civilian locomotives”, he said – an insidious tactic, at a time when Ukraine is short of air defences.

Several drivers have been killed and locomotives targeted inside depots. Leshchenko said that if a Shahed drone came within 50km of a train, it had to be evacuated, and could only continue once the threat has passed. So far this year Russia has hit the network more than 1,500 times – a higher figure than in the whole of 2025. Overall, 249 carriages and 492 locomotives have been damaged.

Once known for their punctuality, trains now suffer regular delays, sometimes lasting as long as 12 to 15 hours. Amid air raid sirens, passengers are forced to disembark and take cover, including during winter. Writing on Facebook, the Ukrainian journalist Tetiana Zaiets described how she hid in April when Russian drones flew overhead.

“It was hell. The train stopped at night somewhere in central Ukraine. I don’t even know the name of the town. Half asleep, I just heard the conductor say ‘evacuation’. We took only our personal belongings and valuables with us. It was raining outside. Thank you to the conductors for handing out blankets,” she posted.

She added: “That’s how we held out for two hours. While kamikaze drones were buzzing overhead, we crawled under a goods wagon. The last carriage in the train was full of children. They were being taken back from hospital. They were crying in their sleep. I thought I’d ended up in some sort of horror film. But no, this is our life.”

Since the incident, Zaiets said she was too frightened to travel by train. “Until the war is over, I won’t be using it,” she said, stressing she respected Ukraine’s “courageous” railway workers.

Last week, an enemy drone hit a train in the Odesa region with 600 people on board, including 15 children. “The train was stopped, we were kicked out. We heard explosions, everything was burning. It was scary,” one passenger, Andriy, told the website Suspline.

Another passenger, Eva, said she was evacuated twice, and “dropped off in a field”. “We sat there and heard something flying. Then we saw a drone very close by.” She managed to collect her belongings and was eventually picked up by a bus, she said.

Leshchenko admitted the Russian strikes were hurting Ukraine’s economy and had slowed the export of grain from its under-fire Black Sea ports. He said Kyiv needed air defences from western partners, so it could protects its trains from marauding missiles and drones. “If the whole country is under attack, they will attack railways for sure,” he said.

Up until this year more than 90% of Ukrainian trains arrived on time. This was in part down to the fact engines never go especially fast, rolling at 55mph. Carriages are clean and comfortable: the best way of getting around a vast country. Stewards look after night train customers and bring them morning tea in filigree holders. There is a trolley on day trains, and patchy wifi.

On international services, border guards scrutinise male passengers, while dogs roam up and down corridors. Since the invasion, men between 18 and 60 have been forbidden from leaving the country, with some exemptions. On trains from Kyiv to Przemyśl, a railway hub in eastern Poland, most travellers are women. Since 2022 about six million people have departed abroad, many exiting by train.

In recent days Russia has launched over 1,500 drones at Ukraine, 800 of them jet-fuel models, which are harder to shoot down. In the past, Moscow would send a swarm of drones a couple of times a week, usually at night. Now the attacks continue without a pause, with one or two drones dispatched every hour, paralysing ordinary life. Air raid sirens in Kyiv are non-stop.

Pertsovsky, Ukrzaliznytsia’s boss, described the loss of his employees on Tuesday as “terrible”. “We are in touch with their loved ones. Everyone is with them to get through this extremely difficult time. The night is bitter with impossibility,” he wrote.

Private equity keeps picking off London-listed firms – and Westminster barely notices

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 16:56:59 GMT

Bodycote is the latest FTSE 250 industrial company set to fall to an overseas bidder, despite the government’s talk of ‘reindustrialising’

The UK is in the business of “reindustrialising”, says the prime minister. If we are, an increasing portion of the activity will be under foreign ownership. Tuesday brought yet another overseas private equity swoop on a FTSE 250 industrial firm.

This time it’s the Macclesfield-based Bodycote, which describes itself as “the world’s largest service provider of heat treatment and specialist metallurgical technologies” – think, for example, processes and coatings to toughen jet engine blades. The buyer is the US buyout firm Veritas for £1.65bn or 940p a share, or £1.85bn including debt. Unless, that is, the rival bidder, CVC, a European private equity firm, comes back for another bite, which the market clearly thinks is a possibility because Bodycote’s shares closed at 955p.

The shame is that one cannot call 940p a stunning price. The valuation “does not appear particularly generous on a take-out basis”, said an analyst at the investment bank RBC, noting that it’s only 25% above the pre-bid level and the implied earnings valuation is merely in line with Bodycote’s 10-year average.

Indeed, nine-tenths of the “reasons for recommendation” section of Bodycote’s announcement sounded like an argument for doing the opposite. The passage started by saying how well the medium-term “optimise, perform, grow” strategy adopted in late 2024 was going. The plan was designed to find efficiencies and shift towards the expanding aerospace and defence sectors in pursuit of enviable financial metrics, including 20%-plus operating margins and a return on capital employed of 15 to 20% through the cycle. Good progress has been made, say the directors.

On the way, there has been enough spare cash for £120m of share buy-backs while maintaining a 38-year record of growing or maintaining the dividend. And the board is “confident in the ongoing execution” of the strategy, with “the majority of remaining improvements under Bodycote’s control”.

It was only in the last sentence that the company also said it was “mindful of increasing structural challenges in certain automotive and industrial markets together with macroeconomic uncertainties which create meaningful risk to delivery of Bodycote’s medium term financial targets”.

In other words, everything is going splendidly apart from a couple of risks – the sectoral one that the strategy is addressing, and the vague “macroeconomic uncertainty” that is a normal state of affairs for most companies. As a reason for accepting a bid at a mere 25% premium, it’s not terribly convincing.

In Bodycote’s defence, one might say the takeover price could yet improve if CVC, which said it was considering its position, comes back. More depressingly, one suspects Bodycote simply lives in that unloved sub-£5bn capitalisation part of the stock market that suffers from lack of attention and lack of regular inward capital flows. It is harder to fight for independence if the unspoken market pressure is to accept a bid for the sake of certainty.

The mini-tragedy in this case is that there was a wake-up call of sorts for investors when Apollo, yet another US private equity outfit, expressed an interest in bidding at 885p in the spring before walking away. The net result, though, is that Bodycote’s 54 years of London stock market life will come to an end one way or another. The company joins a long list of departees this year, which on Tuesday alone also took in telecoms company Gamma Communications for £1.1bn and the Scottish energy firm Capricorn for £292m.

Bodycote can still prosper under private equity ownership, of course. But a leading UK-based global specialist in its field, with 130 sites across 22 countries and 4,000 employees, is yet another bad one for the London market to lose.

The remedies for this rate of exodus have been trawled over in this column many times – and none are easy. But the process surely starts with recognition among politicians that “selling the family silver” – the title of a recent Peel Hunt report that calculated 150-plus bids for UK companies with a market value of more than £100m since the start of 2023 – may not be in the UK’s long-term economic interests. As ever, there was barely a squeak out of Westminster.

HRH Helch: the graffiti artist who left an indelible mark on high-rise Britain

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 16:50:46 GMT

He upset Queen Elizabeth II, defied the developers and had to scrap for every inch of graffiti space in a gentrified, urban landscape

Prolific UK graffiti artist Helch dies

You know you’ve made an impact when the headlines upon your death are filled with words like “iconic”, “infamous”, “world class” and “upset Queen Elizabeth II”. By that measure, graffiti supremo Helch made a pretty serious mark on the world.

He died this week, leaving behind a country pockmarked by his tag, a giant towering HELCH, though sometimes reduced to just a simple upper-case H. It was on railway bridges and motorway overpasses, on derelict buildings and decrepit high rises. From Bristol to London, Helch was everywhere. He was even on a railway viaduct on the way to Windsor Castle, in 60ft high white letters, “ruining” the view of poor old Elizabeth’s home and apparently leaving our late monarch in an absolute rage.

He was only 34, which almost doesn’t make sense. It feels like his work has been around for ever, as much a part of the British urban landscape as red phone boxes and uncollected bins. In a post on Instagram, his gallery, BSMT Space, said “an urban landscape without an H in it seems unfathomable”. And it’s true, that towering letter defined the look of late 2010s Britain.

Unlike 2000s graffiti megastars such as Ben Eine or Sweet Toof, who operated in an east London that was still filled with squalor and dereliction, a place not yet lost to the endless tide of gentrification, Helch’s England was a more polished, sanitised, pristine place. Where his predecessors could run rampant on the wastelands that would soon be newbuilds, Helch had to work in a city where every inch of grit and urban sprawl had been levelled to make way for high-rise apartment blocks no one lives in and co-working spaces no one works in. Helch had to scrap for every inch of graffiti space, he had to hunt out the final concrete canvases left in the new steel and glass urbanity of England.

When you see Helch, you’re seeing the remains of what the country was before the developers came in and sold it all on. When you see Helch, you’re seeing someone lay claim to the city you’re in, or the road you’re on.

It was a comfort to spot a Helch tag as you made your way through London or down some miserable motorway. It meant that someone had persevered, that individuality had won through against the odds. He was just some miscreant from Hayes in London doing what all great graffiti artists do best: leaving his mark, shaping the city in his own image, and upsetting the poshos in the process. But he leaves behind a towering legacy, one that’ll cost the developers a hell of a lot to scrub off, and that makes it worth every penny.

Burnham’s ambitious plans need room to breathe – and Westminster suffocates change

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 16:46:58 GMT

A summer on the road suited the prime minister’s open style, but now the walls of conventional politics are closing in

Nothing stays fresh for long in parliament and no one sounds normal. The air, thick with convention, suffocates originality, tuning every voice to the same Westminster pitch. The need to escape that climate is one reason why Andy Burnham quit his Commons seat to run for mayor of Greater Manchester. Or that is how he tells the story.

Returning after nearly a decade away, the prime minister says he wants to throw open the windows, let in some air. He thinks devolution can cultivate a healthier political culture. He intends to rebalance England’s centre of gravity with a power base in the new No 10 North.

The timing of Burnham’s arrival in Downing Street, just before the summer recess, suited those arguments. He replaced Keir Starmer, then promptly went on tour, posting chatty videos on social media, appearing as the antidote to a stuffy predecessor who, perhaps unfairly, had come to be seen as the archetypal Westminster mechanoid. Starmer, who today announced his intention to stand down as an MP, may find his authentic voice on the outside.

Meanwhile, Burnham has to bring his free-range prime minister act into the battery farm of the Commons. His mandate and legislative programme are inherited from the Starmer era. He is stuck with the same squeezed budgets in the same sluggish economy imperilled by the same turbulent global climate. His room for fiscal manoeuvre is constrained by Labour’s 2024 manifesto prohibition on broad-based tax rises and by the bond market’s punitive vigilance towards anything that looks like undisciplined spending.

In such conditions, politics is reduced to a zero-sum competition for scarce resources. Every promise made to satisfy the needs of one department or constituency contains an undeclared threat to deprive someone else.

Starmer’s leadership was ruined by many things, but few were as crippling as his failure to grapple with those dilemmas. He wouldn’t pick sides between irreconcilable demands within his cabinet. When his own ministers couldn’t read his political instincts or decrypt his priorities, the public had no chance. It was a recipe for paralysis, delivering a congealed gruel of continuity to voters who thought they had ordered piping hot change.

Determination not to repeat that mistake has shaped Burnham’s approach from his first moments in office. He declared a moral mission – the elimination of rough sleeping – before even crossing the threshold of No 10. He followed it up with emblematic policies to demonstrate that regime change brought a new focus on the cost of living.

No one in Downing Street pretends that capping bus fares or cutting VAT on fuel bills is enough to win affection from a sceptical public. The function of modest retail policies is to show that Labour, renewed by fresh leadership, has snapped out of despondency and started listening. A bounce in opinion polls suggests it is working.

But the transition from small-change symbols to big-ticket policy choices is not easy.

It is especially hard if the prime minister is conflict averse and prone to flights of empathic urgency. That is the hazard flagged by Burnham’s critics, based on observation of his career as a minister in the New Labour government and later as Manchester mayor. They are traits that generate spontaneous promises that later have to be diluted or retracted.

In June, Burnham got himself into just such a tangle over a commitment to compensate “Waspi women” who feel they were mistreated by the Department for Work and Pensions when their retirement age was raised. In May, he told a campaigner for party finance reform that he supported the principle of a cap on donations to guard against big money exerting undue influence in politics. A cap has been proposed as an amendment to the representation of the people bill, currently on its way through parliament. But the government, following trade union lobbying, is not backing the move.

The learning curve for any new prime minister is brutally steep.

Things that seem obvious from outside No 10 are revealed to be fearsomely complex. What seems compelling on the campaign trail can feel like a ruinous drain on time and political capital in government. The road is especially hard to navigate for those who arrive midterm, scrambling over unfinished and unpopular business bequeathed by an ousted predecessor.

The retreat from plans to free up prison capacity by releasing offenders early is a revealing case. Burnham understandably doesn’t want his first months in office marred by a parade of stories about villains walking free. But swerving unfriendly headlines isn’t a plan for reforming the justice system or growing its shrivelled budget.

Likewise, the prime minister’s appearance in Kyiv to celebrate Ukraine’s independence day, while important as a display of solidarity with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, came with no account of the sacrifices Britain faces as the price of ramping up its own defences against Russian aggression.

No one is better briefed on that challenge than the chancellor. As defence secretary, John Healey resigned from Starmer’s government in protest at the former prime minister’s reluctance to boost military spending. Relocated to the Treasury, he finds himself managing a downgrade in rearmament expectations ahead of the autumn budget.

The seasonal migration of politics back to parliament threatens a sudden narrowing of Burnham’s options. The prime minister has a theory to counter that threat. His argument is that devolution, as well as bringing fresh air to politics, spurs economic growth.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Loosening the dead hand of Whitehall control over public services is supposed to promote innovation and efficiency. A more responsive government, attuned to local market conditions, will unlock investment.

Assuming that can work, the mechanism is slow. Burnham accepts that it is a 10-year plan. The opposition calculates that the fiscal walls will close in on Labour a lot faster than that.

Kemi Badenoch thinks the economy is the issue that will rehabilitate Tory fortunes. To sharpen her attack on that front, she has sacked her shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, for insufficient pugnacity with the Treasury brief. His replacement, Andrew Griffith, is deemed more dynamic, a quality he once displayed in cheerleading for Liz Truss’s disastrous 2022 “mini-budget”.

In Badenoch’s view, Burnham is a “people-pleaser” who lacks the resolve to whip his MPs behind tough budget choices. He will rely on tax rises to pay for policies that the left see as essential maintenance to the social safety net and the right decry as profligate subsidy for fecklessness. The impossibility of feeding Labour’s big-government appetite with hands shackled by the 2024 manifesto will force the prime minister to seek his own mandate with an early election.

It is a plausible scenario. It is also unclear how the Tories get match fit on that timetable when they are running third in national polls. Badenoch’s personal ratings aren’t so bad, but she lacks insight into the reasons why so many voters think her party is unfit to govern. Discounting Griffith’s contamination by the Truss project when appointing a shadow chancellor is a symptom of that blind spot.

The Tories are flattered into feeling relevant by a sympathetic press and the constitutional crutch of official opposition status. In parliamentary arithmetic, the Conservatives still eclipse Reform UK.

Badenoch welcomes the enclosure of politics in the Commons chamber as much as the Labour leader resists it. The theatre of ritual combat is more her style than his. But the prime minister’s judgment is better in thinking voters are turned off by the whole spectacle. Burnham’s fresh manner has breathed life into a government that was expiring. It will take a different order of political skill to dispel the older miasma of cumulative failure that hangs heavy over Westminster.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

Assisted dying, palliative care and patient choice

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 16:44:04 GMT

Readers respond to an article by Dr Zubir Ahmed, who argued that better palliative care should be prioritised before assisted dying is legalised

I work as a renal physician, including on a transplant ward, so I will have had many of the same experiences as Zubir Ahmed, but I do not share his opinion about assisted dying (As a doctor, I say this: before we even consider assisted dying, fix how we care for the most vulnerable, 26 August).

It is universally agreed that patients with capacity should be able to make decisions about their treatment. Their decision is the one that matters if they have the ability to use and understand the relevant information and can communicate any decision they make. The doctor needs to explain possible options and their likely outcomes in as fair and balanced a manner as possible.

My daily reality, like that of just about everyone working in the NHS (and in other healthcare systems), involves doing the best I can within constrained resources. Palliative care provision and social services are not unique in being limited by the funding and staffing available. To say that patients should not be allowed to choose an assisted death until these reach some arbitrary standard defined as acceptable by Mr Ahmed or others begs many questions, and denies patients the ability to control their destiny now.

Kidney doctors such as me look after patients receiving artificial kidney (dialysis) treatment. This gives many years of good life to many, but when the burden of living has become too much, it is not uncommon for them to decide to stop their treatment. “Thank you for looking after me so well, and for letting me go,” is the most moving thing a patient has ever said to me.

It is essential that safeguards are incorporated into any legislation that allows a patient to choose an assisted death, but we must work out how to craft these safeguards, not deny patients a choice. Dr John FirthCambridge

Zubir Ahmed is right: palliative care needs investment and development before any further debate on assisted dying. Fear of dying badly has increased as NHS services have been squeezed more than ever. Lauren Edwards’ bill would fund assisted dying from the NHS budget, further eroding other services. Specialist palliative care across the UK is patchy, and palliative care in generalist services varies widely.

When a doctor says “there’s nothing more that can be done”, few patients know to ask for a specialist opinion. Sadly, many clinicians are unaware of developments in specialist palliative care and what can be done to relieve distress.

Without access to adequate symptom relief and competent psychological support, you won’t have a real choice when an assisted death is both offered and delivered by the very clinicians who could and should be working to improve your quality of life.

Research reveals that abuse of older people is common, but Edwards’ proposals will do nothing to detect abuse and coercion. The bill does not even require cases of assisted dying to be referred to a coroner; there will be no scrutiny of what really happened. In the last 15 years, 209 cases of assisted suicide have been referred to the director of public prosecutions; eight were prosecuted for homicide or other serious crime (almost 4%). How will these be detected under the current proposals? Andy Burnham is right. This bill is an untimely distraction. Sheila Hollins and Ilora FinlayHouse of Lords

As a former nurse and NHS midwife of more than 30 years, and now a full-time unpaid carer for my 88-year-old mother with dementia, I agree that a choice is only meaningful when a viable alternative exists.

We rightly worry that seriously ill or disabled people may feel they have become a burden. But we must confront what creates that fear: social care that is rationed, unaffordable or unavailable, while relatives are expected to fill every gap regardless of the cost to their own health and future.

I did not freely choose between continuing my career and becoming a full-time carer. I chose not to abandon my mother when suitable, reliable and affordable support was unavailable. Those are not the same thing.

I now provide considerably more than 35 hours of care each week for carer’s allowance of £86.45 – no more than £2.47 an hour at the minimum qualifying hours. Caring has cost me my salary, occupational-pension growth, financial independence and much of my freedom. Yet the state treats family care as an almost limitless free resource.

A humane social-care system would guarantee appropriate professional support to anyone who needs it, including people without relatives. Families could then choose whether to provide care, how much they could safely manage and when they needed to stop. Carers would receive proper financial support, pension protection and meaningful respite.

Before parliament creates another choice at the end of life, it must provide genuine choices throughout life. No vulnerable person should fear being a burden because adequate care is missing – and no relative should have to sacrifice their entire future to prevent that from happening. Jacqueline HyltonLeeds

A national commission on voting reform is essential

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 16:43:55 GMT

Sandy Martin and Joan Ruddock respond to an article on changes to the voting system

Your report (Labour MPs will push Burnham to back voting reform in first 100 days, 25 August) says: “The UK last rejected electoral reform in 2011 after a referendum [on] whether to change to an alternative vote system.” Many people do not realise that the referendum was not about a proportional electoral system. While the alternative vote is the best way to elect a single person, it really doesn’t work for a government.

That referendum was primarily a popularity contest for Nick Clegg, and it is no surprise that he was rejected, predominantly by people who were not aware of the actual terms of the referendum. A national commission, taking evidence from people across the country, followed by a general election that includes a manifesto commitment to changing the system, will be a far more reliable and accurate representation of the views of the British people than a referendum is ever likely to be. Sandy MartinChair, Labour Campaign for Electoral Reform

The amendment to the representation of the people bill on which you report is not the only thing to which the government will have to reply. By law they will have to respond to a parliamentary petition, initiated by me, which calls for the setting up of a national commission in line with the all-party parliamentary group’s proposal.

The petition states that it should be an independent, time limited, expert-led review to build consensus for changing the electoral system for parliament. Already more than 25,000 people have signed – twice the number required to trigger a government response. It is eagerly awaited. Joan RuddockFormer Labour MP and minister

Don’t dismiss ‘Woke 1.0’ – young people’s activism should be encouraged

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 16:43:49 GMT

Far from being crazy, the grandchildren of the radical ‘permissive’ generation are using their voices to fight for progress, as we taught them to do, writes Paul McGilchrist

I can’t help feeling that Nesrine Malik’s critique of “Woke 1.0” was more nuanced and focused than the published responses suggest (Letters, 24 August). Yes, it could be puritanical, dogmatic and wrong-headed at times, but to dismiss it on these grounds is to ignore Malik’s entreaty not to “trivialise and dismiss movements that resonated globally, and which had safety, dignity and equal opportunity at their heart”.

Far from being “crazy”, so called “Woke 1.0” was the roar of the grandchildren of the radical “permissive” generation – on both sides of the Atlantic – using voices they were always encouraged to believe could change the world. They were schooled in human rights like no others before them, and inducted into activism through historical precedent, armed only with just cause and integrity. They were unashamed to wear conviction on their sleeves and prepared to face the inevitable backlash as readily as their often-celebrated countercultural forebears.

Malik argues, persuasively and correctly, that how we “frame” this activism conditions how we appreciate its aims. And it has been comprehensively framed by rightwing reactionaries making space for the recrudescence of attitudes and proclivities which an older progressive generation fought tooth and nail to bury. Paul McGilchristCromer, Norfolk

Writers’ homes are sites of resistance and renewal

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 16:43:44 GMT

David Devanny on the challenges in running the late poet Charles Causley’s home in Launceston, Cornwall

In response to your letters on preserving writers’ homes (25 August) Cyprus Well was the cottage home of poet Charles Causley (1917-2003) in Launceston, Cornwall. We are a small charity, proud to open the doors to aspiring writers, schoolchildren, residents and tourists as much as we can, year-round. We share Causley’s sanctuary of 50 years with those who love his work or write their own, as well as those who just want to immerse themselves in a peaceful and enriching environment.

Like others who run writers’ homes for the public, it’s not easy – particularly with weather impact on the building and demands on shrinking sources of funding. We owe everything to our volunteers and occasional private philanthropy, supplemented by grants and donations from trusts and foundations. It would be wonderful if the town council – some of whom knew Causley in his lifetime – would reconsider their position on supporting us, too.

The trust will keep going as best it can, providing opportunities to visit (and stay in) Causley’s home, bidding for much-needed funding, bringing leading poets to Launceston to work with schoolchildren, as well as in the library and independent bookshop, while championing Causley’s own work and supporting his beloved community.

It’s about the visitor as much as the writer – perhaps that’s the key. Enter a fine writer’s private domain, and you are reminded of the possibility of a world without such places. We can see these homes as sites of resistance and renewal, a mark of the living impact of creativity, and evidence of the importance of preserving it. David DevannyChair, Charles Causley Trust

Fin Tarling’s death casts shadow over Tour of Britain as safety fears loom large

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 16:40:04 GMT

Minute’s applause to take place in Lincoln on Wednesday

Spate of serious recent crashes have put safety on agenda

The death of the Welshman Fin Tarling continues to cast a long shadow over professional cycling and nowhere will that absence be felt more deeply than at the men’s Tour of Britain which begins on Wednesday.

Tarling’s former team NSN Cycling, which includes the Olympic medallist Ethan Vernon, also one of his closest friends, will be brought to the start line in Lincoln for the opening 187km stage, for what is expected to be a minute’s applause.

Tarling was killed while racing in the Volta a Portugal last month when he collided with a non‑race vehicle driving towards him. The race operates a rolling road closure, the same security strategy employed by the Tour of Britain. The police investigation into Tarling’s death is ongoing.

A spate of serious recent crashes, including the high-speed fall endured by the Tour de France champion Tadej Pogacar, which forced him to abandon the Vuelta a España this year while leading the race, have yet again put safety at the top of the agenda.

Tom Pidcock’s tearful tribute to the Tarling family, when winning the World Mountain Bike title in Italy last weekend, revealed the depth of feeling over the teenager’s death.

The double Olympic gold medallist Pidcock, initially expected to start the British race, has opted to focus on preparing for the world championships in Canada by riding warm-up races in Montreal and Quebec.

Tarling’s collision in a race operating under a rolling road closure has been the subject of much scrutiny in the aftermath of his accident and the flaws of that system were highlighted just days later, in the women’s Tour of Britain, when the Australian rider Maeve Plouffe had her own near-miss.

“While the race convoy was still in sight, and I was less than two minutes down [behind], there were cars from the general public coming at me from all directions, including one that nearly hit me on a roundabout,” the 27-year-old said.

Jonathan Day, director of the race organisers, said: “Rider safety is paramount and will always be treated as a priority in our planning and how we operate any race.”

The race organisers maintain that the Tour of Britain is delivered in accordance with the UCI’s road racing regulations, described as the safety and operational standards that govern international and UK-based road racing.

Local authorities, emergency services, commissaires, police and event partners are all part of the race planning process. But the efficiency of rolling road closures has also been questioned by Adam Hansen, president of the CPA professional rider association, who said: “There is a hole in rolling road closures and we have to fix this.”

After an opening stage based on Lincoln, the convoy will travel through Yorkshire and on to the Scottish Borders. The second day’s racing takes the peloton from Boston to Skegness while stage three, through East Yorkshire, starts in Hull and ends in Beverley.

Over the weekend the convoy crosses the Yorkshire moors and dales, before the final stage on Sunday, which starts south of Edinburgh – site of the Grand Départ for the Tour de France next year – and finishes in Earlston.

Alongside Vernon, there is a raft of British talent lining up for the five‑day race including Ben Wiggins, son of Sir Bradley. National time trial champion in the under-23 category, the 21-year-old is now on the radar of several leading World Tour teams.

The Tour de France stage winners Olav Kooij, Filippo Ganna and Tim Merlier are among the leading World Tour names, while Pogacar’s UAE Emirates XRG team will be led by the Giro d’Italia stage winner Jhonatan Narváez.

The move from four days of racing last year to five days in 2026, giving it parity with the women’s Tour of Britain, is hoped to further boost interest as the buildup to the UK-based Grand Départ begins next year.

The hard-right Restore Britain party has got its first major donation of £500,000 from an IT entrepreneur in a sign it may continue to pose a threat to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.
