Sydney’s beaches enter the drone age to get swimmers back in the water after spate of shark attacks

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 16:00:07 GMT

Seventy beaches across New South Wales are part of the $34m dawn-to-dusk drone-monitoring program, which one expert has called ‘the best technology we have at the moment’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

“Hey Taha, what’s the visibility like?” shouts a man with a towel slung over his shoulder.

“Uh, nice,” says Surf Life Saving New South Wales drone operator Taha Kafil-Hussain.

“Good?” the man asks.

“Very good,” Kafil-Hussain assures him.

Thanking him, the early morning swimmer turns and heads down the steps to Coogee beach.

Kafil-Hussain, who Guardian Australia has joined on his early morning shark surveillance flight, says: “When they’re local, they just want to see what the weather, what the water looks like, [if there’s] anything scary.”

The 22-year-old has been flying drones for SLS NSW for four years, but only at Coogee beach for a matter of weeks. Before a shark attack on 34-year-old Sydney teacher and mother Leah Stewart in June, drone surveillance was not permitted at Coogee because it lies directly under the flight path from Sydney airport’s east-west runway.

In an interview with 60 Minutes broadcast on Sunday, Stewart described the horror encounter with a four-metre white shark, after which her left arm was amputated, as “like fighting a dinosaur”. The attack, one of a series of high-profile incidents in Sydney in the past 12 months, has prompted the state government to massively ramp up its shark mitigation program.

Under a $34m initiative by the state government which rolled out on 1 July, 38 of Sydney’s ocean beaches, including Coogee, now receive dawn-to-dusk drone monitoring year round.

Seventy NSW beaches in total are part of the dawn-to-dusk program, while others will benefit from increased surveillance throughout the summer and school holidays. From Tuesday, surveillance hours increased, running from 6.15am to 5pm each day for the start of spring, as daylight increases.

When Guardian Australia meets Kafil-Hussain in mid-winter, he arrives at 6.30am to throw up a marquee, before checking a radio to determine which direction the planes are flying in (drone surveillance at Coogee has been allowed with special permission from the airport).

Not long after, the drone takes off in a whir of plastic from a miniature landing pad, rising 60 metres into the air before heading out to sea. During each 20-minute flight, Kafil-Hussain rakes the bay in sections from left to right, backwards and forwards, leaving a chequerboard pattern on his control screen.

He says he’s looking for “anything moving in a different way than normal”.

“Anything moving against the flow of water, anything that looks a little bit long – anything alive, really.”

He pauses when he thinks he’s spotted something, to zoom in. “Looks like seaweed,” he says.

University of Sydney shark policy expert and associate professor Christopher Pepin-Neff agrees that “drones are the best technology that we have at the moment”.

But they say there are “important caveats that we need to give to the public”.

“On days that are windy, if the shark is too small, the drone operator is not going to be able to see a shark if it’s there.

“I’m slightly nervous that, in the absence of [a] large public education campaign, we have the possibility that we’re going to scare the shit out of people,” says Pepin-Neff.

With more drone surveillance comes more regular shark sightings. The NSW government says there have been more 750 sightings and more than 200 intervention actions by Surf Life Saving NSW since 1 July.

Shark listening stations are now tracking 1,698 white sharks, 938 tiger sharks and 374 bull sharks – the “target sharks” which are most frequently involved in serious shark bites.

Sign up to Breaking News Australia

Get the most important news as it breaks

after newsletter promotion

Kafil-Hussain says he has seen more bull and tiger sharks than whites, and has raised the alarm a few times, most recently for a bronze whaler – involved in rare attacks – which he initially thought was a target shark.

If it’s early and he’s on his own, raising the alarm means making the call to clear the water himself – otherwise he shares what he has seen with lifeguards and they make the decision, with the time from spotting a hazard to fully clearing the water about two or three minutes.

The SLS drones have a speaker attached to them, allowing him to communicate directly with surfers and swimmers.

It’s a technology familiar to followers of the Instagram account Drone Shark App, run by Jason Iggleden, who has been using a drone since 2018 to surveil beaches including Bondi, Tamarama and Bronte.

Videos on the account show an enormous seal barrel-rolling through the water and a swirling vortex of Australian salmon, while in another a whale lingers beneath a kayaker in Tamarama.

“I just had a bit of a vision to help … with getting people out of water with sharks, and just showing them the beauty of what’s out there,” he said.

The licensed and insured drone flyer, who continues to work independently, now passes on any sightings to SLS NSW. He is a firm believer in the drone surveillance, saying the ability to spot target sharks grows with experience.

“I don’t think you really need to consider much more than drones, to be honest,” he says.

Pepin-Neff is supportive of other non-lethal technologies, such as SMART drum lines. They say a trial of new artificial intelligence detection software on drones will take the pressure off humans to discern between more and less dangerous sharks. But their message on controversial measures such as shark nets, here to stay on NSW beaches, and culling, is unequivocal: “They do not work.”

Kafil-Hussain, who drives each day from his home in Parramatta, has now flown drones at most Sydney beaches, from Palm beach in the north to Cronulla in the south. Every beach is different – he sees turtles, dolphins, the occasional whale. Coogee is home to a wobbegong, a low-swimming carpet shark which does not hunt humans but can attack if threatened.

“He’s not around. He’ll pop out eventually,” says Kafil-Hussain.

When Guardian Australia visits the beach, arriving before sunrise, it is already heaving with eastern suburbs dog walkers, swim clubs and surfers. Just weeks after the attack on Stewart, Kafil-Hussain says numbers at the beach have only been growing.

Pepin-Neff says the drone program will “restore confidence” ahead of a busy summer, but there is “no silver bullet”. “Drones are a great tool but they’re not a perfect solution.”

Pepin-Neff swims at fully enclosed beaches, like Marrinawi Cove in Barangaroo, but their advice for those that swim at unenclosed beaches is: “Swim between the flags.”

“The ocean is the wild and we need to treat the beach like the bush.”

The Raygun documentary ducks a big question about the Olympic fame of a ‘dorky white academic’

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 16:00:07 GMT

Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly finds warmth and humor in Rachael Gunn’s ordeal, but never fully reckons with what her notoriety meant for breaking

Early in Netflix’s new documentary, Untold Raygun: Breaking Badly, Australian B-girl Rachael Gunn, recounts a session she had with her sports psychologist prior to the 2024 Paris Olympics.

“Right before the Olympics, I went to my therapist, panicked,” she says. Her therapist asked her what was the worst thing that could happen. And she said, “The whole world could laugh at me.” Her therapist responded: “Do you think that’s reasonable?” Cue Gunn’s hysterical laughter.

Anyone who has ever gone to a therapist will be amused at this anecdote. Nine and a half times out 10, the therapist would have been right. No, they’d say, the worst outcome you can imagine probably won’t come to pass. But in Gunn’s case, what she feared the most did, in fact, happen. Her shenanigans – the sprinkler, the kangaroo hops – in the cypher made her go viral almost as soon as she was done with her sets. (Perhaps if Gunn had been explicit about what she was planning to do in her sets, her therapist would have reacted differently.) Gunn’s performance launched a thousand memes, more than a couple of late-night TV segments, several conspiracy theories, and even a musical at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival.

“She became the most famous breaker on planet Earth overnight,” Flix, a fellow Australian B-girl, says in the documentary. All without winning a single vote from any of the nine judges across her six rounds.

Untold Raygun, which premieres globally on Netflix on Tuesday, really doesn’t dwell on what it means for breaking, an art form created by Black and Brown youth in the South Bronx, that its first Olympic foray will be primarily – if not exclusively – remembered for a white woman from Australia doing the sprinkler instead of the dynamic performances of the rest of the contenders. It’s mostly focused on Gunn herself with little time spent on the greater context of the art form and how it ended up in the Olympics. The documentary features interviews with Gunn, her parents, her husband who introduced her to breaking, and a few dancers who know her from the Aussie scene. Through them, we get a coming of almost middle-age story about an academic who meets a B-boy working at a call center, falls in love with him and the art form he’s passionate about, and somehow ends up centerstage at the Olympics.

Gunn is likeable in the documentary. She comes across as (mostly) self-aware and self-deprecating. Her parents are charming, laughing heartily when asked if they had ever previously associated “Olympian” with their quirky daughter. Sammy Free seems like a sweet fellow who is completely besotted with his wife. (We should all be so lucky to find someone who loves us the way that Free clearly loves Gunn.) But the most useful voices in Untold Raygun are the two Australian B-girls who offer some critical perspective on the place of women in the breaking scene and Gunn’s performances at the Games. They’re harsh, at times, but also fair.

Tinylocks, one of Gunn’s contemporaries, repeatedly invokes “No easy props,” a term that’s something of a hip-hop ethos about having to prove your skill to earn respect. (The phrase is often associated with American B-girl Asia One, who founded a crew called No Easy Props in 1997.) “It was such a male dominated space and B-girls were really fighting to be seen but as more women started entering breaking, it was felt that some girls were getting accolades too early in their careers. The crowd would cheer just for participating,” she says.

It is within the context of “no easy props” that Tinylocks offers her assessment of Raygun’s pre-Olympic performances, as she was coming up in the small Australian scene. “There were one or two times when I was like, ‘Oh yeah, that was fresh.’ Maybe not so much the other times.”

Tinylocks decided to pass on trying to earn the Oceania qualifying spot. “I’m interested in breaking as an art form,” she says, which is a sentiment I heard from other dancers in the scene after the Olympic trajectory was announced by the IOC and the World DanceSport Federation (WDSF). Flix gave it a go at the Oceania qualifier, but said that, at 41, she didn’t expect much. Gunn was surprised that she kept advancing through the bracket until she was in the final battle against B-girl Molly. If you go back and watch the Oceania qualifier, you won’t see any of Gunn’s “iconic” moves from the Paris Olympics in that final. What she threw down against Molly doesn’t stand out in any way – either for good or for bad. Yes, her movements were slow and lacked sharpness, her sets not particularly intricate. But she showed fairly standard breaking foundation movements. If she had done those sets in Paris, Gunn wouldn’t have advanced out of the preliminary rounds but she also wouldn’t have become a global sensation.

The documentary explains the change in her set composition: she realized how far behind she was the top B-girls she was going to be battling at the Olympics. She went to a couple of European battles in the months before the Games and performed poorly in all of them. Gunn and her husband decided to change their approach. Instead of trying to up the difficulty content of her sets through power moves – the acrobatics like headspins and windmills that laypeople associate with breaking – they would go all in on originality, one of the five categories breaking judges evaluate at the Games. (The other four were technique, vocabulary, execution and musicality.) They had gone from hoping to win one battle or even one round to trying to win a single vote from one of the nine judges. Gunn and Free said they looked to Australia for movement inspiration from its famous wildlife (kangaroo) to its dance moves (the sprinkler). They even added a nod to swimming, an Olympic sport at which Australia excels. Despite this strategy, Gunn didn’t get a single vote in Paris.

There’s a world in which this approach could have worked for Gunn but it’s a world where she is much better at breaking fundamentals, where her footwork is sharp and clean, her movements swift but also unhurried. The breaking scene has had its share of well-respected dancers who bring humor and personality to the cypher. B-boys and B-girls often call this “character.” (In fact, one of them, Jeffro, was competing on the men’s side in Paris.) The issue with Gunn’s attempts at character is that those gimmicks were basically all she had. The bunny hop or the kangaroo weren’t simply moments in an otherwise proficient set that ticked other boxes, like technique, execution or musicality. The gimmicks were the main event.

As a point of contrast, let’s consider another athlete who became a meme during the Paris Games: Stephen Nedoroscik. The pommel horse specialist doffed his glasses, Clark Kent style, before he saluted the judges. There the tenor of the online discourse had none of the mockery that suffused the Raygun tweets because Nedoroscik was actually world class in his event. He was the 2021 world champion on pommel horse and won bronze in the event at the Olympics. Something similar took place in the sport shooting event where Turkey’s Yusuf Dikec became a meme due to his nonchalant stance and lack of gear. But because he was actually good at his sport – he won silver – the online hijinks never turned mean.

“People have a lot of opinions about what women do, what women should do, sometimes from women,” Gunn says of the reaction online to her performance. Generally speaking, there is truth to this assertion. Women do get singled out for criticism in a way that often feels disproportionate to the offense. Gunn didn’t commit a crime. She didn’t murder anyone on live TV. And she didn’t cheat her way to the Olympics as many people falsely claimed after Paris. (This is one of the conspiracy theories that Untold Raygun takes pains to dispel.) But it still felt disingenuous for Gunn to invoke this defense as a response to her Olympic performance. The response was not simply about her creative choices but also about the gap between herself and her competitors. She put herself on an Olympic stage where spectators expect elite performance, not a professor who is simply doing her best. The Olympics aren’t really a vehicle for self-expression. They’re supposed to be a vehicle for excellence.

Gunn isn’t the first person to compete at the Olympics whose skills are decidedly subpar. There was Eddie the Eagle, the British ski jumper who competed at the 1988 Olympics in Calgary, who definitely did not fly through the air with the greatest of ease. Eric Moussambani competed in swimming at the 2000 Games though he could barely swim the entire length of an Olympic pool. And in 2018, Elizabeth Swaney, representing Hungary, did nothing of substance in the halfpipe competition, putting together the most basic of runs. What distinguishes Gunn from the other Olympians is that they competed in sports that were already well-established. Though they became well-known, they didn’t become the face of their respective sports. But breaking was new to the Games in 2024 and most viewers weren’t familiar with it except from pop-culture products of the 80s. Gunn left Paris as the most famous breaker in the world. The average person on the street couldn’t tell you who won the breaking competition in Paris but they can probably remember Raygun, if not by name, then at least by description of what she did on the floor.

There was no way for Gunn to have predicted this outcome, even if she, on some level, feared it before she got on the plane for France. But it would have been welcome to see her reckon with it and what it means for the culture and breaking’s chances of getting on the program of a future Games. (The documentary doesn’t mention this so I’ll do it: that breaking won’t appear at LA2028 has nothing to do with Gunn. The decision was made months before she hopped across the cypher.)

Ultimately, Untold Raygun seeks to reassure the viewer that Gunn has survived her very public bout with global humiliation with her spirit and sense of whimsy intact. “I’m a dorky white woman who is an academic,” she said. “And I’m OK with that.”

Last week WDSF submitted breaking for consideration for the 2032 Olympics, which will be hosted by Brisbane. If the local organizing committee decides to give breaking another shot at Olympic glory then perhaps we’ll see Gunn again, but hopefully not at the center of the cypher.

Mark Carney tells US to ‘start being serious’ amid escalating trade war

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 15:48:27 GMT

Canadian PM is set to retaliate against tariffs levied by Donald Trump and criticized US officials over insults

US politics live – latest updates

Mark Carney has rebuked Donald Trump’s administration and urged officials in Washington to “start being serious” amid escalating trade tensions between the US and Canada.

Days before Canada is due to retaliate against Trump’s sweeping tariffs with its own duties on US goods, the Canadian prime minister criticized US officials for insulting his country. “It is beneath their office,” he said.

“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions” about trade, Carney said.

Trump signed an executive order last week directing the US federal government to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America – a move that has been rejected by Canadians.

The US president’s most senior trade negotiator has meanwhile downplayed the potentially disastrous effects of a US trade war with Canada, declaring the spat to be “more their emergency than ours”.

The US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, argued that Canada was more vulnerable after the breakdown in talks set the stage for sweeping tariffs between the two neighbors, telling Politico: “There are no negotiations happening on trade right now.”

The comment comes just more than a week after US-Canada trade talks imploded. The US levied 50% tariffs on $20bn in Canadian goods.

Canada, the US’s second-largest trading partner, announced it would impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of American goods starting on 8 September. Now, US residents are poised to feel extreme pressure from Trump’s tariffs and Canada’s retaliatory measures, including on day-to-day items.

Greer appeared to blame the escalating trade war on Canadian officials, telling Politico: “It’s not clear Canada wants a deal.

“If Canada believes that prohibiting and banning American goods and services is appropriate, then obviously that’s something that the United States should consider as well.”

Unacceptable asks from Canada included lighter taxes on heavy-duty trucks, according to Greer, who said such requests torpedoed the trade talks.

Canadian officials, on the other hand, attributed the collapsed negotiations to a White House disagreement over who was directing trade talks. Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, also said that American negotiators saw the French language in Canada as an “irritant”, but added: “In Quebec, these are rights.”

Trump, for his part, has argued in recent weeks that Canada “wants the benefits” of being a US state, without being one – a preoccupation of the US president – as he lashed out at the country’s leaders. “They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs,” claimed Trump. “No more!!!”

Greer suggested that negotiations broke down after a misunderstanding around what was, and wasn’t, on the table. “Was that political? I don’t know,” he told Politico. “Was it economic? … I’m not sure how much economic sense it makes because the choice is not between the current tariffs and … you know, duty-free trade. Like, that is that. Those weren’t the options.”

Full-blown adulthood: does it actually start at 50?

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 15:36:59 GMT

According to a new survey, that’s the age when people feel most confident and in control of their lives. In other words, they no longer have a chairdrobe ...

Name: 50 (and thriving).

Age: You can work this one out.

Appearance: Cool, calm and collected. Also, very tidy.

Don’t you mean frazzled? Come on, wouldn’t you say you’re more together now than you were at 20, or even 30?

Who says I’m not still in my 20s? Why are we comparing ages anyway? A new survey has found that 50 is the age at which Brits feel “most confident and in control of their lives”.

And what source do we have to thank for this? British Gas commissioned the survey of 2,000 British adults.

Getting the boiler serviced is one way to feel like a grownup, I suppose. The survey found that recycling, putting clothes away and knowing when bin day is were widely-agreed-upon indicators that someone had “got it together”.

What’s wrong with a chairdrobe? It’s a perfectly workable system! It’s a pile of clothes, is what it is. Respondents also said that having a litter-free car, spare batteries to hand and washing up after a dinner party, instead of leaving it till the next day, were signs of adulthood.

I knew I was right to buy that bulk pack of triple As. It’s when you’ve got a spare CR2032 battery that you know you’re really nailing it.

These do seem somewhat low or arbitrary bars for having your life together. Oh, so you want to hold people to owning a car, or buying a house, or becoming a parent? Not in this economy.

True. But surely there are more meaningful markers of maturity than making your bed, or drinking two litres of water a day? As if you do either every day. You’re right, though: the top-rated sign you’ve got your life under control was making regular savings.

Surely it’s what’s on the inside that counts for adulthood, not what’s in your bank account. The next top indicators were enjoying your own company, admitting when you’re wrong and saying no to things you don’t want to do.

OK, those are way tougher than knowing when bin day is. It does get confusing around the bank holidays …

You’re telling me that you have to be 50 to be on top of all this? That’s the average age respondents felt most in control of their lives. But 30% said they felt nowhere near being sorted, while 56% thought no one ever really is.

Didn’t we only just discover that the brain doesn’t reach adulthood until age 32, anyway? Yes, that was a Cambridge University finding last year, and probably more credible than this consumer research.

So, if you think about it, by 50 you’ve only been a grownup for 18 years. Long enough to know to make your bed.

Do say: “Actually, drinking two litres of water a day is excessive for most people.”

Don’t say: “Is it bin day?”

Olivia Rodrigo is standing up for the vulnerable. I wish Taylor Swift would do the same

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 15:21:43 GMT

This weekend, Rodrigo raised millions for charities that benefit women and girls, and she has previously been vocal about Gaza and Ice. With free speech increasingly under threat, her peers should take note

Donald Trump, the 80-year-old president of the United States, spent his weekend whining about a lake and posting memes of Donald’s Ducks. While he was busy with his ducks, Olivia Rodrigo, a 23-year-old pop star, spent her weekend trying to Make America Somewhat Decent Again. On Saturday, Rodrigo hosted the inaugural Daisy Chain Fields festival, bringing together female artists to raise money for women-focused non-profits which have had their funding slashed by the Trump administration. The festival raised $10m (£7.4m) which Melinda French Gates matched, bringing the total to $20m.

In a perfect world a singer holding a benefit concert for feminist charities wouldn’t be radical stuff. But we don’t live in a perfect world, do we? We live in hell. Trump has successfully bullied US institutions into doing his bidding. Universities have defunded diversity, equity and inclusion programmes, many media outlets have kowtowed to the US’s self-styled king and tech CEOs have jumped into bed with him. Women’s rights are going backwards globally and our civil liberties are under attack.

It has become depressingly clear just how many of the rich and powerful are self-serving cowards who will abandon social justice issues as soon as it becomes mildly inconvenient. So it was refreshing to see a young musician rally people together in service of reproductive justice at a festival that was proudly feminist and didn’t pretend to be non-political.

Rodrigo has always used her platform to speak out: she’s never been one of those annoying celebrities who insist that remaining apolitical is some sort of noble act. When Roe v Wade was overturned in 2022, the then 19-year-old musician condemned the decision on stage at Glastonbury. Rodrigo, who is Filipino American, also publicly told the Trump administration not to use her music in their “racist, hateful propaganda” when one of her songs was featured in a government video telling undocumented immigrants to self-deport.

Rodrigo has also not been silent about Gaza: a subject many celebrities are terrified to mention, because empathising with Palestinians is a tried-and-tested way to ruin your career. Last year she wrote on Instagram about how “mothers, fathers and children in Gaza are starving, dehydrated and being denied access to basic medical care ...” Rodrigo also gave a nod to Palestine (which, thanks to Israel’s attacks on maternity wards and healthcare is a reproductive justice issue) at a press conference for her Daisy Chain Fields festival, where she wore a dress made by Palestinian fashion brand Nöl Collective.

Speaking on the New York Times’s Popcast earlier this year, Rodrigo said acknowledging social issues is part of expressing herself. “I think it would just be disingenuous to be like, I don’t feel heartbroken about what’s going on in Gaza. As an artist, I feel like that’s just what you do. And that’s my job,” she said.

Frankly, I think it’s the job of everyone with any sort of platform or power. Celebrities shouldn’t have to get political, some will say. No, of course not. But if you have a huge platform and oodles of money and even just a smidgen of a conscience, then you should probably want to use your resources and reach for good, shouldn’t you? Giving money to charity is one thing, but it takes more courage to show people where you stand, knowing there may be repercussions for it. I hate this idea of not “taking sides”: the world is not a football match; political parties are not “teams”. It is not divisive to stand with vulnerable people.

Taylor Swift, the richest female musician in history, certainly seemed to agree with that at one point. She famously stayed quiet in the lead-up to the 2016 election, but later, when more celebrities were doing so, came out to endorse progressive causes. “I need to be on the right side of history,” she said in the 2020 documentary Miss Americana.

But while Swift did endorse Kamala Harris in 2024, she has been very careful about what she says during Trump 2.0. Unlike all the musicians who have publicly condemned the Trump administration for using their music in offensive posts, she seemingly ignored the use of her songs by Trump for months. In recent weeks her songs have been quietly removed from Trump’s ragebait posts, but Swift has not issued any sort of public statement about it. And she certainly hasn’t said anything about issues such as Gaza or ICE.

There are limits to celebrity activism, sure. But in a world where free speech is under attack, it feels increasingly important for celebrities to speak out. Let’s hope Rodrigo’s festival prompts more of her peers to have some guts.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

‘In my heart until I die’: Argentina says a tearful thank you to Lionel Messi

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 15:05:49 GMT

The Argentinian’s decision to quit international football was met by an outpouring of affection from the country he led to World Cup glory in 2022

Anyone who was present at Lionel Scaloni’s press conference immediately after the World Cup final between Spain and Argentina in New Jersey on 19 July and saw his tears, the sobs which prevented him from speaking while he got up and walked out, could tell this was a man weeping not because of defeat in a single match but because he was fully aware that what that particular group of men had been through for the past eight years had come to an end.

Messi’s announcement that he is retiring from international football, posted on Instagram on Monday complete with photos of three handwritten sheets of some anonymous yet corporate-looking headed paper and a Harry Potter Time Turner pen, to the soundtrack of Brindis sung by Soledad Pastorutti, instantly dominated the news and unleashed a barrage of homages, gratitude and joy from all corners. But it’s not exactly a surprise.

“How crazy that the day has come, dear Leo,” Cristian Romero posted, making it clear that this was expected in spite of the unexpectedness. “The day no one wanted to arrive has arrived,” echoed Giovani Lo Celso, who said he had “nine years listening to you, admiring you and learning by your side”. His international teammates highlight how in their childhood they dreamed of meeting him one day, let alone actually playing with him. Nico Paz says since he was four years old he “used to watch you play with my dad and we would calculate together whether I would be in time to play with you”.

It’s not just his teammates who are expressing gratitude and nostalgia. On a Buenos Aires street corner someone put a red telephone on a table with a sign saying: “What would you say to Messi?” Passersby picked up the receiver and talked into it: “I’m 86 years old and you have given me the greatest joys in my life. You will be in my heart until the day I die,” one gentleman said. A young boy saw the news and “burst into tears even though I was at school”. A well-spoken woman said “we will miss you because you are an extraordinary being”, a little girl added “you’re the best and the greatest”. An old man signed off “bye, son”.

Influencers, journalists, artists, cultural commentators and psychologists all expressed their gratefulness for Messi being a great human being. “Messi led by example,” the veteran sportswriter Matías Martin wrote, while the coach and motivational speaker Matias “Coco” Gallo Bevegni posted that the World Cup winner “taught me more in defeat than in victory”.

The football pundit Morena Beltrán could not hold back the tears as she explained to her older colleagues that for her generation there is a sense of mourning and emptiness which can only be filled by gratitude, which maybe they have already experienced, because they have seen another God. The psychoanalyst Milagros Filgueras praised the decision to hand-write the note, saying some goodbyes need the body involved. The journalist Pablo Perantuono devoted his column to the “epistolary genre”, noting that a handwritten letter in this day and age is almost a countercultural act of originality.

The writer Andrés Burgo highlighted that in 10 of the past 12 World Cups, either Maradona or Messi played, so this truly marks the “end of an era in which grandparents, parents, sons and daughters and grandchildren enjoyed an incredible privilege during almost 45 years. The heir will arrive – we hope – but right now is a time of orphanage. And gratitude.”

Messi revealed that this letter was actually written two days after the final, a cathartic diary-like release, but that on Monday, after “[what happened with] my dad” he was more convinced than ever. The note said: “It’s a decision that hurt and continues to hurt,” but that he understands this is the moment. The poet Valeria Correa Fiz pointed out that he originally wrote “I think”, crossed it out and replaced it with “I understand”. Messi swore he always gave his all, not only these past few years when “everything was won” (he never says “I won”; it’s always “we” or “it” was won) but he has nothing left to give. He’s emptied.

The 39-year-old, however, scored four goals for Inter Miami at the weekend and continues his career at club level, where he clearly still has much to give. He is not retiring from playing football, the thing he loves most. He is retiring from Argentina.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

With two international dates coming up and no rival agreed, no doubt the clarification that there will be no Messi in the squad will impact on the potential fixtures. And not unlike the time when he quit Argentina before, in 2016, the country’s football is in a bit of turmoil.

The context and climate include scandals surrounding the Argentinian Football Association, the pressure by some lobbies to privatise football clubs, which are non-profit organisations, and the international furore caused by several incidents during the World Cup which have landed Argentina with some hefty fines, sanctions and suspensions.

The heaviness of the Argentina flag which for so many years visibly weighed him down, turned idyllic when it became the cloak of victory, mattered very much to his father, Jorge. Messi said he wanted to win another World Cup for him. Perhaps his death has somehow freed him from that aspect of his Argentinianness.

And just like last time, the spontaneous visceral response from the Argentinian people is acceptance and relish at the good times lived. That inexplicable sense of pride that comes from being from the same soil as someone who is very good at something and whose magic is still untarnished by the sordid final match against Spain, or any of the criticisms directed at the squad and fans throughout the tournament. If anything, his final tears in front of the stands, like Scaloni’s tears at the press conference, are mirrored in a nation moved profoundly by the generations we have just lived through, perhaps not realising we were living through them.

The huge volume of emotive, sentimental outpouring is rather lovely, and amid it all an enduring image of three little boys walking down a Buenos Aires street with No 10 Messi shirts on their backs signals the way forward, towards a future unknown.

Forget T-maxxing – the manosphere’s obsession with testosterone is just fear-maxxing

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 15:00:03 GMT

Testosterone replacement therapy comes with serious and potentially irreversible health risks including infertility and early heart disease

Read more in the Antiviral series

Are you tired? Feeling flat and irritable? Finding it difficult to concentrate? Maybe you’re experiencing the seemingly ubiquitous symptoms of modern life. Or, if you’re a man, you may have been told by countless uncredentialed online influencers that you’re probably suffering from “low T”.

For decades, testosterone has been marketed to men as a means to maximise virility. But in recent years, social media has fuelled the “T-maxxing” trend, in which men are encouraged to maximise their testosterone levels through either natural or artificial means.

Low testosterone is being blamed in the rightwing manosphere for a crisis of masculinity; global search interest in the term is up 60% from last year.

Popular podcasters such as Joe Rogan and Andrew Huberman openly talk about taking testosterone, as has the 72-year-old Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has said he uses testosterone replacement therapy as part of an “anti-ageing protocol”.

Elsewhere in the Trump administration, the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, announced in July that soldiers 30 and over would be tested annually to ensure they have the “right testosterone levels”.

Social media is awash with testimonies from men on testosterone replacement therapy who say they have lost weight and regained energy, motivation and libido. Prescriptions for testosterone in the UK and US have risen sharply in recent years.

But the fixation on T-maxxing ignores hard evidence: very few men actually have clinically low levels of the sex hormone, and taking exogenous testosterone – through injections or gels – comes with serious and potentially irreversible health risks, especially when treatment is unwarranted.

Testosterone is a steroid hormone we all produce, but is naturally found at higher levels in men.

Testosterone levels fluctuate throughout the lifetime, says Prof Ada Cheung, an endocrinologist at the University of Melbourne.

Population-based studies show that testosterone rises rapidly during male puberty and that over time “it does tend to decline a bit with age”, she says. “That decline with age we think is largely attributed to the accumulation of chronic health conditions as we get older” – conditions such as obesity, diabetes, high cholesterol and blood pressure. “But it doesn’t mean that every older man needs testosterone [treatment], because that’s not the case at all.”

Testosterone levels also vary through the day and in response to physical stressors such as illness and poor sleep. “It’s always low in the afternoon and highest first thing in the morning,” Cheung says. “Testosterone naturally varies when we eat … and if we’re sick in any way.”

Research suggests that average testosterone levels in men have declined over the last five decades, though they remain within normal reference ranges. Experts, Cheung included, believe the trend may be at least partly explained by lifestyle habits, stress, chronic disease and rising obesity.

Clinically low testosterone – also known as male hypogonadism – is “actually pretty uncommon”, Cheung says. “Less than 2% [of men] would have clinical hypogonadism.” It can can be caused by genetic conditions such as Klinefelter syndrome, or conditions that affect the pituitary gland in the brain, which regulates sex hormone production.

“Why people often get confused is that the symptoms of low testosterone are very non-specific, like fatigue, low mood, poor concentration, erectile dysfunction, low motivation,” Cheung says. Far more commonly, she points out, these issues are caused by other factors, such as stress, depression, obesity, and iron or thyroid issues.

But these symptoms are frequently used to promote testosterone screening and treatments on social media, says Dr Brooke Nickel, a senior research fellow at the University of Sydney’s school of public health.

Research she co-authored, published in January in the journal Social Science & Medicine, found that young men are being aggressively marketed to by testosterone influencers and wellness companies. Their analysis of 46 popular posts – from accounts with a total following of 6.8 million and which had amassed a combined 659,000 likes – found that nearly three-quarters of accounts had vested financial interests, such as being the sellers of testosterone tests and therapies.

“The narratives that they were discussing were closely mirrored to those promoted within the manosphere, where hormone levels were being presented as a measure of manhood,” she says.

Testosterone tests, they found, were primarily targeting younger men – a group for which mass screening for low testosterone is medically unwarranted. None of the posts, unsurprisingly, presented any evidence to support claims made.

Nickel describes such posts as “fearmongering” – using common experiences to suggest “there’s something medically wrong and that testosterone is a solution”.

“Once you start testosterone and you are on it for a while, it’s very hard to wean. It’s not just a short-term thing,” Cheung says. Taking testosterone shuts off the body’s natural production of the hormone, as well as sperm production.

The American “looksmaxxer” Braden Peters, also known as Clavicular, is by his own admission infertile from steroid abuse.

“People can become infertile and it can take months to years to recover – and the recovery is not always guaranteed, which is probably one of the most serious concerns,” Cheung says.

Doctors have reported people taking testosterone presenting with gynaecomastia, (male breast enlargement), severe atrophy of the testicles, and early heart disease. Testosterone replacement therapy also increases the risk of blood clots.

For patients who do have clinical hypogonadism, “it’s often a lifelong commitment when we start treating someone with testosterone therapy”, Cheung says. “It can lead to things like sleep apnoea, acne, prostate issues, urinary difficulties, mood and libido fluctuations, so it’s not without risk.”

Men frustrated by barriers like financial costs and stigma when seeking out testosterone through regulated medical channels have reported getting the hormone through underground sources with relative ease, Australian research has found.

That poses its own health risks: Australian testing of anabolic steroids obtained from underground markets has found traces of carcinogenic heavy metals such as lead, arsenic and cadmium, as well as product mislabelling.

If men are concerned about symptoms and believe low testosterone may be an issue, they should contact a health practitioner, Cheung says. “If you’re worried, go and see your GP and have a conversation, rather than listening to someone trying to tell you something on social media.”

Donna Lu is an assistant editor, climate, environment and science at Guardian Australia. Antiviral is a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claims

Norway’s new king swears oath of allegiance with daughter at his side

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 14:40:34 GMT

Haakon VIII promises to uphold 1814 constitution but his queen misses ceremony because of post-surgery ‘complications’

King Haakon VIII swore an oath of allegiance before Norway’s parliament on Tuesday in the first major stage in the passing of the crown since the death of his father after 35 years on the throne.

Wearing a ceremonial uniform, Haakon, who became king when Harald V died on Friday, promised to uphold Norway’s 1814 constitution with his 22-year-old daughter, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, by his side.

“I promise and swear that I will govern the kingdom of Norway in accordance with its constitution and laws, so help me God, the almighty and omniscient,” the 53-year-old king pledged to cabinet ministers and MPs in the main chamber of the 169-seat parliament.

Haakon’s wife, Mette-Marit, 53, was unable to attend the 17-minute ceremony because of complications after a lung transplant in June. Her doctors said such complications were not uncommon.

Are ​Holm, a pulmonologist at Oslo university hospital, said the queen had had “complications on some occasions with the operation, including today. As a ​result, she must be put under observation ​throughout the day today.”

Harald, whose funeral will be held in Oslo on 9 September, with heads of state from around the world invited to attend, was widely appreciated in Norway for his warmth, unassuming lifestyle and dedication to preserving national unity.

Tens ⁠of thousands of Norwegians have flocked to the royal palace to lay flowers, drawings, candles and flags.

A poll for the public broadcaster NRK found the monarchy’s popularity had risen over the past few months. The first survey since Harald’s death at the age of 89 found that about 72% of Norwegians supported the monarchy, compared with 54% in May. In February, while the royal family was mired in a succession of scandals, support for the institution fell to 60%.

Mette-Marit has faced strong criticism for her association with Jeffrey Epstein, while her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, is appealing against a four-year sentence for two rape convictions.

Responding to Haakon’s oath, Masud Gharahkhani, the parliament’s president, who arrived in Norway as a child refugee from Iran, said Harald had personified “the values that underpin our liberal democracy”, including compassion.

There will be no formal coronation of the new king and queen because Norway abolished the ceremony more than a century ago but Haakon may, like his father and grandfather, choose to have his accession consecrated at Trondheim’s Nidaros Cathedral.

Harald, who will be buried in the royal mausoleum at the Akershus Fortress in Oslo, died while being treated in hospital for haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells.

After a reckoning and the toppling, what is replacing Britain’s symbols of empire?

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 14:30:00 GMT

In this month’s newsletter: communities are reshaping how empire is remembered in public life. Plus, holding royalty to account in Jamaica and repairing centuries of harm in California

Don’t get Cotton Capital delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

Hello and welcome to the Cotton Capital newsletter. I’m Nadine White and this month we’re asking: after the toppling, what comes next?

Britain spent much of 2020 arguing about what should come down. Statues of enslavers and colonial figures were toppled, defaced or quietly removed. Edward Colston ended up in Bristol harbour. Robert Milligan was taken down outside London’s Museum of Docklands, while campaigners renewed calls for Cecil Rhodes to come off his plinth at Oriel College, Oxford. But six years on, one of the most persistent battles is still playing out.

The longstanding Hackney MP Diane Abbott has highlighted ongoing calls for the removal of a statue of Robert Geffrye, the 17th-century merchant whose wealth was built partly through investments in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. The statue remains prominently displayed outside the Museum of the Home, formerly the Geffrye Museum, despite a 2020 public consultation finding strong support for its removal.

Abbott argues that the issue is not about erasing history, but refusing to honour those who profited from slavery in public spaces. “We must never forget that,” she wrote. “But we must not honour it.”

If you’ve walked through most British towns and cities recently, you’ll know the landscape hasn’t changed all that much. The vast majority of imperial monuments are exactly where they have always been: on plinths, in parks, above doorways and worked into the stone of public buildings.

The toppling of Colston became globally symbolic precisely because it was so unusual.

Elsewhere, changes were smaller and more localised: in the London borough of Lewisham, Sir Francis Drake primary school became Twin Oaks primary school after a community consultation; in Tottenham, north London, Black Boy Lane became La Rose Lane, honouring the Trinidadian-born activist and publisher John La Rose.

So, six years on, a quieter question has started to emerge: what is actually replacing Britain’s imperial symbols?

A different kind of intervention

Across the country, a new memorial landscape is slowly taking shape, often pushed forward by artists, campaigners and community groups unwilling to wait for institutions to act.

At the International Slavery Museum in Liverpool, the Black British-Caribbean artist Rayvenn Shaleigha D’Clark is creating iron entrance panels that reinterpret materials historically tied to enslavement and control. “Bronze and iron carry deep historical associations with the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans when they were used to confine, control and restrict,” she told me. “This project considers how those same materials can now be reclaimed and subverted within a contemporary context.”

For D’Clark, artists have a particular role to play in how Britain faces its difficult histories. “Through their work, artists can help make visible stories that have often been hidden, overlooked or excluded from mainstream historical narratives.” This is a different kind of intervention to pulling something down, but no less intentional.

In London, The Wake, a memorial honouring victims of the transatlantic slave trade by Khaleb Brooks, is due to be unveiled outside London Museum Docklands in 2027. Standing seven metres high, it will include a bronze cowrie shell that people can enter, offering a space for reflection.

Meanwhile, campaigners are working to preserve and publicly display the anchor of HMT Empire Windrush, the passenger liner that brought over the first wave of people from the Caribbean after the second world war to help rebuild Britain, turning a physical relic of migration into a national site of memory.

These projects are unfolding against considerable resistance – one that’s worth taking seriously. A recent YouGov poll found that 60% of Britons oppose paying reparations for slavery, with 24% in support.

At Oxford’s Oriel College, after years of campaigning, the Rhodes statue stayed put. The college opted instead for contextualisation – exhibitions and commissioned artwork exploring Rhodes’s legacy. Critics saw it as compromise dressed as engagement. Supporters argued it was more thoughtful than removal alone.

In Glasgow, the city council confirmed in July that all 11 statues returning to the revamped George Square will come with material explaining their links to enslavement, colonialism and imperial conflict. The monuments – among them William Gladstone, Sir John Moore and Field Marshal Colin Campbell, who helped crush the 1857 Indian Rebellion – will form part of the city’s Legacy of Slavery and Colonialism Trail when the square reopens at the end of October.

Internationally, the mood has also shifted in complicated directions. In the US, a new Christopher Columbus statue was recently installed at the White House using fragments of a monument toppled during the 2020 protests – a signal that the reassessment of empire is far from settled.

What has changed, perhaps irreversibly, is that Britain can no longer treat its imperial symbols as neutral background scenery. Whether those symbols stay or go, they are now contested in a way they weren’t before.

The question isn’t really whether empire should be remembered – it’s whose version of that memory we choose to keep and whose we’re still, quietly, walking past every day.

British corporation continued trafficking of enslaved Africans to Guyana 40 years after abolition | Chris Osuh

Trafficked on the last US slave ship, Cudjo Lewis never returned home to Benin. But his descendant has | Adria Walker

Sign up to Cotton Capital

Starting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the world

after newsletter promotion

Jamaica | Jamaican officials will head to the UK this month to petition King Charles on their claim for reparatory justice from Britain. They will ask Charles to use his authority to request legal advice from the judicial committee of the London-based privy council on whether the forced transportation of Africans to Jamaica was lawful from the privy council, the final court of appeal for some Commonwealth countries.

Jamaica’s culture minister, Olivia Grange, said the request was being made to the king “in his capacity as head of state of Jamaica from whom we expect protection”.

The unprecedented move has the full support of Ghana’s president, John Mahama, who has said global discussions on reparations have reached “a defining moment”. Our Caribbean correspondent, Natricia Duncan, will be keeping an eye on all the latest developments. Angela Foster, assistant editor

Manchester | The links between Manchester’s historic Portico library, the Peterloo Massacre and transatlantic enslavement have been explored by a walking tour inspired by research for the Portico Reunited project, which aims to reposition Peterloo in its global context.

The Portico and Peterloo: A Transatlantic Moment marked 207 years since the Peterloo massacre, in which 18 people were killed and hundreds injured while protesting for the vote in August 1819. It was a turning point in British history and led to the founding of the Manchester Guardian.

Hugh Hornby Birley led the anti-democracy militia who charged the crowd on that fateful day. What is less well known is that Birley, who was a board member of the Portico, owed his position as leading cotton manufacturer to the enslavement of African people, including on the Rabot Estate in St Lucia. Chris Osuh, community affairs correspondent

Sea Islands | California is gearing up to become the first US state that requires corporations to investigate their historical records and submit an affidavit disclosing whether they benefited from enslavement.

The Truth in Disclosure Act passed in the California state legislature in late August and will be sent to Governor Gavin Newsom’s desk to become law. Under the legislation, entities with an annual revenue of more than $100m will declare under oath if the corporation “bought or sold persons subjected to slavery, used persons subjected to slavery as collateral, provided loans to purchase persons subjected to slavery, insured such transactions or the persons subjected to slavery, or provided related or other services to aid or otherwise facilitate those transactions”.

Introduced in February by assembly member Isaac Bryan, it seeks to highlight the lasting impact of enslavement and follows the work of the California Reparations Task Force, which offered recommendations to repair centuries of harm in a 2023 report (pdf).

“For too long, corporations have been allowed to benefit from the economic engine of slavery while avoiding any public accounting of that history,” said Bryan. “Californians deserve to know which companies built their wealth on the backs of enslaved people – and they deserve that truth under oath.” Melissa Hellmann, senior reporter on Guardian US’s race and equity team

Finally made it to the V&A East for The Music Is Black exhibition, which traces 125 years of Black British music, and have been rinsing the playlist ever since. It begins with a sombre look at attempts to stifle Black creativity and expression during enslavement, with a slave voyage map showing that more enslaved Africans were taken from the west Africa coast to Brazil than any other country, manumission papers and the “Slaves’ Bible”, which had any passages on freedom and equality edited out to curb rebellion. It moves on to the music Black people brought with them through migration – jazz, blues, lover’s rock, trip-hop in Bristol, ska in Coventry, jungle and grime – effortlessly conveying the role Black musicians have played in shaping the music scene in Britain. No stone is left unturned in this thoroughly immersive exhibition. Angela

This month marks the 25th anniversary of the Durban declaration and programme of action, which acknowledged the transatlantic slave trade as a crime against humanity. It was adopted in September 2001 at the World Conference Against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance in Durban, South Africa, and was a major turning point for the global reparations movement – although there is still much to be done.

‘Not just Hollywood crap’: Mike Leigh on the East End communist who brought world cinema to the UK

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 14:05:03 GMT

A new season celebrates Contemporary Films and its founder Charles Cooper, who bet on Britain taking to Ingmar Bergman, Yasujiro Ozu, Satyajit Ray – and a young Mike Leigh

Occasionally, vital pieces of the cultural jigsaw disappear without anyone really noticing. This, sadly, was the fate of Contemporary Films, the British film distributor that popularised sophisticated, grownup international cinema – foreign language mostly – in the UK, and heralded the arrival of the auteur generation with directors such as Ingmar Bergman, Satyajit Ray, Andrzej Wajda and Yasujiro Ozu.

Contemporary, and its founder Charles Cooper, weren’t the only game in town – Kenneth Rive’s Gala was a fellow traveller – but Contemporary got there first, setting up shop in 1951, first with short films for the then popular film society sector, and moving into features with the 1952 Japanese film Children of Hiroshima. Its marketplace clout faded rapidly in the early 1990s, when it was a victim of changing industry practices. But amazingly, the company is still with us – and is planning a 75th anniversary series of screenings to showcase its history.

Such is Contemporary’s lustre that, along with screenings of films such as Miloš Forman’s A Blonde in Love, Bergman’s Wild Strawberries and Jack Hazan’s David Hockney documentary A Bigger Splash, the great and good are turning out in support, led by Mike Leigh, whose feature film directing debut, Bleak Moments, was picked up by Contemporary in 1971. “It was a great honour,” Leigh says. “One was used to seeing ‘Contemporary Films’ on all the movies one saw that weren’t just Hollywood crap.”

Bleak Moments, a studiedly funny and weird film based on Leigh’s own stage play, is about a woman living an isolated life with a sister with a learning disability and a boring job. It was financed by Albert Finney, still riding high on his 1960s acting successes. As a homegrown, off-kilter feature, it was a slightly unusual item for Contemporary to pick up. “We were fresh on the block and innocent,” says Leigh, “and you take everything for granted in some way. But actually, when you think about it, they were pretty remarkable and they embraced this thing.”

Now a Palme d’Or and Golden Lion winner, Leigh undoubtedly understands the impact the company had on his own development. But it is its effect on the wider culture, the openness and cosmopolitanism that Contemporary helped to foster, that is arguably its most important contribution. “I grew up in Manchester,” says Leigh, “and I saw movies all the time, but I never saw a film that wasn’t in English. I saw only Hollywood and British movies. So when I came to London, world cinema suddenly presented itself. I have recollections of seeing Russian films, Italian neorealism, you name it. It was all going on, and Contemporary was very much at the centre of that.”

Cooper, the driving force behind it all, was an East End Jew – the son of a butcher from Ukraine – and a committed communist who saw cinema as a way to build awareness. Before the second world war, he brought Soviet films to the UK via Kino, the film section of the Workers’ Theatre Movement, then spent the war in New York running a film section for the International Workers Order.

Deported from the US in 1950, Cooper set about supplying films to hungry fans in film societies, of which there were an estimated 200 across Britain. The increasing interest in foreign “art” films meant Cooper was in tune with the intellectual times, with his special interest in eastern European and underclass-oriented films.

Part of Cooper’s strength, it seems, was his devotion to family life and willingness to involve his children in his day-to-day. His daughters from his first marriage agree. Adi Cooper, now a board member of Social Work England, says: “Charles was in the right place at the right time in terms of capturing a market for the sort of films he was interested in, which branched out from political ones into what you would now call, I guess, arthouse cinema. He was prepared to take a risk on people who were unheard of here at the time, some of whom went on to have a much wider appeal.”

Her twin, Sue Cooper, a founder member of 1970s punk act Poison Girls, says: “There wasn’t much separation between work and home with Charles. He really was passionate about film and politics, and he was very motivated to expose people’s thinking to different cultures. He was basically an internationalist and a humanist.” They regale me with anecdotes about screenings in the basement of their Wembley home (“The room is crammed full of people! I’m two feet from the back wall gazing up at this film called Alexander Nevsky”) to messing about in the school holidays at the company’s Frith Street office (“pasting press cuttings into scrapbooks and getting seven and sixpence for three hours’ work”).

Also key to Contemporary’s success was the relationship Cooper nurtured with George Hoellering, the Hungarian émigré who ran the celebrated Academy cinema on London’s Oxford Street which, throughout the 1950s and 60s, was the flagship venue for these kind of films. “They were joined at the hip,” says Pete Lawley, Contemporary’s current managing director. “They were the gold standard of the time.”

Hoellering died in 1984, by which time Cooper had his own cinemas: the Paris Pullman and Phoenix cinema in London and another Phoenix in Oxford. Lawley, who came on board in 2023, outlines Contemporary’s decline: as Cooper’s health began to fail in the late 1980s, he passed control to his second wife, Kitty Furstenberg, who in turn sold it on to their friend Eric Liknaitzky, who died in 2023. Although Contemporary did acquire some of the key indies of the late 80s and early 1990s, including Patricia Rozema’s I’ve Heard the Mermaids Singing, Jane Campion’s Sweetie and Hal Hartley’s The Unbelievable Truth, it seems the shift to home entertainment formats in the 90s passed Contemporary by. Instead it stuck to occasional re-releases of tried and tested classics from their archive.

Lawley says Contemporary has kept going by licensing clips from their catalogue; he has been sorting through the copious company documentation and says he is now working on plans for the future. “It’s very important to me,” he says. “I really want to keep it going. It can’t be about the money, let’s put it that way. It may be small, but there’s something worthwhile to build upon.”

Contemporary 75 begins with a screening of Bleak Moments and Mike Leigh in conversation. at the BFI Southbank, London, on 3 September and runs until 11 October at cinemas across London

Jess Cartner-Morley’s September style essentials: slipper-soft shoes, miracle hair mist and a worth-the-wait cardigan

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 14:00:01 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Got that new term feeling? Embrace the September reset with tailored blazers, hints of cashmere and a surprisingly excellent tee

Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

Nobody has handed me a timetable in decades, but I still love that new-term energy, and this edit leans right into it. A blazer that is properly tailored, rather than assembled from buttons and hope. Closed-toe shoes to ensure a proper soft landing after months of sandals. A T-shirt from a brand I was fully prepared to be sniffy about, until it made me eat my words. And a packing solution, because the only sane way to deal with the end of summer is to plan a holiday, obviously.

There’s also a genius lip colour for lip balm addicts like me, a bag doing a very convincing impression of something 10 times its price, and one long-sold-out cardigan that was worth every month of the wait.

Onwards, into the good stuff.

Herringbone wool blend blazer

A blazer with a waist is so elegant, but proper tailoring is usually expensive. High-street versions tend to rely on button placement to create shape, which is uncomfortable and doesn’t give a smooth curve. This herringbone beauty has proper internal structure to give a beautiful line that holds. Classy details: peak lapels, flap pockets at the hip, back vent, inner pocket. Snap it up.

Soft leather shoes

Cheap shoes are a false economy if they’re not comfortable. Those plastic heel stiffeners that are used to stiffen synthetic uppers give me blisters just looking at them. Zara shoes are highly variable in this regard, but these are a delight. Like slippers! And the narrow profile and high fastening – sort of a jazz shoe silhouette – are quite chic and now. I’ve got them in ecru, which is low in stock, but they also come in this black shade.

Sora fitted T-shirt

I’ll be honest: I didn’t think a fashion brand founded by an influencer would be my sort of thing. I’ve never worn an “airport fit” in my life and I don’t intend to start now. But Molly-Mae’s brand Maebe has some excellent bits. This T-shirt has subtle shoulder pads – removable if that’s not your thing, but I like them – and the draped, gathered waist creates shape without clinging. Good to have our prejudices challenged, no?

Compression cubes, set of four

… but there is always more to learn. Specifically, this summer I realised the difference between regular packing cubes and compression cubes. Sorry if this is obvious and I was being thick, but packing cubes just keep your stuff organised. Compression cubes come with two zips – one to close the cube, a second one to squeeze all the air out – and reduce the space your clothes take up by at least half. As a hand-luggage-only person, this is a revelation. These aren’t the cheapest but Antler knows its stuff, and it’s worth investing in quality because you need to be able to give that zip a good yank.

For more, read the Filter’s test of the best packing cubes

Wonderskin lip stain in Crush

I read that “this went viral on TikTok” and thought “not for me then”, so apologies that this sat on my desk for months. Now I am OBSESSED, as the young people say. I can’t wear lipstick, as my every-five-minute lip-balm habit smears it off before breakfast. This is a stain. Paint it on – it’s an absolutely bonkers metallic navy colour, so you look insane for one or two minutes until it dries – then wipe it off with a damp cotton pad. Your lips are then stained a gorgeous colour that doesn’t budge however much Vaseline you smear on top, while the formula doesn’t dry them out. I have it in “Crush”, a rosy pink shade.

Juliette soft large tote

The trapezoid shape and gusseted side panels caught my eye – squint and you’re looking at The Row’s Marlo tote – but the details reeled me in. There’s a flat base to minimise rummaging, bottom studs to keep it off germy floors, a removable laptop sleeve and drink bottle holder, a D-ring top closure, an internal zip pocket and a sleeve to pass over luggage handles for when you are travelling. (You can have your initials embossed here if you are fancy.) The chocolate colourway is sold out, but the black and “whiskey” are also divine.

One for Smoothness hair mist

I recommend quite a lot of hair products, but as Fleabag so rightly said, “HAIR IS EVERYTHING”. I promise you that for every one I mention there are endless others that I don’t because they don’t do what they promise. I have fine, dry hair, which generally means I have to choose between products that make it shiny and smooth but also flat and boring, or products that give volume and bounce but leave it crunchy and horrible. Gielly Green has a gorgeous salon in central London where I occasionally go for a treat – when they wash your hair the chair converts into a flat bed so you don’t crick your neck, which is heaven – and it makes this excellent spray: spritz it on to damp hair before you blow-dry.

Cashmere micro-bandana

I love Rise & Fall and I know a lot of you lovely people do too. If you don’t know it yet, it’s a British brand that buys products direct from the manufacturers of the finest materials. So you get cashmere sweaters and organic cotton bed linen made by the people who make them for the fanciest brands – without the retail mark-up. A bit of an in-the-know secret, but we don’t gatekeep here. This micro-bandana, available in poppy and buttermilk, will take the edge off the first chills of autumn.

Fit and Flare dress

Dresses are tricky at the moment. Plenty to choose from if you want trad-wife puff sleeves and waftiness, but no thanks. You’re grand if you want Maga newsreader spray-on shift dresses, but again, not for me. But I’ve found a goodie! This is a textured shirt dress, not too short, with a detachable belt if you want more shape.

Doriane cardigan

I tried this on in Sézane’s Marylebone store a few months ago, but didn’t buy it because, do you really need another black top etc etc. Anyway, I couldn’t stop thinking about it (the little lozenges of skin that run between the buttons just make it a bit fun, if you know what I mean) but it was then consistently sold out. It’s now back in stock, so I’ve got mine and I love it. Also, Sézane has had a rebrand this season – French girl chic is growing up, we love to see it – so definitely worth a browse.

Autistic boy who took replica knife to school has exclusion quashed by high court

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 14:00:00 GMT

Boy’s mother says she hopes case will help others, as judge says exclusion should be ‘a tool of last resort’

The mother of a 10-year-old autistic boy who had his permanent exclusion from a primary school quashed by the high court has said she hopes the ruling helps other children.

The boy, who cannot be named, was permanently excluded from his primary school, part of the Lift academy chain, after coming to school in July 2025 with a replica butterfly knife, which he handed to a friend to use against another child during an altercation in the playground.

The knife was described as having unsharpened blades and rounded ends, and when the child used it against the other child no significant injury was caused.

The judge said there had been differences of opinion about whether the knife was made of metal or plastic and that it may have been closer to a “fidget toy” than an unsharpened or training version of a weapon.

The school excluded the boy, first temporarily and then permanently, on the basis of the incident.

In his judgment, the deputy high court judge Alan Bates identified a range of concerns with the way the school and the governors disciplinary panel had reached their decision, including whether the decision was proportional.

He said that permanent exclusion should be “a tool of last resort” and that those considering whether to exclude a child should make a careful assessment of whether allowing the pupil to return to the school would seriously harm the welfare of the pupil or of others at the school.

As a result of this case, the judge recommended the Department for Education (DfE) update its guidance about permanent exclusions from schools, saying it could “fairly” be said to be unclear or incomplete.

According to DfE data, in the autumn term of the 2024-25 year there were 3,700 permanent exclusions from schools in England, 85% in secondary schools, 14% in primary schools and 1% in special schools. It is highly unusual for a school exclusion case of this kind to reach the high court.

“I am so happy about this high court ruling,” the boy’s mother said. “I hope it will help the lives of many children and young people in other schools. Both my son and I were so upset about the school’s decision to permanently exclude him. We didn’t think things had been dealt with fairly. I just felt that they wanted to get rid of my son.

“It was a long and complicated process to fight this and at one point I nearly gave up. But the situation was so upsetting and frustrating that I was determined to continue to challenge the exclusion.”

A spokesperson for Lift schools said: “We respect the court’s judgment and are carefully considering its implications. We are reviewing the published detail and will be reflecting the findings in our own exclusion guidance, training and governance arrangements so that future decisions clearly evidence the factors considered and the reasoning behind them.”

Angelo Monni of Duncan Lewis solicitors, representing the boy, said: “The decision provides important guidance for schools, academy trusts, governors, local authorities and families, and is likely to significantly influence how permanent exclusion decisions are approached in future. The judgment provides important guidance that will need to be followed by schools, and is a vindication for our client and his mother.”

A DfE spokesperson said: “We will carefully consider the judgment and the judge’s observations. Permanent exclusion should only ever be a last resort, used to protect the education or welfare of the pupil or others in the school community. Headteachers must consider any contributing factors, including whether a pupil’s behaviour may stem from an unmet need or a special educational need or disability. We’ve recently updated our statutory exclusion guidance and will keep it under review, so schools, governing boards and independent review panels have the clarity they need.”

Gaps in NHS end-of-life care ‘denying ill children chance to die at home’

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 13:00:58 GMT

Campaigners say some care boards in England flouting their legal duty, resulting in ‘cruel’ postcode lottery

Seriously ill children are being denied the chance to die at home because the NHS in many parts of England is flouting its legal duty to provide the care needed to make that happen, critics say.

The widespread failure to provide at-home end-of-life care is forcing children who want to die at home to instead do so in hospital. Campaigners have described it as “cruel”.

The postcode lottery in palliative care means some of the almost 89,000 under-19s in England who have a life-limiting condition may not get their wish to die at home. Medical advances mean their numbers have almost trebled since 2003-04, and the complexities of their illnesses have increased. About 1,600 die each year.

Nick Carroll, the chief executive of the charity Together for Short Lives, said: “It is shocking that children with serious illnesses are waiting to leave hospital because the health and care system is not taking responsibility for their community care. To deny families the chance to spend precious moments together at home before their child dies is simply cruel.”

He accused the NHS of neglect for not ensuring that all children who want to can die at home with specialist teams including doctors, nurses and therapists on hand during their final days. “Families have every right to be upset as they continue to be overlooked,” Carroll said.

The NHS’s 42 integrated care boards (ICBs) are legally obliged under the Health and Care Act 2022 to ensure such care is provided around the clock at home when a child is dying. But 15 (36%) of them do not commission such services, freedom of information requests by Together for Short Lives show.

Only 13 (31%) were able to show they were doing so. Ten (24%) were providing some but not all of the care they should, and three (7%) said they were still organising such care.

The lack of provision means very sick children are ending up having to seek help at A&E or be admitted to hospital, some of whom then die there rather than at home.

Carroll said: “Our research shows that many families, simply because they live in a certain area, may be denied the chance to have their child die in the safety and comfort of their own home because ministers and the NHS have failed to put the right care in place. That should shame us all.”

He blamed the situation on ICBs’ precarious finances and on their “widespread assumption that palliative care is primarily for older adults, despite thousands of children across England living with life-shortening and life-threatening conditions”.

He said while an early draft of the government’s forthcoming “modern service framework” for palliative care specifically mentioned babies, children and young people, that reference was not included in the most recent version.

Sarah Buchan Cooke said it made a huge difference to the whole family when her son Dylan was able to die at home in January 2023, just before he turned four, after a long spell in hospital. He had Sandhoff disease, a rare neurodegenerative condition that left him needing 24/7 care.

Great Ormond Street children’s hospital and Haven House, a children’s hospice, both in London, supported the family in Dylan’s final days.

“At the end of his life it was a beautiful thing to have him at home. I can’t really imagine it any other way. I’m very aware of how fortunate we were,” Buchan Cooke said.

“It breaks my heart to think of other families in our situation not being able to have that same level of care and support. You’re the one who knows your child best. That ability to choose [between home and hospital] means everything.”

In March, Rachel de Souza, the children’s commissioner for England, highlighted that some children, including with life-limiting illnesses, were spending months and sometimes years in hospital because of a lack of “safe or appropriate” alternatives elsewhere.

Delays in arranging packages of care, a shortage of children’s social care placements and housing issues were “leaving children and their families in impossible situations”, de Souza said. Such children are disproportionately from poor backgrounds or ethnic minorities, data shows.

The NHS Alliance, which represents ICBs, did not respond directly to the findings. It agreed with the charity that access to end-of-life care for children should be universal but emphasised that commissioning such services could be “complex”.

Ian Perrin, the alliance’s assistant director of integrated care, said: “Every child with a life-limiting condition, and every family supporting them, should be able to access high-quality, compassionate palliative and end-of-life care, regardless of where they live.

“ICBs recognise the vital role that children’s hospices, community services, specialist teams and voluntary sector partners play in supporting children and their families. As the services are delivered through a range of organisations and arrangements vary across the country, this can make commissioning complex and difficult to compare consistently.

“However, ICBs remain committed to working with families, providers, charities and national partners to reduce unwarranted variation, improve access to care and ensure more people can receive care closer to home.”
