The rich and powerful are already trying to sway the next election – I have a plan to stop them

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 12:00:58 GMT

A bill proposing a cap on donations is up for debate this week. We must seize this chance to keep big money out of our politics

Christopher Harborne gave Reform £9m in one day – more than double the amount all trade unions combined gave Labour nationally and its MPs directly for the entirety of the last general election. Once such “largesse” in our politics was rare, now it is commonplace. In 2015, just 1% of donations were from individuals and companies giving £1m or more – by 2024, that figure was a third. The chequebooks of the rich and powerful are already circling the next election. The question for Labour is, are we prepared to pay the price if we refuse to stop them?

The prime minister deserves credit for recognising how toxic this has become and the public support for action too. As a result, on Wednesday, measures to cap what overseas donors can give will come before parliament in the representation of the people bill. Yet focusing on location rather than the level of a donation misses how wealthy individuals can set up a UK shell company or use a UK postcode to continue to dominate our democracy. With several British millionaires already funding political entities and parties and others waiting in the wings, our goal must be to ensure no one – near or far – can buy Westminster.

Labour is yet to commit to this because some are uneasy that capping individual donations could lead to calls to cap collective donations from membership organisations and trade unions. This is not the first time this fear has led to inaction. The Phillips review of party funding in 2007 collapsed over this dilemma, despite support from major Labour donors including Lord Sainsbury for a cap. With hindsight, we can see how this opened the door for the crisis we now face.

That is why I have proposed an amendment to the bill – new clause 120 – that would introduce an immediate £500,000 annual cap on donations, falling to £100,000 in the following calendar year. This would give the government until the end of the second year to establish a permanent cap. Whatever level is ultimately chosen could not exceed £500,000 and would have to be approved by parliament, giving all MPs the chance to shape the final scheme.

Critically NC120 explicitly exempts trade unions from the cap if they abide by the existing rules around political funds. Thousands of working people pooling their contributions through a democratic membership organisation is not the same as one extraordinarily wealthy individual writing a cheque for millions of pounds. Since 1913, there has been legislation on how trade union funds can be used – making the comparative lack of parity in how we regulate moneys given by companies and individuals even more startling.

Most of us could never dream of having £100,000 to give to a political party. We make ourselves heard by voting, campaigning, volunteering, joining political parties and organising collectively. Safeguarding such organisations on all parts of the political spectrum is therefore also part of a healthy democracy because they allow people who could never wield significant financial power individually to act together.

The government has now said it will consider lowering the amount of money political parties are permitted to spend. This is welcome if it happens, but is only half the solution to stopping the voices of ordinary people from being increasingly drowned out by those of billionaires and big business. Without a donation cap, too, donors will circumvent rules by using local groups, parties will stockpile funds and enforcement will be retrospective at best.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

If passed, the proposal coming before parliament would mean the government would not have to agree on the formal limit now. We would only have to agree that there should be one for all donors – whatever passport they hold – and to act before the next election. Such a deadline would also prevent disagreement about details becoming a convenient excuse for doing nothing at all.

In common with Donald Trump, Nigel Farage is clear he intends to keep taking the sums in question and celebrates those giving. Inevitably, when political parties can accept unlimited individual donations, politics degenerates into a fundraising arms race. One party attracts a multimillion-pound donor, so another goes searching for its own to be able to compete.

As a democratic as well as socialist movement, Labour cannot stand by as our democracy disintegrates under these pressures. Opposing donation caps is at odds with helping to organise the will of working people against the dominance of capital. Political power should not simply belong to whoever has the most money. Without a meaningful cap, each new quarterly donation report for Westminster politics will provide another nail in the coffin for our hopes of doing things differently. If we fail to seize this moment, the largest wallets will become the loudest voices in deciding Britain’s future.

Stella Creasy is Labour and Cooperative MP for Walthamstow

‘We’re hunky in our own way’: Modern Family’s Mitch and Cam on their hilarious and groundbreaking love

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 11:59:31 GMT

Jesse Tyler Ferguson and Eric Stonestreet proved that opposites really do attract in the smash hit sitcom. But beyond the bickering and and pranks, there was a romance so special that it changed many fans’ lives

Opposites attract. And spend most of their time arguing. But the love between Cameron and Mitchell Tucker-Pritchett remained strong throughout the 11 years of Modern Family.

The two met at a games night when Mitch rolled his eyes every time Cam “got a little boisterous”. They married in two of the most romantic and near-disastrous TV episodes in living memory and raised two adopted children, Lily and Rexford. Being a groundbreaking gay TV couple came at a price: critics wanted more PDAs and less fighting, but Cam and Mitch’s love shone bright.

“Mitch and Cam were a gay couple raising a child on TV, so the microscope was zoomed in with a little more focus so a lot of their flaws were heightened,” says Jesse Tyler Ferguson, who plays Mitch. “But I think, when you sit back and look at it, you can see how much love there is between those two people and the family they created.”

The chemistry between Tyler Ferguson and TV partner Eric Stonestreet is so strong that talking to them is like watching an episode of Modern Family. “There was never any doubt, even in the early years when we were getting to know each other, that this was going to be someone who’d be in my life for ever,” says Tyler Ferguson. Stonestreet remains tight-lipped, but the affection is powerful. “If I’m in your world jacking with you, then you can take it to the bank that I’m in love with you,” he says.

Modern Family ran from 2009 to 2020, when Cam and Mitch drove off to live happily ever after in Missouri. Tyler Ferguson and Stonestreet live in different cities, but still see each other and talk regularly – and their love for the characters lives on.

ES: We met when the producers were testing potential Cams with their already-cast Mitchell.

JTF: It was like speed dating, meeting all these different guys and waiting for chemistry to happen. I was certainly drawn to Eric as a person. He was very kind, sweet and excited to be there. Do you want to bring up the Z snap or not?

ES: I’ll set it up and you finish it. I’d had three auditions and I’d learned where the laughs were and had a take on the character, so I was very confident. Then we get to the big moment – the network test – and I wasn’t feeling it. So …

JTF: The room was a little less warm than Eric had been experiencing before. In this moment where he thought that there should be a laugh and there wasn’t one, he panicked and did a gay Z snap.

ES: To this day I have no knowledge of where that came from. I knew it was a ridiculous thing to do and I left thinking I’d messed up. But Jesse was very kind. I remember you saying: “Really good job, that was awesome.”

JTF: The most iconic romances develop when opposites attract, like Sam and Diane in Cheers or Ross and Rachel in Friends. Mitch lived a very sheltered life as far as being in the closet and he finds a lot of comfort in Cam’s free spirit.

ES: Here are these two imperfect people who’ve found each other and the perfectness in each other. That makes the characters likable immediately. It gets the relationship so much further down the road when it’s not two hunky dudes. Well, we’re hunky in our own way.

JTF: The whole PDA thing was so interesting to me. When you looked at all the couples on the show, there’s not a tonne of PDA between Jay and Gloria either, but because we were the gay couple we took the heat.

ES: What really hurt my feelings in the beginning was people saying because I was straight I didn’t want to kiss Jesse. First of all, that’s stupid and secondly I’d been in a very gay cult classic movie called Girls Will Be Girls where I’d made out with a drag queen, so please, girl.

JTF: The writers’ response to that is that Mitch has a fear of PDA and then they made this wonderful episode called The Kiss where there’s a moment between Mitch and his dad showing affection and then in the background you see Cam and Mitch kiss. I found it so moving.

ES: I got caught up when people were saying Mitch and Cam argue a lot. There were times when I’d look at Jesse and go,“Here we go again,” but it was our job to make those arguments relatable.

JTF: I wish they had a better ground plan for their house. We’d always say it’s strange that they only have one bathroom and it’s right off the kitchen.

ES: It’s sprawling in Missouri, trust me.

JTF: Only in hindsight. I grew up gay and closeted in Albuquerque, New Mexico, and didn’t have anyone on television who was aspirational for me, like “I could get married and have kids”. To know that Eric and I are that for people makes this job feel like a gift.

ES: I don’t even know how to process it when a 14-year-old kid to comes up to me now and says: “I’m gay and I love your character and thank you so much.” The fact we have an effect on people’s lives who weren’t even born when we shot Modern Family is unreal and I’m so grateful.

JTF: Tears. People wanting to give me a hug and being so moved. That’s the good version. There’s also the ones where people are screaming and running down the street.

ES: People will come up to me and say: “I watched three episodes during my chemo and you helped me get through those treatments.” I was in New York City seeing a Broadway show and this woman stops me and she says: “Seeing you here tonight has brought my daughter back to life. You were my daughter’s favourite character and the last time I saw her laugh was watching you on Modern Family and you being here right now is like her being here.” I lost it and gave her the biggest, warmest hug I could.

ES: My dad was this big, burly guy and sometimes they’re the most romantic ones. You feel like you’ve won a different kind of prize because it’s not all out there for everyone to see. I think I’m romantic – I have the best gift for our one-year wedding anniversary [Eric is married to Lindsay Schweitzer].

JTF: I do my best to be romantic. Small acts of affection are very important to me and I show my love by planning date nights. I’m a great cook and I like to cook for Justin [Mikita, Jesse’s husband].

ES: I have the portrait that was above our fireplace of Mitch, Cam and Lily and a basket of fake lemons just because it was an inside joke with one of the producers, Chris Lloyd.

JTF: There were a few pieces that we fought over. I have this painting from the Cam and Mitch house and I don’t remember the details of why I was in a scene, but I ended up taking it.

ES: I’m more Mitchell off camera and Jesse’s more Cam. He’s breezy and will let things go and I’m the one who’s uptight and constantly worrying about everything. I really enjoyed strapping on my loafers and poufing my hair up because it gave me the chance to be a better version of myself, which is what Cam is.

JTF: Eric is very thoughtful as a friend and one of his love languages is pranks. He’s really good at the long-game prank, so he will show affection by creating scenarios that will bring joy to people but also give him pleasure. A lot of our relationship is him ruthlessly pranking me and teasing me and it all comes from a place of love.

JTF: It’s a long game. There are different phases of love – it has peaks and valleys that come with kids, jobs and getting to know each other and you have to allow fights to happen. My father-in-law always says: “We’ve been married 52 years, 33 happily” and he never specifies which they are.

ES: We wanted Mitch and Cam to reflect real relationships. My wife, Lindsay, gives me permission to be myself and I desperately want her to be herself and although Mitch would raise a judging eyebrow every once in a while at something Cam would do, they love each other in the face of imperfection.

JTF: I have the utmost faith in them and their relationship, so I think they’re still together. Absolutely.

Jesse Tyler Ferguson stars in Tru at the Menier Chocolate Factory, London, from 19 September to 14 November.

‘I was scared to tell my old teammates’: Victoria Pelova on making leap from Arsenal to Spurs

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 11:00:03 GMT

While move across north London has been amicable, the Dutch midfielder is relishing clash with former club

There is not the same intensity to club rivalries between women’s teams as there is between their men’s counterparts, but as the game grows that is changing. Increasingly, there is animosity from fans if a player leaves for a rival side.

Victoria Pelova’s move from Arsenal to Tottenham firmly bucks the trend, though. Despite arguably having her best years ahead of her, the 27-year-old departed with a lot of well wishes and love.

“I was really scared to tell my old teammates that I was going here,” Pelova says. “My close friends knew about it, obviously, but everyone responded so well. Everyone tells me that it reflects on the person I am. So, I’m actually really glad about that.”

Pelova has been an Arsenal fan favourite despite limited minutes in her three years at the club, during which she was hampered by an anterior cruciate ligament injury sustained on international duty in June 2024. Why is she so liked? She comes across as fun and is loved by her teammates, with a wicked and dry sense of humour.

Pelova was not worried what people would make of her move to Spurs, but the Netherlands midfielder did think about it. Ultimately, it was “an easy decision” to join Martin Ho’s squad.

“The way Martin approached me, what he said about how he sees me as a player, the videos he showed me and how he wants me to be, I’ve actually never had a coach talking like that about me. So, for me, it was a good decision. I talked a lot with my mum about it and she immediately said yes. That was actually the most important thing for me, what my mum thought.”

At the start of June, Pelova shared online that her mum had died. A carousel of moving photos of the pair through the years was captioned: “Your biggest fear was leaving me behind. My biggest fear was losing you. Rest now, Mum.”

Pelova is not ready to talk about the loss, but it sits in the background of the interview. Not having to move home as a result of her leaving Arsenal was important. “It does really help me that I have friends and family around me that take care of me,” she says.

Reflecting on her spell at Arsenal, with her ACL injury coming at a time when it was believed she would start to get more playing time, she says: “There was a private situation going on, my mum was ill, and I didn’t get minutes. So, it was a really tough time and people didn’t know what I was going through.”

The goal now? “To be happy again, in football and outside football, and just day by day see how it goes.

“It sounds like I have not been happy, but I have been happy in the last year and in being with my friends. But when you’re not playing as regularly as you want to it’s inevitable that you’re not going to be totally happy, and when I’m the happiest person, I will be the best footballer I can be.”

The fresh start at Tottenham has been rejuvenating. “It’s nice to have no one know you. For me, that’s the way to go. I don’t know if I can explain it, but I feel like when everyone knows you, they focus on the things they know.”

Ho made an instant impression on Pelova. “All the coaches I’ve met are always like: ‘Oh, you can play there and there and there.’ Martin was like: ‘You’re this for me.’ He knew exactly where he wanted me and what he wanted from me. That, right away, set the tone for me and it was where and how I see myself as well. What I’ve seen so far is that he’s so detailed. He just wants to make you better. He’s very strict, but he wants to make you a better player and that’s why I’m here.”

after newsletter promotion

Ho has “a lot” of confidence in her, and that is hugely freeing. “That’s the part I don’t have to worry about … and I can focus on other things.”

Pelova’s experience of Tottenham had been playing against them, and the more difficult that got, the more it contributed to her decision to join. “Defending was so hard,” she says of facing Spurs last season. “So, I already liked the style Martin had the team playing. I also already know Caitlin Dijkstra; I’ve known her for eight years and we lived together in Amsterdam so we know each other so well. She’s like my sister. I know Lize Kop, they’re also one of my closest friends. So, that has made the transition easy because I can always rely on them.

“I’m quite social so I’ve been trying to get to know everyone, the youngsters. It’s quite a hard job in the beginning, it’s intense, but I like it. On the pitch, you’re building relationships, pre-season is always heavy, you just need to grind, but it has been good.”

Pelova has belief in herself and her body, too. “We train really hard. That’s different to what I’m used to. So, obviously it goes up and down, but I’m confident that in a few weeks everything as a team will have progressed so much. Always with new players, it needs time. I’ve been in football a really long time so I know how it goes.”

Asked about Tottenham’s chances of disrupting things at the top, she flips the question, then says she relishes being outsiders. “You need to put us on as underdogs. The underdog position is the place to be.”

Now, Pelova is ready for the intensity of pre-season to end and for the games to begin at home against West Ham on Sunday. One, in particular, stands out, and it comes on 25 October at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. “Please, stop pre-season,” she says with a laugh. “I just want to start. I can’t wait to play against all the teams. I can’t wait to play against Arsenal.”

Happy 60th anniversary, Notting Hill carnival – a symbol of all that London can be

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 10:15:26 GMT

Its founders understood the power of culture to challenge racism, build understanding and turn strangers into neighbours. We need that now as much as ever

Sadiq Khan is the mayor of London

This bank holiday weekend, the streets of Notting Hill once again set the stage for one of the greatest celebrations on Earth.

Children danced through the streets in a blaze of colour. Costume-makers with deft fingers created masterpieces from feathers, sequins and gems. Street vendors served up world-class pepperpot, Trinidadian roti and jerk chicken, and sound systems and steelpan bands shook the streets with the unmistakable sound of carnival.

On its 60th anniversary, Notting Hill carnival proved itself to be bigger, bolder and more vibrant than ever. It’s now the world’s second-largest street festival, attracting people from around the globe and generating a whopping £400m for our economy each year.

But carnival has always been much more than just a party. It’s a loud and proud celebration of Caribbean culture and the extraordinary contribution that Caribbean communities have made to our capital city. For me, it represents London at its very best: people of different ages, backgrounds, colours and creeds coming together, sharing in the joy of one another’s traditions and cultures, and celebrating the incredible diversity that has come to define the city we all call home.

That’s why I was delighted to step forward with an additional £4.66m of funding – more than triple the amount we provided last year – to help ensure Londoners and visitors could once again enjoy this incredible event. The money we made available was vital for supporting organisers to implement increased safety measures, including doubling the number of stewards and allowing more signs and temporary CCTV cameras to be installed.

The 60th anniversary of carnival is a landmark moment for London and I was determined City Hall should pull out all the stops to assist because it’s also a reminder of how far we’ve come as a city.

From the late 1940s, thousands of Caribbean migrants sailed to London as part of the Windrush generation, to help rebuild a postwar nation on its knees. Despite coming at Britain’s invitation, however, many of the new arrivals found themselves unwelcome in their new home. Forced to live in cramped, poor-quality housing, they were frequently excluded from public spaces and jobs, and subjected to widespread racism and abuse – fuelled by the far right and fascist groups who sought to stir up hatred and division.

In 1958, racist violence erupted on the streets of Notting Hill, with Black Londoners attacked and homes damaged. The following year, Black Londoners across the city demanded justice after the police failed to properly investigate the racist murder of Kelso Cochrane, a young carpenter from Antigua.

It was in the face of this appalling racism and violence that the seeds of carnival were planted. First, Trinidadian activist and journalist Claudia Jones decided to organise Britain’s first Caribbean carnival at St Pancras town hall. Broadcast on the BBC, the carnival used the power of music and dance to help heal a hurting community and show the rest of the country the richness and joy of Caribbean culture.

A few years later, local activist Rhaune Laslett organised a community fair designed to bring her diverse Notting Hill neighbourhood together. It was then that something magical happened. As their set finished, Russ Henderson and his steelpan band carried on playing as they walked up Portobello Road, taking the crowd with them. A neighbourhood party became a street procession – and the rest, as they say, is history.

Sixty years later, the seeds planted by Claudia, Rhaune, Russ and countless others have grown into something extraordinary. Today, London without carnival is almost impossible to imagine. It’s become a much-loved fixture of our city’s cultural calendar, and for many Londoners, one of the most highly anticipated weekends of the year.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

But as the event has grown, the challenge of keeping carnival-goers safe has grown with it. That’s why this year I again stepped in to provide the necessary funding to support the delivery of a safer carnival. And let me be clear: as long as I’m mayor, carnival will remain where the local community wants it to be – on the streets of Notting Hill.

Our city has come a long way since those first celebrations. But we know that racism has not disappeared. Indeed, the frightening rise of nativist populist movements in recent years demonstrates that the urgent work of tackling prejudice and building a fairer city is far from finished.

But what carnival’s founders understood is the extraordinary power of culture: to challenge racism, build understanding and turn strangers into neighbours. They responded to a moment of division and fear with unadulterated joy – and in doing so, they helped shape a more open and inclusive London for all of us.

So to everyone who has carried carnival forward over the past 60 years – the pioneers, organisers, masqueraders, musicians, costume-makers, volunteers, police officers, paramedics and generations of Londoners who have made it their own – thank you. Here’s to another 60 years of celebrating our incredible communities and this beautiful city we have built together.

Sadiq Khan is mayor of London

It’s September. Time to put your knees away

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 10:00:02 GMT

From May to August, social media is awash with photos of brown knees. But summer’s almost over and they’re all starting to blur together

It’s the start of September, so time to bid adieu to the classic holiday selfie: two brown knees. If it’s on the socials there might be a caption – #bestlife, #bliss – and if it’s in a text it needs no explanation at all, because its message is universal. I am in a hot place. I am doing what I please, mainly supine. I have knees.

Everyone’s knees look the same, which is weird given the sheer variety of body shapes, and everyone’s background is mainly the same: a body of water, conceivably a mountain. There might be a cocktail to the side, but there will never be anything interesting, such as a dog, because that would dispel the serenity. It would be good if the knees were just a frame, and between them some distant, barely legible scene were playing out, such as a sword fight or a harras of many-coloured horses, but that would run counter to the vibe: “I am completely at peace and definitely not seeking out horses and lying near them for clicks.”

The knees arrive in May and by August you will have seen most of your friends’, except that since they are all interchangeable, you don’t remember who’s been where and you have no way of telling whose bliss is the greatest. It would really help if someone would sunburn their knees, but if they do, that’s an image they’ll never share, ditto any mosquito bites or knee imperfections or pastiness. But then, I don’t need a gritty, warts-and-all portrait of the holiday season – I just want to be confident that everyone I’ve ever met and many, many people I haven’t have fully hinged legs.

Knee season is countercyclical (almost) with football season, so for the rest of the year we see only elite knees, and that’s fine too. None of this is a criticism, and nobody here thinks there was anything to be said for a time before phones.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Colin Kaepernick knelt 10 years ago. America responded with a clear warning to Black people

The Guardian Tue, 01 Sep 2026 07:30:47 GMT

A decade after Kaepernick’s quiet protest shook the NFL, his exile looks less like an aberration than a blueprint for the culture war that followed

America likes nice round numbers, perfect for anniversaries and reflections, and it has, suddenly, been 10 years since Colin Kaepernick first protested police killings – more accurately, police killings of Black people that went unpunished either internally or by the courts – by taking a knee during the national anthem for the entirety of the 2016 NFL regular season. He never played in the league again.

Ten years covers a lot of ground, especially in these years of American darkness, and many of the important details surrounding Kaepernick, his banishment and significance have disappeared, time replaced by more time and more darkness – time moving faster than ever, at internet speed, where nothing matters, where nothing sticks. We consume by clip, by click, by meme, and knowledge by meme is not knowledge at all.

Much of the Kaepernick story was reduced to his personal banishment, but second to Barack Obama, Kaepernick is the face that propelled white anger into a “culture war” that continues earnestly into its second decade. It has traveled through the NFL, through Hollywood, the White House, and now is corroding the WNBA. Obama’s ascent to the White House confirmed the unlikely prospect that a Black person could be elected president, ostensibly the ultimate symbol of American possibility. It was not a universal sentiment.

In the annals of American protest, which has included suffragettes breaking windows, students blocking traffic, Black Panthers armed in public, economic boycotts and marches on Washington, Kaepernick was mild by comparison – he gave voice with 60 seconds of silence. “To me, this is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way,” he explained on 26 August 2016 after a preseason contest between his San Francisco 49ers and the Green Bay Packers (he sat on the bench during the anthem for that game, he would kneel for the first time the following week). “There are bodies in the street and people getting paid leave and getting away with murder.” Combined, however, Obama and Kaepernick represented the realization of the deepest of white fears, the assumptions and expectations of Black equality that has consumed a segment of the collective white American psyche since emancipation.

Ten years later, one view of the Kaepernick legacy can be seen through a harsh, retrofitted lens: sports leagues would largely purge the troublemakers and co-opt the protests, reducing them into useless, corporate-friendly gestures; an American electorate that voted Donald Trump into power twice, as his unapologetic, unambiguous racism reflected theirs; media outlets responding in agreement, coalescing around Trump’s whiteness, appeasing their rightsholders, readers and viewers by making the conscious choice – a clear and egregious dereliction of journalistic duty – to silence the voices within who make them uncomfortable; a player class that was never nearly as bold as its greatest legends well aware of Kaepernick’s fate, unwilling to repeat it, and operating as puppets.

They didn’t have far to go. While Trump called NFL players “sons of bitches” in his first term and demanded Kaepernick be banned from the league, NFL players undermined him. Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott assured his bosses in 2018 that he was no radical, not merely by playing football but demeaning Kaepernick’s protest. “For me, I believe in doing something, action. It’s not about taking a knee,” Prescott said, undermining centuries of evidence to the contrary about the efficacy of physical protest. Even the most devout Cowboys fan could probably not name a single example where Prescott took action. He simply didn’t want to get involved.

Michael Vick, ex-convict, killer of dogs, but redeemed by the NFL following his prison sentence, told Kaepernick to “cut his hair” if he sought a pathway to forgiveness. Hall of Famer Ray Lewis told Kaepernick to “keep his mouth shut”. It should be noted that Kaepernick was exiled from the NFL for kneeling – kneeling – while Lewis, connectable to an incident that resulted in two killings as an active player, was fined $250,000 by the NFL for pleading guilty to obstruction of justice and never missed a game.

Whether hostile or oblivious, white Americans have treated this nation as a personal possession they choose to share with others, quite different from a nation that belongs to all that must be shared collectively. This country, Black people know and are harshly reminded by their white countrymen whenever they have the temerity to forget, is theirs, and that proprietorship is codified by the everyday speech of white Americans – We let you attend our schools, live in our neighborhoods, be part of our communities, play in our professional sports – and is mirrored by Black speech alike. It is the fatal language of integration.

Such assumed proprietorship demands white people receive deference for their benevolence, explains their rage when they don’t get it. It also means they believe they can revoke the privilege of being American whenever that proprietorship is challenged, as Kaepernick discovered 10 years ago. The result was a continuum. Kaepernick losing his job has now become a political philosophy at the highest levels of government: Black people have not earned their positions through the grind of hard work, but from diversity initiatives.

Only in witnessing the slow-motion murder of George Floyd in 2020 during a global pandemic and the White House overreacting by rolling tanks through town and shooting at white people on the steps of their own houses did the country have a collective moment that it had all gone too far, that Kaepernick had been right all along. Even NFL commissioner Roger Goodell admitted, by pressure not conscience, that the league was wrong in its crackdown on player protest – but only briefly. The simmering hostility, never quieted, has increased anew.

The January 6 riots ended the period known as athlete activism, and in the wider sense, the Kaepernick era. They also ended whatever shreds of credibility remained from this nation of laws, and exposed the players as having surrendered. Wired to accept challenges and refuse defeat, the players were finally vindicated as hordes of white, real Americans, the ones who told them there were other ways to protest, wore T-shirts to stand for the flag and kneel for the cross, countered the Black Lives Matter protest without cleverness or style with Blue Lives Matter, and – at the order of the President of the United States – stormed the most symbolically important legislative building in the world. The players – perhaps mollified by Goodell’s apology, or Obama’s advice to NBA players to stop their protests after a weekend work stoppage following Jacob Blake’s shooting in Kenosha, general fatigue or knowing they were overmatched – didn’t say a thing. A cop – a member of that sacred occupation for which they ostensibly held so much respect – died in the aftermath of the January 6 riot. The mob ransacked the Capitol, and the American media tripped over itself debating whether to even call it a riot. It made sense. This is theirs, and you cannot trespass or riot on your own property.

There is the lesson of Kaepernick and there is his legacy. They are not the same. The lesson was largely directed toward other players. It was a threat. Kaepernick was the NFL’s Metacomet at Plymouth, head on a stake for the world to see, a warning for the rest to stay in line – and they have. What passes for protest today is a player writing something mildly profound on their cleats, but only on the designated game days when the NFL allows it.

The devastating rest is the legacy, far darker and yet in its own sense inspiring. The inspiration lies in the freedom of acknowledgment. There is no reason to continue the naive exercise of negotiation, of waiting for permission, of believing the moral arc of the universe bends toward justice, of believing equality is a shared American goal. It is not. What the country has become in these 10 years, with its 1,500 pardons, the proud anti-Blackness from this White House, the malleable ethics of a cowering corporate media that has largely stamped out the voices it once embraced as a “racial reckoning” – has proven it. Look at the wreckage.

Howard Bryant is the author of 11 books, including The Heritage: Black Athletes, A Divided America, and the Politics of Patriotism and Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America.

U. S. Launches Airstrikes on Iran for Second Time in Three Days

The New York Times September 01, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

U. S. Central Command did not say precisely what it was trying to destroy in Iran, but it said the attacks were aimed at Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

By Pranav Baskar and Farnaz Fassihi

The U. S. military said on Tuesday that it had struck military targets in Iran in retaliation for Iranian attacks on ships and U. S. forces in the region, raising the risk of the conflict escalating once again.

Hours later, the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps announced that the country had launched a “regretful response” to America’s strikes, though the group did not say how it was retaliating or where. It also accused the United States of bombing sites on the southern coast of Iran, including several civilian locations.

The exchange of strikes came after the two countries traded attacks on Sunday, puncturing a monthlong calm since President Trump pulled back after concerns over dwindling U. S. munition stockpiles, and unveiled a campaign to strangle Iran’s economy. The hostilities underscore that the conflict, which began six months ago, appears far from a durable solution.

U. S. Central Command did not specify where it was striking in Iran, but it said the attacks were targeting Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. Iranian state media said projectiles had hit sites in Chabahar and Konarak, two southern port cities east of the Strait of Hormuz.

In a social media post, Mr. Trump said the U. S. attacks were “large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait.” He added that “If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level.”

Two Iranian officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the U. S. attacks, said the strikes hit several sites across Iran’s southern shores, including a military base in Bandar Abbas, the perimeter of the commercial airport on Qeshm Island, and targets in Sirik and Jask. The officials said the attacks caused significant damage.

The deputy governor of the Hormozgan Province, Ahmad Nafisi, told state television that a wedding ceremony and a residential home were struck in the city of Kuhestak. Mr. Nafisi said two people were killed and at least 20 people were wounded. Central Command did not immediately comment.

Oil prices jumped and were up about 4 percent after the U. S. military said it had retaliated over Iranian strikes on commercial ships. Two ships were attacked within minutes of each other on Monday, according to Marisks, a risk consulting firm.

The U. S. military said on Sunday that its forces had bombarded Iranian troops on Larak Island that were preparing to launch rockets armed with mines into the Strait of Hormuz, the vital shipping corridor for oil and gas. Such an artillery weapon would be unusual, and it was not possible to independently confirm the military’s report.

The Iranian foreign ministry said several people were killed and wounded in Sunday’s strikes, but did not provide specifics.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said it retaliated by firing at bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates that host U. S. military personnel. The Jordanian authorities said that they had intercepted eight missiles in their airspace, while the Emirati military said it had “responded to” a drone from Iran. There were no reports of damage or casualties.

Even as the fighting slowed in recent weeks, there had been few signs of resolution to the issues at the heart of the war that Mr. Trump began in late February alongside Israel. A “memorandum of understanding” between Tehran and Washington quickly broke down after it was signed in late June.

Since then, Iran has fired on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz, severely curbing the ability of U. S. allies to export oil and gas, and gaining significant leverage. Iranian officials have demanded steep and immediate concessions in exchange for reopening the strait, which U. S. officials have rejected.

The Trump administration has sought to squeeze Tehran economically by enforcing a naval blockade on Iranian ports and increasing sanctions on Tehran. But thoroughly enforcing sanctions is notoriously hard, and Iran’s case would require messy run-ins with allies and powerful rivals capable of retaliation, most notably China.

Jenny Gross contributed reporting.

Pranav Baskar is an international reporter at The Times, based in New York.

Farnaz Fassihi is the United Nations bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of the organization. She also covers Iran and has written about conflict in the Middle East for 15 years.

OpenAI Is About to Release Its First AI Model With ‘Critical’ Cyber Abilities

Wired September 01, 2026

OpenAI announced Tuesday that its forthcoming AI model, Astra, is its first to reach the company’s threshold for what it calls “critical” cyber capabilities. OpenAI says it plans to publicly release a version of Astra “soon,” but will make the model’s advanced cyber capabilities available only to select partners in its Daybreak Blue early-access program at launch.

In a briefing with reporters, OpenAI safety and security leaders said the company has concluded that Astra reaches the critical cybersecurity capabilities outlined in its preparedness framework, which sets thresholds and protocols for when its AI models pose new levels of risk. The company says an AI model has reached its critical cyber threshold when it can independently find and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities in real-world software. OpenAI leaders said the company has followed its procedure for this situation, which is to halt further development until appropriate safeguards and security measures can be implemented.

OpenAI previously said that it paused some training workloads related to the development of Astra and a future AI model for several weeks. Executives say the company has now resumed said work on Astra, and the future AI model, after putting additional safety and security controls in place. OpenAI says the multi-week pause was productive, and it is now confident that it can release Astra broadly in a safe way.

The announcement comes as Silicon Valley grapples with the advanced cybersecurity capabilities of cutting-edge AI models, and tries to assure users, lawmakers, and other companies that it can keep them under control. In July, OpenAI disclosed an incident in which agents running two of its models exploited vulnerabilities in what was supposed to be a siloed testing environment, gaining access to the internet and hacking the open source AI platform Hugging Face. (OpenAI notes that Astra was not one of the models involved in this case.)

Other AI companies, such as Anthropic and Meta, have disclosed similar incidents in recent weeks. On Monday, Anthropic also said it has paused some AI training workloads while it hardens its safety and security practices.

OpenAI says it’s implementing a multi-step approach to limit everyday users from accessing Astra’s advanced cyber capabilities, including a new “misalignment monitor.” If someone asks Astra to help them find an exploit in a real-world software system, for example, the model is supposed to refuse to answer. OpenAI says it has also made Astra more robust to jailbreaking attempts, and in tests it successfully refused unsafe queries at a significantly higher rate than previous models.

However, OpenAI notes in a blog post that its misalignment monitor may “occasionally flag legitimate activity as potential cyber misuse or unauthorized behavior, leading to it inadvertently being slowed, paused, or stopped.” OpenAI says the guardrail can be triggered in some cases even when a user is engaging in activities that don’t appear related to cybersecurity. When this happens, ChatGPT and Codex users may be asked to review the model’s action before proceeding, OpenAI said.

Partners in OpenAI’s Daybreak program—which includes digital infrastructure providers like Cisco, Cloudflare, and Palo Alto Networks—will get early access to a less restricted version of Astra with more robust cyber capabilities. The goal of the program is to ensure these companies can use advanced AI models like Astra to harden their defenses before similarly capable models are made broadly available. OpenAI leaders also said the company has been working closely with government partners to ensure they’re aware of Astra’s cyber skills and can get access to them.

Astra is not only capable of finding novel software vulnerabilities and developing ways to exploit them for hacking, but is also able to “chain” multiple exploits together, a technique used to bore deeper and deeper into a target system and gain access that wouldn’t be attainable using just one vulnerability.

According to figures from OpenAI, Astra outperforms industry leading AI models such as GPT-5.6 Sol and Anthropic’s Mythos on cybersecurity benchmarks such as ExploitBench, which Astra scored 100 percent on. However, these capabilities are broadly in line with the rising hacking abilities of AI models that OpenAI and Anthropic have been forecasting for months. In April, for example, Anthropic emphasized that Mythos Preview was able to autonomously develop exploit chains.

As the AI and cybersecurity industries have scrambled to adapt, though, many cybersecurity experts have emphasized that key digital security defenses and longstanding best practices are still durable. However, AI puts organizations and systems that haven’t fully implemented these protections at even more urgent risk.

The Diamond Moon and Other Astronomical Events to See in September 2026

Wired September 01, 2026

August set the bar high for stargazers, with two eclipses and the peak of the Perseids meteor shower. But it’s not time to put away your telescopes, with some lesser-known astronomical events set to arrive across the sky this month.

The Pleiades will appear next to the moon, Venus will reach its brightest point of the year, Neptune will be in its best position for spotting with a telescope, and as an encore to the Perseids, there will also be a smaller meteor shower.

Here are some dates worth marking on your calendar for the month to come.

September begins with an easy opportunity to spot two of the brightest objects in the night sky. Venus will appear near Spica, the most intense star in the constellation Virgo. Both objects will be visible to the naked eye.

The exact timing of Venus’ appearance is September 2 at 00:17 UTC. This means that, depending on the your location, the conjunction could occur in the afternoon or evening of September 1.

Milky way stars photographed with a wide-angle lens.

It should be easy to tell the two celestial objects apart. Venus will shine much more brightly, looking like a white dot that doesn’t twinkle as much as the stars. Spica will appear nearby as a considerably fainter bluish dot. The two will be approximately 1.5 degrees apart.

A handy trick is that 0.5 degrees in the sky is roughly the average diameter of a full moon. Therefore, once you find the brightest point in the sky—which will be Venus—you can find Spica about three moons away.

The moon will be accompanied by one of the most famous star clusters in the sky. On the night of September 3, it will appear approximately 1.1 degrees from the Pleiades—close enough to observe both objects in the same region. The moon will be about 59 percent illuminated, according to Star Walk’s calculations.

The Pleiades, also known as “the Seven Sisters” or M45, is a star cluster located in the constellation Taurus. Six or seven of its members are usually visible to the naked eye under good conditions, although the cluster contains hundreds of young stars. These stars were born at approximately the same time and remain gravitationally bound together.

Astronomical photograph of the Pleiades. From Earth, six or seven stars can usually be seen, but they form a gigantic cluster. The moon will appear next to them on September 3.

The proximity to the waning moon offers a good opportunity for spotting them. To the naked eye, they will appear as a small group of bright points next to the moon, as if they were diamonds. Binoculars will allow you to make out many more. The encounter will happen again on September 30, when the two objects will once more be separated by just one degree.

September also has its own meteor shower. The Epsilon Perseids will peak September 9 and 10, producing up to eight meteors per hour.

A meteor shower, captured in Spain.

The number of meteors is lower than that of the famous Perseids in August. However, this shower has one advantage: Its peak will occur just two days before the new moon, making the sky ideally dark for viewing.

Conditions will be especially favorable from the northern hemisphere, and, as with any meteor shower, it is recommended to find a dark location away from light pollution.

Venus is usually one of the easiest objects to spot in the night sky, but toward the end of September it will shine even brighter. The planet will reach an apparent magnitude of approximately -4.8. By comparison, the full moon has a magnitude of -12.7, and Sirius—considered the brightest star in the sky—barely reaches -1.46.

Look for the planet after sunset, near the western horizon. Viewing conditions will be best from the southern hemisphere.

Unlike the other events on this list, the equinox isn’t something we can go out and observe directly. Instead, it’s an astronomical moment that marks a specific point in Earth’s orbit and, with it, the change of season.

The September equinox will occur on September 23 when the Sun crosses the equator as it moves southward. The event marks the astronomical beginning of fall in the northern hemisphere and spring in the southern hemisphere.

Spotting Neptune is considerably more challenging than spotting other planets. The most distant planet in the solar system (sorry Pluto) is forecasted to reach opposition on September 26. This means that Earth will be approximately between Neptune and the Sun.

This positioning means Neptune will remain visible for much of the night and will be at one of its closest distances to our planet for the year. Therefore, September offers one of the best opportunities in 2026 to try to spot it.

One of the few great photos we have of Neptune.

It’s too faint to be seen with the naked eye. You’ll need a telescope and to know its position among the stars of Pisces. Even then, it will appear as a tiny bluish disk.

September will end with a particularly famous full moon. The full moon closest to the September equinox is traditionally called the Harvest Moon. The term does not describe a distinct physical phenomenon, nor does it mean that the moon will change color, size, or brightness. It’s a traditional name related to the harvests of the northern hemisphere.

Sonos Has New Devices, a New OS, and Yes, a New App

Wired September 01, 2026

Sonos has a new app. Stop me if you’ve heard this one before.

The smart speaker company, long a darling of the audio industry, undid much of the goodwill it earned with its multiroom speakers through a bevy of software updates that broke its app in 2024. Almost all app users hated it, citing the loss of features like volume control and accessibility tools meant to help blind people use the wireless speaker system. Sonos eventually owned up to the mistake, considered bringing back the old app again, then booted its CEO and marched its new leaders out to apologize profusely to win back the company’s furious customers.

Now, Sonos says it has a brand-new app update, infused with lots of generative AI features. The company also announced a new soundbar and its second pair of over-the-ear headphones. Sonos representatives say it doesn’t want to be seen as a speaker company anymore, but as something bigger and more holistic.

“For years people have been seeing us as a speaker company,” says Brandon Holley, the interim hardware lead at Sonos. “What we actually are is an audio operating system.”

The company is calling that operating system Sonos 27, and it manifests in a few ways. First and foremost: updates to the Sonos app.

Sonos knows that the words “new Sonos app” might strike fear in the hearts of its users.

“When I say that out loud, I know exactly what comes to mind,” Sid Patel, vice president of software at Sonos, tells WIRED. Patel says the app was developed with a “customer-centric feedback listening approach” that involves reaching out to the community and being active in forums like Reddit. New features to make the app easier to use will include improved tab navigation, better room sorting, and changes to volume knobs on the app itself. In the fall, Sonos will release system health views that let you diagnose connection issues for each product.

The big feature is Sonos 27voice, the company’s generative AI integration, which is being released in early access. It lets you talk to the speakers like you would Amazon’s Alexa or a Google Home speaker, allowing you to request music based on your mood. It also has a Model Context Protocol, which can connect to your AI service of choice if you want to ask ChatGPT to play music on your speakers.

The company is highlighting its Sonos Custom Agents, which let users customize their agents to do various tasks throughout the system, like triggering speakers in a certain room at a certain time. You can also change the voices used if maybe you’d like the AI in your kitchen to sound like a fancy French chef, or have your bathroom speaker talk to you like a pirate.

“Obviously AI is something that's very hot these days, clearly,” Patel says. “So we have integrated various pieces of AI into our system.”

When asked what products Sonos 27 and its AI features would work with, a Sonos representative wrote via email that Sonos 27 will work in Sonos’ S2 app, but not the S1 app—the version that controls some older Sonos equipment. So owners of older Sonos hardware won't be able to access these new AI features.

“Sonos 27 is designed to take advantage of newer hardware capabilities, so not every product will support every new feature,” the representative wrote. “We want to be transparent about those limitations while continuing to support products with security and ongoing updates for as long as the hardware allows.”

Despite the stated effort to be transparent, Sonos says it won’t release details about compatibility or upgrade paths for each product until “a later date.”

Sonos Fabric

Sonos has an official name for the network its products use to sync across rooms: Sonos Fabric.

“Sonos Fabric is the name of the magic that has existed for what Sonos was built on,” Patel says. “The idea of, you have one speaker, two speakers, three speakers, and how they magically work together in a home theater setup or a bonded setup or group.”

Two new features are coming to that newly christened technology. One is what Sonos calls portable surround, which enables users to take devices from one room to another and have them sync there. So if you have a main soundbar by your TV but want to bring in another couple of speakers from other rooms to act as surround sound speakers for movie night, the Sonos products can detect their location and moderate which audio to play where.

Second is the ability to switch audio between the speakers and headphones, which Sonos calls Headphone Linking.

Sonos Ace Ultra

Sonos’ first pair of over-ear headphones arrived in 2024, right during the height of the Sonos app woes. The Sonos Ace were very good, except the headphones didn’t work within Sonos’ speaker ecosystem. Sonos wants to fix that problem with its follow-up headset, the Sonos Ace Ultra.

It has 35 hours of battery life and can connect to devices via USB-C and 3.5 mm. More importantly, it can connect to other Sonos speakers via Wi-Fi. The Ace Ultra runs on Sonos Fabric, which means it can connect to your wider Sonos system and let you switch playback between speakers and the headphones

“With a single push of a button, you'll be able to suck music into your headphones,” Patel says.

Sonos Beam Ultra

Sonos introduced a new soundbar, called the Beam Ultra. It’s an upgrade of the company’s existing Sonos Beam with nine drivers, four more than the past Beams. They’re also upward-firing drivers that bounce the sound off your ceiling for better acoustics. The Beam Ultra has AI-enabled features, like AI speech enhancement that aims to make dialog more discernible in loud scenes. The Beam Ultra can connect via Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and wired HDMI eARC.

This is a lot of change for Sonos, something the company hasn’t always handled gracefully. Sonos’ home systems already aren’t the easiest to set up, sometimes requiring separate apps for older products. The company may be rejiggering itself as an “audio operating system,” but its software has long been the source of its troubles with getting its products to work right. Will AI smarts fix that? Maybe for its newer devices. But anyone with an existing system may still struggle.

The AI features on products and in the Sonos 27 app will be opt-in, meaning you can avoid them entirely. “That really is our new approach to our app release,” Patel says. “We're going to bring our customers along. We're going to listen more.”

That would be a good plan. Sounds like Sonos’ speakers will be listening more, too.

Using High-Energy Laser, US Shoots Down Drones Near Mexico Border

Wired September 01, 2026

This week, the US Army used a high-energy multipurpose laser to shoot down three drones near the US-Mexico border, which official reports claimed were “posing a physical threat to US military personnel and CBP partners,” referring to Customs and Border Patrol.

The operation took place between the night of August 25 and the early morning of August 26 in the vicinity of the Rio Grande Valley in Texas and was led by the Joint Task Force Southern Border (JTF-SB), which operates under US Northern Command. Authorities confirmed that, during the operation, agents used technology derived from the Army’s High-Energy Multipurpose Laser (AMP-HEL) system, a military program focused on implementing high-energy lasers for new defense capabilities.

Available information suggests that this initiative began in September 2025, when AeroVironment, a company specializing in defense technology, delivered the first two functional prototypes of these laser-based weapons to the US Armed Forces. Two new, improved systems were delivered as the program was expanded in December of the same year. According to the manufacturer, this particular platform, called the Locust Laser Weapon System, is designed to be mounted on military vehicles, as the Army has done with the versions its received.

Operating at 20 kilowatts, the Locust system relies on an extremely concentrated beam of light that, in various phases, allows for the detection, tracking, illumination, damaging, or destruction of targets at a distance. Locust and other high-energy laser (HEL) systems typically use sensors, cameras, radars, or other means to locate an object. Once identified, the system focuses the light beam on the target with great precision, even when it is moving. It then uses an additional electrical energy charge to increase the beam’s power and convert it into heat. This ultimately damages or disables the drone, the exact outcomes depending on factors such as distance, exposure time, and the target’s characteristics.

In addition, Locust’s most recent versions—such as the one delivered to the military last December—include radar and command-and-control systems. These make it easier to integrate the weapon into a more complex mobile defense platform, rather than using it as a stand-alone device.

The exact location of the operation remains unknown. Nor is there any concrete information regarding the origin of the neutralized drones or the entities responsible for their operation. However, Curtis Taylor, commander of JTF-SB, suggested that the aircraft could be linked to criminal cells involved in drug trafficking and operations in Mexican territory.

“Cartel networks are increasingly employing unmanned aircraft systems to facilitate illicit human smuggling and actively spy on our personnel and law enforcement partners. By integrating layered countermeasures alongside advanced directed-energy capabilities like this laser system, we have made it clear that we will not tolerate hostile surveillance. We also greatly appreciate the support of our Mexican Army partners as we work together to combat this threat to the border region,” the major general stated in a press release.

The official statement also does not specify the exact models from the AMP-HEL program that were used in the operation. However, the international press has linked the action to the campaign against illegal immigration and drug cartels that President Donald Trump has been waging since he began his second term.

During his election campaign, Trump promised to combat both issues by implementing drastic measures, especially along the US-Mexico border. To that end, his administration has deployed a wide variety of technologies, HEL systems being just part of the growing toolkit.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

You may be scoffing as you read this. The best folding phones? Really? Aren’t those just gimmicks? I'm here to tell you they're pretty darn useful. And yes, there are quite a few now, so you have options. Folding phones are an evolution of the traditional single-screen slab of glass we've all been using for nearly two decades—and we might even see a folding iPhone in 2026.

They largely come in two forms: a folding flip phone or a folding book-like phone, enabling you to either relive the glory days of small phones or expand your multitasking options while on the go. A folding phone is a personal decision—arguably even more than a traditional smartphone, since it hinges (heh) on what style you prefer. We have tested almost all of them, and these are our favorites.

Samsung

The Galaxy Z Fold8 features fresh proportions for a form factor that feels just right and purpose-built. It is shorter and wider than the Galaxy Z Folds you might be used to, yet when you open it up, it feels even more tablet-like than ever. The crease is significantly less obvious than previous models, and the Fold8 is lighter and easier to handle than the larger Fold8 Ultra. You lose a little bit of screen real estate, but it's marginal.

The front 5.5-inch screen has a nice 10:16 aspect ratio that doesn't cause ridiculous letterboxing. I also found I opened the inner 7.6-inch screen far more often than with the Ultra, and you can comfortably have three apps side by side in split-screen mode. The Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset ensures the smoothest of rides with apps and games. The Fold8's 4,800-mAh battery (Samsung's first with silicon-carbon battery technology) lasts about five to six hours of screen-on time.

Where the Fold8 loses ground compared to the more expensive Ultra is the camera. The Fold8 has a 50-megapixel main sensor and a 50-megapixel ultrawide, with two 10-megapixel selfie cameras on the outer and inner screens. The Ultra adds a more powerful 200-megapixel main camera and a 10-megapixel telephoto offering 3X optical zoom, making it the better choice for photographers. That said, the Fold8 still takes great photos and will serve just fine for most folks.

If you've been on the fence about foldables, the Fold8 could be the tablet-phone combo to tempt you down. It's pricey at $1,900 (the Ultra is $200 more), but there are already offers popping up, and we'll see more as we head into the holiday season.

Motorola

Amazon

Motorola

Flip phones are perfect if you want something that comfortably fits in your pocket or a small clutch. Motorola's Razr Ultra isn't just compact, but it's also the most fashionable smartphone today. You can buy it with suede-like Alcantara or a sustainably sourced wood on the back—both look and feel fantastic. It's also reasonably durable, with an IP48 rating for some dust protection, a titanium-reinforced hinge, and Gorilla Glass Ceramic for more durable displays.

Not much has changed over last year’s Razr Ultra 2025. You get the same Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite chipset, 512 GB of storage, and 16 GB of RAM. The 4-inch OLED screen on the front lets you add multiple widget panels, so you don't need to open the phone as frequently. Once you do, though, you'll enjoy a super-bright, colorful 7-inch AMOLED screen. The big upgrade is the 5,000-mAh silicon-carbon battery, which can easily last two days between charges and is impressively huge for a phone this small.

The 50-megapixel main camera delivers great photos, and there's a reliable 50-megapixel ultrawide and a 50-megapixel selfie camera. While it's a good camera, it still doesn't quite match candybar phones from the likes of Google and Apple. Still, I love being able to take a selfie with the phone closed and see a preview with the front screen, and my wife loves it when I take a picture of her because she can see a preview of herself on the other side of the phone and can correct my poor angle. Video capture is also good, with Dolby Vision support that makes clips look sharp, colorful, and not too grainy in low light.

You'll hear a lot about Motorola's AI features on this phone—there's even a dedicated “AI” button—but the long and short of it is that most of these features aren't very helpful. Pay Attention is the only one I've found myself using due to the nature of my job; it starts a recording with real-time transcription and an AI summary at the end, but most flagship phones can do that these days. Don't buy it for Moto AI, buy it because it's a flipping-cool Razr.

You can get a cheaper folding phone if you're willing to make a few sacrifices. The regular Razr flip phone has a similar design to the Ultra, but with slightly smaller screens. It also makes do with a slightly souped-up MediaTek chipset and less RAM, which means slower performance, but nothing too frustrating. It has the same titanium-reinforced hinge as the Ultra and an IP48 dust- and water-resistance rating.

The camera is still solid, offering pleasing shots in good conditions, but it struggles a little with low light and high-contrast scenes. The outer display is smaller, but still customizable. Battery life is good and should last a couple of days when you need it to.

The fact that you only get three Android upgrades is disappointing, and the Razr has the same unimpressive Motorola AI features as the Ultra. But weighing up the package at this price, the Razr is the most affordable, but still worthwhile, way to try a folding phone.

A polished update to Google’s Pixel line, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold brings several minor improvements. One of the few folding devices with a proper IP68 dust- and water-resistance rating plus the ability to withstand 10 years of folding, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold may be your most durable option. It's also the only folding phone with Qi2 25W wireless charging support, meaning you can magnetically stick it to MagSafe or Qi2 wireless chargers.

Even with a slimmed-down body, it's noticeably thicker and heavier than Samsung’s folding options, which makes it more cumbersome to use. Despite a smaller battery than last year's model, it has enough stamina to get through most days, and that's mostly because the new Tensor G6 chipset is more efficient. Google added floating Bubbles for better multitasking, so you can have an expandable chat floating over two other apps in split-screen mode. There are also enhancements for Gemini, including some useful contextual pop-ups in chats to add links to your calendar for events or open destinations in Maps.

Despite the “Pro” in the name, the Fold lacks most of the Pro features available in the cheaper Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL. You do get the new HiLight feature, a group of color LEDs in the camera module’s flash that light up different colors based on who is calling or while you chat to Gemini. But you miss out on a much more powerful camera system and features like instant Night Sight, 120X digital zoom, and better video capture. You can still capture excellent photos on the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, but they're not the best that Google offers. That's a bitter pill when you're coughing up $1,900.

Honor

Amazon

Despite the sizable camera bump, the otherwise super-svelte Honor Magic V6 (4.1 mm open, 8.8 mm closed) is a lovely foldable that's easy to handle and feels close to a regular phone when closed. It brings better battery life, faster charging, and greater durability over last year's Magic V5, and also has a versatile camera and a responsive fingerprint sensor in the power button. Honor’s MagicOS is packed with potentially useful foldable and AI features, but also some bloatware.

The biggest enhancement this year is the long-lasting 6,660-mAh silicon-carbon battery, and Honor is promising better durability than before, with an IP68/69 rating for water resistance. There’s also a snazzy new red finish. The Honor Magic V6 is the best book-like foldable for folks in the UK, Europe, or other markets where the phone is sold, though you can always import it into the US. Read more in our Best Phones You Can't Buy in the US guide.

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra for $2,100: The Z Fold8 Ultra is a refined release with a 6.5-inch cover display that opens to an expansive 8-inch screen that feels like two 6.5-inch displays side by side. It's fast and smooth, with a 5,000-mAh battery, but it's the camera that earns it the “Ultra” title. It's an impressive combo, including a 200-megapixel main shooter, 50-megapixel ultrawide, and a 10-megapixel telephoto lens that supports 3X optical zoom. Sadly, it lacks Qi2 support for magnetic wireless charging, and the camera module makes it rock when lying flat on a surface. But the main reason it misses out on a place above is that the smaller Fold8 is so much easier to handle.

Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 for $1,200: We haven't had a chance to spend much time with the Flip8 yet, but based on what we have seen, it's a close second to Motorola's Razr Ultra. It is the lightest and thinnest flip phone in the world with a redesigned chassis. It has a 4.1-inch cover screen, and it flips open to become a 6.9-inch candy bar. It's also more durable than ever and boasts the same excellent chipset and performance as Samsung's larger Fold models. The 4,300-mAh battery is solid, but the camera system is relatively basic, comprising a 50-megapixel main shooter backed by a 12-megapixel ultrawide.

Motorola Razr Fold

Motorola Razr Fold for $1,900: The first book-style foldable from Motorola is good, but not great. The front screen feels very much like a normal phone, and you can open it to enjoy the vast 8.1-inch display inside. Sadly, the Razr Fold lacks the top-end processor of the year, which is disappointing at this price. The highlight is the massive 6,000-mAh battery, which can stretch to nearly three days of use. Thankfully, it does come with seven years of software updates (unlike Motorola's Flip family). Motorola has also added a telephoto lens to the capable camera, though it can't compete with Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

Motorola Razr+ 2026 for $1,100: The awkward middle child in the Razr lineup lacks the bells and whistles or top-notch specs of the Ultra, but still costs more than $1,000. You can get very close to the same experience from the cheaper Razr and save hundreds. Even battery life is unimpressive, because it has the smallest capacity of the Razr family. The cover glass isn’t the ceramic glass mixture as on the Razr Ultra. I found out the hard way after dropping the phone once, roughly a 4-foot drop onto asphalt, and the front screen shattered. Get a screen protector!

Oppo Find N6

Oppo Find N6 for $1,929: With an 8.12-inch internal display, the Find N6 is a beautifully engineered folding phone that’s impossibly slim and light. Despite its promise of being creaseless, the fold is still discernible. You’ll hardly notice it when the screen is on, though you’ll feel it if you use the optional stylus. Performance is impressively slick, with enough stamina to see you through a busy day, and the camera system is excellent. It’s a big step up from last year’s N5, with a 200-MP main shooter, 50-MP telephoto, and 50-MP ultrawide. The global model can use familiar Google apps, but you’ll have to import it, as this phone won’t officially be released in the West.

Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold for $1,799: The only reason to consider the Pixel 10 Pro Fold right now is if you see it on sale. Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold is superior, but the 10 Pro Fold isn't far behind this year's release. It's still a reasonably slim device with a large front screen that feels like a normal phone, an excellent 8-inch inner screen, and a triple-camera system that delivers great results, though not as great as the Pixel 10 Pro series. Read our Best Pixel Phones guide for more.

Xiaomi Mix Flip for $899: Xiaomi’s first flip phone has a lovely design with excellent displays inside and out, long battery life with fast charging, and flagship-level performance, which makes a nice change, as flip phones often have middling specs. It also boasts a solid dual-lens camera, opting for telephoto instead of ultrawide alongside the capable main shooter, which is more useful for most folks. The software lets the party down a little; there’s no IP rating, and it is pricey, but I had fun with this flip phone.

Things to Know Before Buying

Folding phones are more fragile than normal phones. Folding phones have more parts than a traditional smartphone, not to mention a hinge. Companies advertise how many folds these devices have been tested for—usually around 200,000 or 500,000 folds—but a single drop can be incredibly damaging. They are not as dust-resistant, and some aren't as water-resistant (only the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is IP68-rated in the US), so you'll want to be especially careful. Use a case, and it may be worth investing in the manufacturer's device care policy.

Don't remove the built-in screen protector. Most of these folding phones have a film over the inner screen. You might be tempted to remove it, but don't—it can damage the display. The packaging usually includes instructions not to remove it and how to care for your device.

There's a small learning curve to the software. Flip-style folding phones are fairly straightforward, but book-like folding phones that double as tablets have new multitasking tricks that will take some getting used to if you want to make the most of them. I recommend taking some time to run through these features so you understand how they work.

They're expensive. Do you need one? Nobody needs a folding phone. If you think you'll benefit from one, know they're frequently discounted during big sale events like Black Friday, and you can also knock a few hundred dollars off if you trade in an eligible device.

Which Type of Folding Phone Is for You?

Folding flip phones are for people who want a compact device. Think of a normal phone you can fold in half. That's pretty much what you get, plus a screen on the front to monitor widgets and texts. This does mean you can flip the phone to answer a call and flip it shut to end one—super cool. You can put the phone at a 90-degree angle, and some apps will adapt to show controls on the bottom and important details at the top, like in video calling apps or when watching videos on YouTube, though this depends on the phone. Folding flip phones typically have mediocre battery life, and their cameras aren't as good as their non-folding counterparts.

Folding book-like phones are for people who want the big-screen experience. Are you constantly watching full-length movies on your phone? Or do you always find yourself jumping back and forth between two apps? Then these are for you. They have good battery life and better cameras (though not as good as non-folding phones), but they're far more expensive. These include the short-lived triple-screen folding devices like Samsung's Galaxy Z TriFold. They're thick and heavy, though we're seeing newer models that are surprisingly thin. Still, you may have a hard time fitting them in your pockets.

Is Now a Good Time to Buy?

If you're team Android, this is a good time to buy. Samsung and Google just updated their foldables, and Motorola released its first big foldable in the summer and won't announce the Razr 2027 lineup until the spring. For folks outside the US, we probably won't see new foldables from Honor or Oppo until the spring, too.

If you're considering an iPhone, Apple is likely to unveil a new folding phone soon, so you might want to wait and see what it looks like.

My Favorite Folding Features

Whichever style you go for, my favorite feature of folding phones is the ability to see the viewfinder on the external screen and snap a selfie with the high-quality rear cameras—just set the phone down slightly folded so it stays upright, and there's usually a button you can click in the camera app to send the preview to the external screen. You can usually trigger the shutter hands-free with a palm gesture. (Motorola's Razr Ultra lets you start and stop video recordings with hand gestures, too!) It's excellent when traveling if you want to take a photo of yourself next to a point of interest.

Many of these phones offer similar functionality with translation—Samsung and Google, for example, let you show your words translated on the external screen so the person you are speaking to can see it, and then they can tap a button on the screen to have the phone start translating their words, which you'll see on the internal screen. It's a much nicer system than using Google Translate on a candy bar phone.
